text_cree: kayâs ayîsiyiniwak mistahi kî-kitimâkisiwak, oskac ôtê ê-ayâcik, nama kêkway ohci kî-pakitinikôwisiwak.
text_en: The people of old were in a piteous state, when first they lived here on earth. The Higher Powers had put them down here with nothing at all.
label: literal
rationale: No figurative language detected; the description of the people's state and divine placement is literal.
footnote_en:
[1] LB: Unfortunately I did not record the gesture.
[2] LB: Probably kîh-ohtinamwak .

text_cree: nama kêkway ayiwinisa ohci ayâwak; nama kêkway môhkomân.
text_en: They had no clothes, no knives.
label: literal
rationale: Plain statement of lacking possessions; no non-literal expression.
footnote_en:
[1] LB: Unfortunately I did not record the gesture.
[2] LB: Probably kîh-ohtinamwak .

text_cree: nayêstaw oskan kî-omôhkomâniwak.
text_en: All they had for a knife was a bone.
label: literal
rationale: Literal statement about using a bone as a knife.
footnote_en:
[1] LB: Unfortunately I did not record the gesture.
[2] LB: Probably kîh-ohtinamwak .

text_cree: nama kêkway ohci ayâwak iskotêw.
text_en: From the beginning they had no fire.
label: literal
rationale: Straightforward statement of having no fire from the beginning.
footnote_en:
[1] LB: Unfortunately I did not record the gesture.
[2] LB: Probably kîh-ohtinamwak .

text_cree: acosis piko kî-ohci-nipahêwak pisiskiwa, oskana ê-kikamohtâcik wîpisisiwâhk.
text_en: With merely an arrow they killed animals, fastening bones to their arrows.
label: literal
rationale: Describes hunting method literally.
footnote_en:
[1] LB: Unfortunately I did not record the gesture.
[2] LB: Probably kîh-ohtinamwak .

text_cree: nama kêkway; kî-kitimâkisiwak.
text_en: They had nothing; they were in a piteous state.
label: literal
rationale: Reiterates their lack and pitiful state in literal terms.
footnote_en:
[1] LB: Unfortunately I did not record the gesture.
[2] LB: Probably kîh-ohtinamwak .

text_cree: kîtahtawê iskotêw kî-osîhtamâsôwak, ômisi ê-tôtahkik; ê-kisitêyik, piyisk êkota kî-otinamwak iskotêw.
text_en: Presently they made fire for themselves, doing it like this; when it was hot, they got fire from it.
label: literal
rationale: The footnote about not recording the gesture does not describe figurative language; the sentence itself is a literal account of fire-making.
footnote_en:
[1] LB: Unfortunately I did not record the gesture.
[2] LB: Probably kîh-ohtinamwak .

text_cree: piyisk asiniya ê-pakamahwâcik, ê-wâsaskotêpayiyit, êkotê êkwa kî-ohtinamwak iskotêw ayîsiyiniwak.
text_en: Also they pounded a stone, and when it sent out sparks, from this, too, the people got fire.
label: literal
rationale: The footnote suggesting a verb form does not describe figurative language; the sentence literally describes obtaining fire from sparks.
footnote_en:
[1] LB: Unfortunately I did not record the gesture.
[2] LB: Probably kîh-ohtinamwak .

text_cree: êkwa asiskiy kî-otaskihkowak.
text_en: Their pots and kettles were of earth.
label: literal
rationale: Literal statement about materials of pots.
footnote_en:
[1] LB: Unfortunately I did not record the gesture.
[2] LB: Probably kîh-ohtinamwak .

text_cree: mîna kî-wâtihkêwak, pahkêkin ê-asiwatâcik, asiniya ê-kisâpiskiswâcik; êwako ohci wiyâs ê-kîsisahkik.
text_en: Also, they would dig a hole and put in a hide, and heat some stones; in this way they cooked meat.
label: literal
rationale: Literal description of cooking method.
footnote_en:
[1] LB: Unfortunately I did not record the gesture.
[2] LB: Probably kîh-ohtinamwak .

text_cree: êkwa kîtahtawê amiskwayâna kî-otayôwinisiwak.
text_en: Then in time they began to have beaver-pelts for their clothes.
label: literal
rationale: Literal statement about acquiring beaver-pelt clothing.
footnote_en:
[1] LB: Unfortunately I did not record the gesture.
[2] LB: Probably kîh-ohtinamwak .

text_cree: ôta ê-pê-takohtêyit, sakicihcênitôwak; atamiskotâtôwak.
text_en: When the others arrived there, they shook each other by the hand and greeted each other.
label: literal
rationale: No figurative language detected; literal description of greeting.
footnote_en:
[3] LB on ayîsiyiniw :  Here unmistakably “Indian”; below nêhiyaw : “Cree” (kept in translation) is probably meant in the same way.  The proper term wâpiski-wiyâs : “white-flesh, white man” alternates with môniyâw : “Canadian” (kept in translation).
[4] LB on atimwah : Properly “dogs”, but often used for misatim : “horse”; that this is here the case is shown by the next sentence.

text_cree: cikêmâ êkosi nistam kâ-isi-wâpamât ayîsiyiniw wâpiski-wiyâsa.
text_en: For, indeed, thus it was that the Indian first saw the Whiteskin.
label: literal
rationale: Literal statement; 'Whiteskin' is the conventional term, not figurative per footnote [3].
footnote_en:
[3] LB on ayîsiyiniw :  Here unmistakably “Indian”; below nêhiyaw : “Cree” (kept in translation) is probably meant in the same way.  The proper term wâpiski-wiyâs : “white-flesh, white man” alternates with môniyâw : “Canadian” (kept in translation).
[4] LB on atimwah : Properly “dogs”, but often used for misatim : “horse”; that this is here the case is shown by the next sentence.

text_cree: kahkiyaw kêkway kî-miyik kita-ôh-pimâtisit: môhkomân, pâskisikan, kita-âpacihtât kahkiyaw kêkway pâskisikêwin.
text_en: They gave him everything to live by: the knife and the gun and all kinds of ammunition for his use.
label: literal
rationale: No figurative language detected; literal listing of items given.
footnote_en:
[3] LB on ayîsiyiniw :  Here unmistakably “Indian”; below nêhiyaw : “Cree” (kept in translation) is probably meant in the same way.  The proper term wâpiski-wiyâs : “white-flesh, white man” alternates with môniyâw : “Canadian” (kept in translation).
[4] LB on atimwah : Properly “dogs”, but often used for misatim : “horse”; that this is here the case is shown by the next sentence.

text_cree: êkosi êkota ohci kiskinôhamawâw kita-isi-pamihtât pâskisikan.
text_en: So then he began to be taught how to take care of a gun.
label: literal
rationale: No figurative language detected; literal description of being taught.
footnote_en:
[3] LB on ayîsiyiniw :  Here unmistakably “Indian”; below nêhiyaw : “Cree” (kept in translation) is probably meant in the same way.  The proper term wâpiski-wiyâs : “white-flesh, white man” alternates with môniyâw : “Canadian” (kept in translation).
[4] LB on atimwah : Properly “dogs”, but often used for misatim : “horse”; that this is here the case is shown by the next sentence.

text_cree: êkota ohci êkwa ati-miyw-âyâwak ayîsiyiniwak.
text_en: From that time on the Indians were well off.
label: literal
rationale: No figurative language detected; literal statement about well-being.
footnote_en:
[3] LB on ayîsiyiniw :  Here unmistakably “Indian”; below nêhiyaw : “Cree” (kept in translation) is probably meant in the same way.  The proper term wâpiski-wiyâs : “white-flesh, white man” alternates with môniyâw : “Canadian” (kept in translation).
[4] LB on atimwah : Properly “dogs”, but often used for misatim : “horse”; that this is here the case is shown by the next sentence.

text_cree: kîtahtawê êkota ohci piyisk atimwa ayâwêwak, ê-otâpahâcik.
text_en: At a certain time after this they began to have horses to pull their loads.
label: metaphor
rationale: Footnote [4] states 'atimwa' properly means 'dogs' but is used for 'horses', a conventional metaphorical use.
footnote_en:
[3] LB on ayîsiyiniw :  Here unmistakably “Indian”; below nêhiyaw : “Cree” (kept in translation) is probably meant in the same way.  The proper term wâpiski-wiyâs : “white-flesh, white man” alternates with môniyâw : “Canadian” (kept in translation).
[4] LB on atimwah : Properly “dogs”, but often used for misatim : “horse”; that this is here the case is shown by the next sentence.

text_cree: ôtê piko nimitaw ayîsiyiniwak okî-ayâwâhtâwâw kayâhtê misatimwa; nama wîhkâc ohci ayâwêw ayîsiyiniw nâtakâm kâ-itapit.
text_en: And, strangely enough, it was only the people in the south who had horses; the Indian who dwells in the north from that time to this has never had horses.
label: literal
rationale: No figurative language detected; literal description of horse distribution.
footnote_en:
[3] LB on ayîsiyiniw :  Here unmistakably “Indian”; below nêhiyaw : “Cree” (kept in translation) is probably meant in the same way.  The proper term wâpiski-wiyâs : “white-flesh, white man” alternates with môniyâw : “Canadian” (kept in translation).
[4] LB on atimwah : Properly “dogs”, but often used for misatim : “horse”; that this is here the case is shown by the next sentence.

text_cree: êkwa tâpwê âpihtâ-kîsikâhk itohtahik mayaw ê-nipât; êkotê ê-pawâtahk, wîhtamâkôwisiw nipâkwêsimôwikamik.
text_en: Then truly he was taken to the place of the noonday sky, even as he slept; dreaming of that place, he was told by the Higher Powers of the Sun-Dance Lodge.
label: literal
rationale: Describes a vision experience literally; no figurative language.
footnote_en:
[5] KR:  Close-quote missing in book.
[6] LB on k-ôh-pikonahkik :  The actor “they” probably refers to the Thunderers.

text_cree: êwako tahtw-âskiy kita-tôtahkik ayîsiyiniwak kî-miyâwak.
text_en: The people were given the annual performance of this rite.
label: literal
rationale: Straightforward statement about receiving a rite; no figurative language.
footnote_en:
[5] KR:  Close-quote missing in book.
[6] LB on k-ôh-pikonahkik :  The actor “they” probably refers to the Thunderers.

text_cree: êkwa ispî kiskinohamawâw tânisi ta-tôtahk; okîsikôwa kî-kiskinôhamâk.
text_en: And at the same time he was taught how to perform it; by the dwellers in the sky he was taught.
label: literal
rationale: Literal description of being taught; 'dwellers in the sky' is a conventional term for spiritual beings.
footnote_en:
[5] KR:  Close-quote missing in book.
[6] LB on k-ôh-pikonahkik :  The actor “they” probably refers to the Thunderers.

text_cree: mâskôc nawac nawac ta-miywâsin kâkikê ta-pakitinamâht ayîsiyiniw; êwako nititêyihtênân.
text_en: Surely it would be well, if it were always permitted to the Indian; so we think.
label: literal
rationale: Expresses a wish/opinion literally; no figurative language.
footnote_en:
[5] KR:  Close-quote missing in book.
[6] LB on k-ôh-pikonahkik :  The actor “they” probably refers to the Thunderers.

text_cree: tahki kêkway kita-miyo-ohpikin.
text_en: Crops would always grow well.
label: literal
rationale: Literal statement about crops growing well.
footnote_en:
[5] KR:  Close-quote missing in book.
[6] LB on k-ôh-pikonahkik :  The actor “they” probably refers to the Thunderers.

text_cree: namôya maci-kêkway nipâkwêsimowikamik.
text_en: The Sun-Dance Lodge is not an evil thing.
label: literal
rationale: Literal denial of evil nature.
footnote_en:
[5] KR:  Close-quote missing in book.
[6] LB on k-ôh-pikonahkik :  The actor “they” probably refers to the Thunderers.

text_cree: wiyawâw, "kahkiyaw kêkway maci-kêkway nêhiyawak maci-manitowa atoskawêwak," itwêwak ayamihêw-iyiniwak.
text_en: To be sure, “The Cree perform all kinds of evil things for the Evil Spirit,” say the missionaries.
label: literal
rationale: Literal quotation of missionaries.
footnote_en:
[5] KR:  Close-quote missing in book.
[6] LB on k-ôh-pikonahkik :  The actor “they” probably refers to the Thunderers.

text_cree: namôya niyanân nêhiyaw ôta askihk ohci kiki-pakitinâw; maci-manitôwa mîna manitôw okosisa namôya ohci kiskêyimêw nêhiyaw; mîna maci-manitôw kâ-isiyîhkâsot namôya nêhiyaw kiskêyimêw.
text_en: On the contrary: the Cree was not put down here on earth with these things; the Cree has never known and does not know an Evil Spirit or a Son of God; and the Cree does not know him who is called the Evil One.
label: literal
rationale: Literal statements contradicting missionary claims; no figurative language.
footnote_en:
[5] KR:  Close-quote missing in book.
[6] LB on k-ôh-pikonahkik :  The actor “they” probably refers to the Thunderers.

text_cree: âta kita-kî-tâpwêhtahk nêhiyaw, nawac manitôwa ê-kitimâkêyimikot, êkâ wîhkâc yôtinwa kâ-nipahikot.
text_en: But rather, well may the Cree believe that the Spirit looks with kindlier pity on him, since he is never killed by winds.
label: literal
rationale: Argument about the Spirit's pity; 'looks with kindlier pity' is a conventional expression.
footnote_en:
[5] KR:  Close-quote missing in book.
[6] LB on k-ôh-pikonahkik :  The actor “they” probably refers to the Thunderers.

text_cree: nama wîhkâc nêhiyaw nipahik yôtin.
text_en: Never is a Cree killed by wind.
label: literal
rationale: Literal statement about wind not killing Cree.
footnote_en:
[5] KR:  Close-quote missing in book.
[6] LB on k-ôh-pikonahkik :  The actor “they” probably refers to the Thunderers.

text_cree: nama wîhkâc nipahik nêhiyaw piyêsiwa.
text_en: Never is a Cree killed by the Thunderers.
label: literal
rationale: Literal statement about Thunderers not killing Cree.
footnote_en:
[5] KR:  Close-quote missing in book.
[6] LB on k-ôh-pikonahkik :  The actor “they” probably refers to the Thunderers.

text_cree: nama wîhkâc nêhiyaw nipahik iskotêw.
text_en: Never is a Cree killed by fire.
label: literal
rationale: Literal statement about fire not killing Cree.
footnote_en:
[5] KR:  Close-quote missing in book.
[6] LB on k-ôh-pikonahkik :  The actor “they” probably refers to the Thunderers.

text_cree: êkota ohci nititêyihtênân, nawac nêhiyaw ê-kitimâkinâkôwisit.
text_en: That is why we think that the Cree is favored by the Higher Powers.
label: literal
rationale: Conclusion that Cree is favored; no figurative language.
footnote_en:
[5] KR:  Close-quote missing in book.
[6] LB on k-ôh-pikonahkik :  The actor “they” probably refers to the Thunderers.

text_cree: mâskôc ê-kisiwâhât manitôwa, nipâkwêsimowikamik ê-kipihtinahk, êwako ohci mâh-mistahi kâ-ôh-pîkonahkik môniyâw-ôtênawa, nititêyihtênân; mîna iskotêw tahto-kîsikâw kâ-ôh-pîkonahk wâskahikana; tahto-kîsikâw misiwê nikiskêyihtênân ê-saskitêki wâskahikana, mayaw ôtênâhk êtohtêyâhko.
text_en: Perhaps it is because he has angered the Spirit by putting a stop to the Sun-Dance Lodge, that in such numbers they break up the Canadian's towns; so we think; and that every day fire destroys the wooden houses; every day we learn that everywhere houses have caught fire, every time we go to town.
label: literal
rationale: Describes destruction literally; footnote [6] clarifies that 'they' (the Thunderers) break up towns, but this is a reference clarification, not figurative language.
footnote_en:
[5] KR:  Close-quote missing in book.
[6] LB on k-ôh-pikonahkik :  The actor “they” probably refers to the Thunderers.

text_cree: mîna nipêhtênân tahto-nîpin ê-pîkwâstahki piko itê ôtênawa.
text_en: And every summer we hear that in many places towns have been destroyed by windstorms.
label: literal
rationale: Literal report of windstorm destruction.
footnote_en:
[5] KR:  Close-quote missing in book.
[6] LB on k-ôh-pikonahkik :  The actor “they” probably refers to the Thunderers.

text_cree: namôya maci-kêkway kâ-kî-miyikoyâhk manitôw, mawimoscikêwina, nayêstaw kita-isi-nitotamihk miyo-kêkway.
text_en: It is not an evil thing which the Spirit has given to us, but ways of worship, only that good things may be prayed for.
label: literal
rationale: Literal statement about what the Spirit gave.
footnote_en:
[5] KR:  Close-quote missing in book.
[6] LB on k-ôh-pikonahkik :  The actor “they” probably refers to the Thunderers.

text_cree: êkosi nikî-isi-pakitinikonân manitôw ôta askîhk kâ-nêhiyâwiyâhk.
text_en: Thus did the Spirit set us down here on earth, us who are Cree.
label: literal
rationale: Literal description of being placed on earth; 'set down' is a conventional phrase.
footnote_en:
[5] KR:  Close-quote missing in book.
[6] LB on k-ôh-pikonahkik :  The actor “they” probably refers to the Thunderers.

text_cree: âtiht mâmaskâc mastaw ê-ihtakohki nîmihitôwina êkâ ê-kipihtinahk wâpiski-wiyâs, nanâtohk ê-isi-mêstinikêhk; mâka nipâkwêsimôwin nama kêkway mêstinikâniwa.
text_en: Strange, that some dances which arose much later are not stopped by the White Man, dances in which various things are used up, while the Sun-Dance involves no waste.
label: literal
rationale: Literal contrast between dances; 'strange' expresses opinion but not figuratively.
footnote_en:
[5] KR:  Close-quote missing in book.
[6] LB on k-ôh-pikonahkik :  The actor “they” probably refers to the Thunderers.

text_cree: nêhiyawak êkota tahtw-âskiy kî-miyâwak nîso-kîsikâw êkâ kita-mîcisocik, kita-nitotahkik kahkiyaw kêkway kita-miyo-ohpikiniyik, kita-nitotahkik ta-kimiwaniyik.
text_en: It was given to the Cree, every year, for two days to go without eating, and to pray that all things might grow well, and to pray for rain.
label: literal
rationale: Literal description of the Sun-Dance requirements.
footnote_en:
[5] KR:  Close-quote missing in book.
[6] LB on k-ôh-pikonahkik :  The actor “they” probably refers to the Thunderers.

text_cree: êkosi kâ-isi-pakitiniht ôta askîhk kitimâki-ayîsiyiniw.
text_en: It was thus that the poor Indian was set down here on earth.
label: literal
rationale: Literal restatement of the Indian's placement on earth.
footnote_en:
[5] KR:  Close-quote missing in book.
[6] LB on k-ôh-pikonahkik :  The actor “they” probably refers to the Thunderers.

text_cree: êkwa kotak awa oskinîkiw kâ-kiskêyihtahk ê-wî-kakwê-nipahiht, wawêyîw; asiskîwinisôw; wâpiskâyik asiskiy âpacihtâw.
text_en: Then another man, a youth, who knew that they were going to try to kill him made himself ready; he painted himself with clay; he used white clay.
label: literal
rationale: Literal description of the youth preparing himself with paint.
footnote_en: [1] LB: The words suggest flying; probably I missed a word that said this; compare the return journey, below.

text_cree: êkwa sipwêhtêw; nipîhk êsa waskic pimohtêw, mistahi ê-manitôwit.
text_en: Then he set out; he walked over the surface of the water, so great was his spirit power.
label: literal
rationale: Literal account of walking on water through spirit power, with no flying suggested.
footnote_en: [1] LB: The words suggest flying; probably I missed a word that said this; compare the return journey, below.

text_cree: êkwa ê-takohtêt êkotê ispimihk, wîkiyihk pakicîw ôhi kâ-wî-kakwê-nipahikot.
text_en: Then, when he arrived up aloft, at the others' dwelling he alighted, at the dwelling of those who were going to try to kill him.
label: literal
rationale: Literal description of arriving and alighting; the footnote notes that the words suggest flying, but this is still a literal event in the narrative.
footnote_en: [1] LB: The words suggest flying; probably I missed a word that said this; compare the return journey, below.

text_cree: wâpamêwak; "kihiw," itêyimêwak.
text_en: They saw him; they thought he was an eagle.
label: literal
rationale: Literal statement that the others mistook him for an eagle, not a figurative expression.
footnote_en: [1] LB: The words suggest flying; probably I missed a word that said this; compare the return journey, below.

text_cree: ê-tipiskâyik êkwa, ê-kîwêt, mosci-pimihâw êkwa.
text_en: When darkness came and he went home, he merely flew.
label: literal
rationale: The sentence describes an action in a narrative context; 'flew' could be metaphorical but with no clear evidence and a conservative approach, it is treated as literal.
footnote_en: [2] LB: Unless I greatly misjudge, the informant here gives a more favorable account of the Mitewin than could be got from other Sweet-Grass Cree.  He spent some years at an institution for the blind at Winnipeg, where he may have consorted with Ojibwa.

text_cree: ê-wâpahk nitomêw êsa kahkiyaw kâ-mitêwiyit ayîsiyiniwa, kita-osîhtâyit mitêwikamik.
text_en: On the next day he summoned all the people who took part in the Medicine Ceremony, to have them build a Medicine Lodge.
label: literal
rationale: The sentence describes a straightforward summoning and building activity with no figurative language.
footnote_en: [2] LB: Unless I greatly misjudge, the informant here gives a more favorable account of the Mitewin than could be got from other Sweet-Grass Cree.  He spent some years at an institution for the blind at Winnipeg, where he may have consorted with Ojibwa.

text_cree: "êkwa kiyâm pêyak ê-ayât awiyak maskihkiy, kita-itohtatâw," êkosi itêw ayîsiyiniwa; "âhkamêyimok; wîcôhkamawik;" "osâm mistahi kinipahikonawak," itwêw; "kîsihtâyêko ôma kâ-osîhtâyêk mitêwikamik, mîna kahkiyaw kîsihtâyêko, tahto ayîsiyiniwak ka-wî-itohtêcik kîsi-pîhtokêtwâwi, êkospî ka-pê-nitominâwâw," itwêw awa oskinîkiw; "êkwa pîhtokêyâni, nistikwânihk ka-pakamahonâwâw," itwêw awa oskinîkiw; "nika-pimitâcimon, pîhtokêyâni," itwêw; "êkwa mîna nîstanaw atimwak ka-mowâwâwak," itwêw; "êkwa kahkiyaw kika-nîmihitonâwâw," itwêw awa oskinîkiw; "êkwa kî-nipahiyêko, ka-pakocêninâwâw." "ohpimê kika-astânâwâw." "wêskwâhtêmihk ê-askîhtakwâk kika-anâskânâwâw." "êkwa ê-mihkwâk iskwâhtêmihk isi kika-anâskânâwâw." "tâpiskôc nipêwinis kika-isîhtânâwâw," itwêw êsa; "êkotê niyaw iskwâhtêmihk itê isi, sâkâstênohk êkotê isi nika-aspiskwêsimon." "êkwa kapê-tipisk kika-nîmihitonâwâw," itwêw êsa; "ka-mowâwâwak ôki atimwak." "êkwa nîso môhkomâna itakotêwa êtiskwêsiniyân." "kîspin kêkway mihko wâpahtamêko, êkosi nika-sâkohâwak akâmaskîhk kâ-ayâcik ayîsiyiniwak," itwêw êsa.
text_en: “And please let anyone who has any medicine bring it there,” he told the people; “Work with zeal; help me in what I am doing; too many of us are being killed,” he told them; “When you have finished the Medicine Lodge which you are building, and have completed everything, and when as many persons as mean to go there, have entered the lodge, then you are to come and call me,” said that youth; “And when I enter the lodge, you are to strike me on my head,” said the youth; “I shall be crawling along the ground, when I enter the lodge,” he said; “Also, twenty dogs you will eat,” he said; “And all of you will dance,” said the youth; “And when you have slain me, you will cut me open. Off to one side you will place it. Opposite the doorway you will lay blue mats. And red matting you will lay toward the doorway. You will make something like a small bed,” “And there my body, towards the doorway, facing the direction whence comes the light of day, I shall lie with my head on it. And all night you are to dance,” he told them; “You will eat those dogs. And two knives will hang by my head as I lie. If you see any blood, then I shall be defeating those persons who are across the sea,” he told them.
label: simile
rationale: The footnote speculates about a literal object ('entrails') and does not indicate figurative language, but the sentence itself contains the simile 'tâpiskôc nipêwinis' ('like a small bed').
footnote_en: [3] LB: Object presumably the entrails ?

text_cree: tâpwê nîmihitôwak kapê-tipisk.
text_en: Accordingly they danced all night.
label: literal
rationale: The sentence describes a literal action of dancing all night.
footnote_en: [4] Perhaps read okî-nâspitsi-nipahâhtâwâw : “they had killed him beyond the possibility of revival”.

text_cree: ê-pê-wâpaniyik, kîtahtawê kâ-wâpahtahkik mihko môhkomânihkânihk ê-pahpahkikawiyik.
text_en: As dawn approached, there at one time they saw blood dripping from the blades of the knives.
label: literal
rationale: The sentence literally describes seeing blood dripping from knives at dawn.
footnote_en: [4] Perhaps read okî-nâspitsi-nipahâhtâwâw : “they had killed him beyond the possibility of revival”.

text_cree: êkwa tâpwê cîhkêyihtamwak ê-nîmihitocik, nayêstaw atimwa ê-môwâcik.
text_en: Then truly did they put their heart into the dance, and only dogs they ate.
label: idiom
rationale: 'Put their heart into the dance' is a conventional idiom meaning dancing with great enthusiasm.
footnote_en: [4] Perhaps read okî-nâspitsi-nipahâhtâwâw : “they had killed him beyond the possibility of revival”.

text_cree: pîsim ê-pê-sâkêwêt, êkoyikohk natawâpênawâw awa oskinîkiw.
text_en: When the sun rose above the horizon, they went to view that youth.
label: literal
rationale: The sentence literally describes the sun rising and the group going to view the youth.
footnote_en: [4] Perhaps read okî-nâspitsi-nipahâhtâwâw : “they had killed him beyond the possibility of revival”.

text_cree: êkwa êkota wâpahcikâtêw ê-âpisisihk.
text_en: There it was seen by all that he returned to life.
label: literal
rationale: The sentence literally states that everyone saw the youth return to life.
footnote_en: [4] Perhaps read okî-nâspitsi-nipahâhtâwâw : “they had killed him beyond the possibility of revival”.

text_cree: kahkiyaw êsa kî-sâkôcihêw anihi nîstanaw ita ayîsiyiniwa.
text_en: He had overcome all of those twenty persons.
label: literal
rationale: The sentence literally states that he overcame the twenty persons.
footnote_en: [4] Perhaps read okî-nâspitsi-nipahâhtâwâw : “they had killed him beyond the possibility of revival”.

text_cree: kahkiyaw êsa okî-nâspici-nipâhtâwâw.
text_en: It appears that they had all gone to sleep beyond hope of revival.
label: idiom
rationale: The footnote suggests an idiomatic reading 'beyond the possibility of revival,' which is a conventional expression for permanent death.
footnote_en: [4] Perhaps read okî-nâspitsi-nipahâhtâwâw : “they had killed him beyond the possibility of revival”.

text_cree: êwako pêyak âcimôwin; êkota ohci namôya êkoyikohk miywâsin mitêwikamik.
text_en: That is one story; but since then the Medicine Lodge has not been so good a thing as all that.
label: literal
rationale: The sentence states a fact about the Medicine Lodge without non-literal comparison or fixed expression.
footnote_en: [5] CHECK pistispowihtocik

text_cree: kahkiyaw kêkway mac-âyisak ahpô ayîsiyiniwak kî-nâ-nipahitôwak, maci-maskihkiya ê-âpacihtâcik, ê-piscipôwihtocik.
text_en: All kinds of evil beings or person have killed one another, by using bad medicines to poison one another.
label: literal
rationale: The footnote refers to 'pistispowihtocik' (likely the word in this sentence) but only asks to check it, giving no figurative information; the sentence describes killing by poison literally.
footnote_en: [5] CHECK pistispowihtocik

text_cree: piko isi isi-kaskihtâwak êsi-nisiwanâcihitocik kayâs ayîsiyiniwak.
text_en: The old-time people were able to do all manner of things in the way of destroying one another.
label: literal
rationale: Describes abilities of old-time people literally, with no figurative language.
footnote_en: [5] CHECK pistispowihtocik

text_cree: êwako wiyawâw ocipwêwak nîkân kâ-kî-miyikôwisicik mitêwiwin; kêhciwâk kî-itohtêwak mitêwi-manitôwa.
text_en: It was the Ojibwa who first were given this Medicine Ceremony by the Higher Powers; they went into the actual presence of the Spirit of the Mitewin.
label: literal
rationale: Relates historical facts about the Ojibwa and the Medicine Ceremony in literal terms.
footnote_en: [5] CHECK pistispowihtocik

text_cree: êkota ohci kahkiyaw kêkway nipîhk kâ-otaskîyit, êyakonik mawimostawêwak kâ-mitêwicik; môhkiciwanipêkohk mîna kâ-otaskîyit kahkiyaw mawimostawêwak; mîna tahto kêkway kâ-sâkikihk ôta askîhk, êwakoni kî-kiskinôhamâkôwisiwak kita-isi-mawimostahkik.
text_en: Since then, those who participate in the Medicine Rite, worship all those beings that have their home in the waters; they worship also that being who has his home in springs; and they were told by the spirits to worship as many things as grow forth out of this earth.
label: literal
rationale: Lists worship practices literally; 'home' in the translation is a conventional term for dwelling, not a metaphor.
footnote_en: [5] CHECK pistispowihtocik

text_cree: anohc kêyâpic mihcêt kêkway ê-pwâtawihtâcik maskihkîwiyiniwak, kaskihtâwak nêhiyawak omaskihkîmiwâwa ohci; cikêmâ kî-miyikôwisiw nêhiyaw maskihkiy; iyikohk êspîhcâk askiy, kahkiyaw kêkway kâ-wâpahtamihk, niyîpihki kâ-ohpikihk, êspîhcâk askiy, misiwê kî-têpastâwân nêhiyaw omaskihkîm.
text_en: To this day, many things which the physicians fail of doing, the Cree can do them through their medicines; what wonder, since the Cree was given medicine by the Higher Powers? Over all the extent of the earth, everything that is seen growing forth in the summer time, as far as the earth extends, everywhere the medicine of the Cree was placed within his reach.
label: literal
rationale: The Cree original says medicine was 'placed' not 'within reach', so it is literal; the English idiom is translator's choice.
footnote_en: [5] CHECK pistispowihtocik

text_cree: misiwê itê itâpiyêko ka-wâpahtênâwâw nêhiyaw ê-kî-miyiht wîsta kita-ohci-pimâtisit.
text_en: Wherever you may look, you will see that which the Cree, for his part, was given, that he might derive from it his continuance of life.
label: literal
rationale: States that the Cree can derive sustenance from what was given, without figurative expression.
footnote_en: [5] CHECK pistispowihtocik

text_cree: mîna âpihtaw ê-mâyâtaniyik maskihkiy kî-miyâw.
text_en: Also, as half of the gift, he was given bad medicine.
label: literal
rationale: Refers to being given bad medicine as a literal fact.
footnote_en: [5] CHECK pistispowihtocik

text_cree: wiyawâw êwakoni mitêwak kâ-kî-kiskinôhamâkôwisicik; kahkiyaw kêkway kî-wîhtamâkôwisiwak kit-si-nanâtawihiwâkêcik, ahpô nipîhk kahkiyaw kêkway kâ-ohpikiniyik, kita-pâsahkik kahkiyaw kêkway maskihkiy.
text_en: Those same Medicine Dancers were the ones to whom it was taught by the Higher Powers; they were shown by the spirits every way of doctoring people, all the things, even, which grow in the water, that they might dry all kinds of medicinal herbs.
label: literal
rationale: Describes what the Medicine Dancers were taught, in plain language.
footnote_en: [5] CHECK pistispowihtocik

text_cree: ohcitaw nitâyimôtên kayâs nêhiyawak kâ-isi-pimâtisicik.
text_en: I tell this because I wish to discourse upon how the Cree lived of old.
label: literal
rationale: The footnote mentions only a typo check, not figurative language, and the sentence is a plain statement of intent.
footnote_en: [6] CHECK kanapamikowisit - either PCT or lexfile has typo

text_cree: nimiywêyihtên manitow wiya ê-itêyihtahk, awa nâpêw kâ-pê-natawêyihtahk nêhiyaw tânisi kâ-kî-isi-pimâtisit.
text_en: I am glad that the Lord had it in mind that this man should come here and desire to know how the Cree used to live.
label: literal
rationale: The footnote does not discuss this sentence; the expression 'had it in mind' is a conventional way to express divine intention but remains literal in the Cree original.

text_cree: mitoni mâka kahkiyaw miyo-kanâpanikôwisit ayîsiyiniw, êkwa kayâs nika-âyimôtên.
text_en: How well the people of old were taken care of, in everything, by the Powers, of that I shall now speak.
label: literal
rationale: The footnote likely points to a typo in 'kanapamikowisit', not to figurative language, and the sentence is a literal statement about being taken care of.
footnote_en: [6] CHECK kanapamikowisit - either PCT or lexfile has typo

text_cree: nama kêkway wiyasôwêwin ohci-ayâw nêhiyaw; kipahotôwin nama kêkway; nama kêkway maci-ihtiwin; wiyawâw piko ayîsiyiniwak omitonêyihcikaniwâw kî-âpacihtâwak.
text_en: Originally the Cree had no kind of law; there was no such thing as imprisonment; no such thing as crime; people simply used their own considerate judgment.
label: literal
rationale: The footnote does not refer to this sentence; the description of law, imprisonment, and judgment is entirely literal.
footnote_en: [6] CHECK kanapamikowisit - either PCT or lexfile has typo

text_cree: ayisk nêhiyaw nama kêkway ohci mâyi-tôtam; namôya ohci mâyi-tôtawêw nêhiyaw kisê-manitôwa.
text_en: For the Cree did not, by his original nature, do wrong; it is not in the nature of the Cree to do wrong to God.
label: literal
rationale: The footnote does not apply; the assertion about the Cree nature and wrongdoing is a literal moral claim.
footnote_en: [6] CHECK kanapamikowisit - either PCT or lexfile has typo

text_cree: êkwa nêhiyaw tipiyaw wiya manitôwa kî-kakêskimik; êwako ohci yôspisiwin kâ-ôh-ayât nêhiyaw.
text_en: The Cree was instructed by God himself in person; that is why the Cree has gentleness.
label: literal
rationale: The footnote does not describe figurative language; 'God himself in person' is an emphatic but literal statement.
footnote_en: [6] CHECK kanapamikowisit - either PCT or lexfile has typo

text_cree: ayisk kisêwâtisiw, manitôw kâ-kî-pê-kakêskimât ayîsiyiniwa.
text_en: For he has kindness of heart, since God came and instructed the people.
label: literal
rationale: The footnote is not about this sentence; 'kindness of heart' is a common compound that does not rise to a metaphor or idiom in this context.

text_cree: êkwa mîna piko iskwêwa kî-nâ-naskwêwasimik; êkosi kî-wiyasôwâtêw.
text_en: At that time only the woman made rejoinders to Him; therefore He pronounced the law for her.
label: literal
rationale: The footnote is a linguistic gloss on a verb form and does not indicate any figurative language; the sentence describes actions plainly.
footnote_en: [7] LB: For kîh-nâ-naskwêwasimik .

text_cree: pêyak, nipâkwêsimôwin.
text_en: One is the Sun-Dance.
label: literal
rationale: The sentence is a plain statement identifying one practice as the Sun-Dance; the footnote does not indicate any figurative meaning.
footnote_en: [1] LB: The insistence upon prompt return to work and upon absence of black magic (“it is never in anger”) are, of course, pleas for the dances, some of which have been forbidden by the government. The informant spoke much more freely when notes were not being taken;  when dictating he broke off at frequent intervals with, “That is all.” Then, when reminded of some feature he had left out, he would go on for a while.  This accounts for the form of our text.

text_cree: ê-nitotamâht manitôw, kahkiyaw ayîsiyiniw kita-ohpikit ôta askîhk.
text_en: The Sun-Dance consists of this, that God is entreated that every human being may grow up and thrive here on this earth.
label: literal
rationale: This sentence literally describes the purpose of the Sun-Dance; the footnote commentary does not suggest non-literal language.

text_cree: êwako nipâkwêsimôwin, nîso-kîsikâw piko aniki kâ-nîmihitocik nipiy êkâ ê-minihkwêcik, êkwa mîciwin êkâ ê-mîcicik nîso-kîsikâw.
text_en: The Sun-Dance consists of this, that for two days and no longer the dancers drink no water and for two days eat no food.
label: literal
rationale: The sentence states the rules of the Sun-Dance without any figurative language; no footnote indication otherwise.
footnote_en: [1] LB: The insistence upon prompt return to work and upon absence of black magic (“it is never in anger”) are, of course, pleas for the dances, some of which have been forbidden by the government. text_cree: mayaw kâ-pôyohk, sêmâk kahkiyaw kîwâniwiw, ê-nitawi-atoskêhk.
text_en: As soon as it is over, at once all go home and return to work.
label: literal
rationale: The sentence describes the participants' prompt return to work, which is a literal description; the footnote mentions it as a plea but does not treat the language as figurative.

This accounts for the form of our text.

text_cree: namôya wîhkâc ê-kisiwâsihk, êwako mîkiwâhp kâ-âpacihtâcik nêhiyawak.
text_en: It is never in anger that the Cree use this lodge.
label: idiom
rationale: Per the footnote, “it is never in anger” is a plea meaning absence of black magic, a conventional non-literal expression (idiom) rather than a literal statement about anger.

This accounts for the form of our text.

text_cree: awa kâ-wî-nipâkwêsimôwinihkêt, "kitâpahta ôma!" "kitâpam awa, nôhtâ kisê-manitôw, kitawâsimis ê-wî-kanawêyihtamawak kita-pîhtwât!" "miy sôhkisiwin awa kitawâsimis kâ-kanawêyihtamawak cistêmâwa." "kanâci, êkâ kêkway ta-sêkihikocik ayîsiyiniwak." "ita mânokêyâni, kitawâsimisak kâ-wî-mânokawakik, kita-kitâpahtahkik wîkiwâw ta-okimâwihk êkâ awiyak kita-âhkosit;" "kahkiyaw kiyâm kita-miywêyihtamwak ôki kitawâsimisak, tahto kê-pê-nitawâpahkêcik ôma pîsim piyêsiw wîki kâ-wî-osîhtâyân, ohtin mîna." "êyakonik kita-kisêwâtisiwak koyahâkanak, kâ-sôhkahk kipimâcihiwêwin, êwako kita-miyihcik kahkiyaw ayîsiyiniwak." "ôma nîpawiyâni nama kêkway kita-sêkihikwak." "wâh-pimohtêci kitawâsimis, pêyâhtik kita-pimohtêw awa piyêsiw, nipiy kita-sâpopatât ohci ôma askiy, êkâ ta-pîkopayik." "kisêwâtotawin; kitimâkihtawin!" "êkosi ê-itwêyân anohc, kahkiyaw ta-miywamahcihohk."
text_en: He who is about to give the Sun-Dance, “Look upon this thing! Look upon this tobacco, God, my Father, which I shall keep for Thy child to smoke. Give power to Thy child for whom I keep the tobacco. Moderate him, so that mortal men be not frightened by aught. There where I set up the lodge which I am about to erect for Thy children to look upon, let no one be ill; let all Thy children rejoice in it, as many as shall come to look upon this lodge of Sun and Thunderbird which I shall build, and of the Wind. May these Thy appointed creatures be propitious, so that Thy firm gift of life may be given to all men. When here I stand let them not by aught be frightened. When Thy child is about to walk abroad, let this Thunderbird go gently, drenching this earth with rain, that it may not break apart. Be kind to me; hear me with pity! Thus do I now speak, that all may live in health.”
label: literal
rationale: Bloomfield's footnote comments on a recording error in 'taw-okimâwahk', not on figurative language; the passage is a direct prayer with no non-literal expressions.
footnote_en: [2] LB on taw-okimâwahk : Doubtless error of record.

text_cree: kîspin piyêsiw ê-miyât êwako mîkiwâhp, kâ-mânokêt ayîsiyiniw, mistahi âpacihiwêw.
text_en: If the Thunderbird gives a man this lodge, and he has set it up, he does much good to people.
label: literal
rationale: The sentence is a straightforward conditional statement about a person receiving a lodge from Thunderbird and doing good; the footnote does not mention any figurative language here.
footnote_en: [3] LB: Informant had explained that not anyone, but only he who had been so commanded in a vision by a Thunderer, could give a Sun-Dance.

text_cree: kahkiyaw awiya âpacihêw, êkâ ta-nôhtêyâpâkwêyit, ta-miyoskâkoyit nipiy.
text_en: He does good to each and every one, that they need not thirst and that water may benefit them.
label: literal
rationale: The sentence describes the beneficial effects on people in plain terms; no figurative language is indicated in the footnote.
footnote_en: [3] LB: Informant had explained that not anyone, but only he who had been so commanded in a vision by a Thunderer, could give a Sun-Dance.

text_cree: êwako ohci ayîsiyiniwak, pêyak kâ-nipâkwêsimôwinihkêt.
text_en: This is why; for the sake of mankind is why one gives a Sundance.
label: literal
rationale: The footnote clarifies the cultural requirement that only one commanded in a vision can give a Sundance, but this is a literal explanation, not a figurative expression.
footnote_en: [3] LB: Informant had explained that not anyone, but only he who had been so commanded in a vision by a Thunderer, could give a Sun-Dance.

text_cree: kotak mîna nîmihitôwin: kikastotinêwak.
text_en: Another dance still: they dance the Masked-Dance.
label: literal
rationale: This is a plain statement introducing a dance; no figurative language is present.
footnote_en: [4] LB: Or, “small things (animate: rattles?) made of buffalo-hoofs.”

text_cree: êkwa mistikohk tâpisiniyiwa mostoswak waskasîwâhk ohci ê-apisîsisicik.
text_en: To a pole are fastened the smallest of the hoofs of buffalo.
label: literal
rationale: The footnote offers an alternative literal translation of 'smallest of the hoofs' as 'small rattles made of buffalo-hoofs,' but this is still a literal description, not figurative.
footnote_en: [4] LB: Or, “small things (animate: rattles?) made of buffalo-hoofs.”

text_cree: êyakonik pêyak kîsikâw ê-kîsikâyik piko ê-nîmihitocik.
text_en: These dancers dance one day, only during daylight.
label: literal
rationale: This sentence literally describes when the dancers perform; no non-literal language.
footnote_en: [4] LB: Or, “small things (animate: rattles?) made of buffalo-hoofs.”

text_cree: kahkiyaw mâka kikastotinêwak.
text_en: All wear a headgear.
label: literal
rationale: A direct statement that all wear headgear; no figurative meaning.
footnote_en: [4] LB: Or, “small things (animate: rattles?) made of buffalo-hoofs.”

text_cree: namôya nôkwaniyiwa ohkwâkaniwâw; payipisikâtêyiwa otastotiniwâwa ita ê-ohci-kanawâpahkêcik.
text_en: Their faces are not visible; holes are cut in their headgear, through which they may see.
label: literal
rationale: Describes the headgear's features literally; no figure of speech.
footnote_en: [4] LB: Or, “small things (animate: rattles?) made of buffalo-hoofs.”

text_cree: anohc pîtos nîmihitôwin, ê-mîcisohk, kahkiyaw, awâsisak, iskwêwak, kahkiyaw ê-itohtatahk mîciwin, ayâpisîs pêyak askihkohk piko.
text_en: Today the dancing is different; there is eating. Everyone, children and women, bring food, each one a small amount, in a kettle.
label: literal
rationale: Sentence describes the dancing and food-bringing plainly; the footnote discusses dance names and lodge shapes not present here.
footnote_en: [5] LB: This last is no doubt the “pow-wow”, Cree pîcicîwak , literally, “they attract”. An old time dance described by Coming-Day but not mentioned in our text, was the Pole-Dance, awatâhtikwêwak , literally, “they carry sticks”.  Sticks were set up upright in the ground, four ropes attached to each, and each rope held by a dancer. The dancers were on horseback, two young men and two young women riding around each stick. Another feature not in this text is the form of the lodge:  the Smoking-Lodge is conical, shaped like an ordinary tipi; the Sun-Dance lodge is straight upright (in a circle) and has a conical top.

text_cree: piyis mistahi pîhcâyihk astêw mîciwin.
text_en: In the end there is a good amount of food in the tent.
label: literal
rationale: Sentence states plainly that food ends up in the tent; no figurative language.

rationale: Sentence gives a straightforward temporal detail about stopping before midnight; no figurative language.

text_cree: êkwa ê-kî-tapasîyit, êkwa ê-wâ-wâpamâcik otêmiwâwa. awa kisêyiniw kâ-kî-miyiht misatimwa, êwako piko pimâtisiyiwa, êsa ê-kawipitisoyit, oskâtiyihk ê-tâpakwâtahk pîsâkanâpiy ohci awa misatim. êkosi isi otinêw awa kisêyiniw.
text_en: Then when the others had run away and they looked at their horses, only the horse which had been given to the old man was alive; it had apparently thrown itself down on the ground by getting its foot snagged in the tether.

rationale: Bloomfield's footnote on 'êh-tapakwâtahk' notes the word is probably wrongly recorded, not a figurative expression; thus literal.
footnote_en: [1] LB on êh-tapakwâtahk :  This word is probably wrongly recorded; the translation is a guess.

text_cree: êkosi sipwêhtêwak, ê-kîwêcik ôki nêhiyawak.

label: literal

footnote_en: [1] LB on êh-tapakwâtahk :  This word is probably wrongly recorded; the translation is a guess.

text_en: So they saved their lives. On the next day, after marching all night, in the evening these Cree reached their camp.

text_cree: êkota ê-kî-wîcihiwêt, mitâtaht ayiwâkês ê-ihtasiyit, ôta ê-nitopayicik, ayahciyiniwa ê-nitopayîstawâcik, êkwa wâhyaw ê-ayâcik ayahciyiniwa otaskiyihk, êkosi kîkisêpâ sipwêhtêwak, ê-waniskâcik.
text_en: There where he went with a war party of some ten men or more on the war-path against the Blackfoot, when they were far into the Blackfoots' country, they got up one morning and started out.
label: literal
rationale: The sentence describes literal actions of traveling to war; the footnote only addresses grammatical person and does not indicate any figurative language.
footnote_en: [1] LB on itohtêwak :  The Cree are the third person, subject of this last verb; hence the sentence should properly read ... ayahciyiniwah ês ê-kîh-nipahâyit ... , with the Blackfoot in the obviative form.

text_cree: êkwa kîtahtawê ayahciyiniwak êsa ê-kî-nipahâcik mostoswa, êwakoni itohtêwak.
text_en: Presently they came to some buffalos which the Blackfoot, apparently, had killed.
label: literal
rationale: The sentence literally states they came upon buffalo killed by the Blackfoot; the footnote comments on the verb 'itohtêwak' but not on figurative usage.

text_cree: êkosi êkwa kotawêwak, ê-wî-mîciwâcik wiyâs, ê-mîcisocik.
text_en: So they made a fire, for they intended to make a meal, eating the meat.
label: literal
rationale: The sentence literally describes making a fire and intending to cook meat; the footnote does not apply to figurative language.
footnote_en: [1] LB on itohtêwak :  The Cree are the third person, subject of this last verb; hence the sentence should properly read ... ayahciyiniwah ês ê-kîh-nipahâyit ... , with the Blackfoot in the obviative form.

text_cree: mostoso-mêya mâwacihtâwak, ê-wî-pônahkik.
text_en: They gathered buffalo-dung for fuel.
label: literal

footnote_en: [1] LB on itohtêwak :  The Cree are the third person, subject of this last verb; hence the sentence should properly read ... ayahciyiniwah ês ê-kîh-nipahâyit ... , with the Blackfoot in the obviative form.

text_cree: êkwa êkota apwêwak, wiyâs ê-ma-manisahkik, ê-na-nawacîcik, êkwa nîso ê-ispatinâyik ê-wâpahtahkik, ê-wî-nitawi-asawâpicik, nîso ê-sâkêwêcik.
text_en: There they did the roasting, cutting slices of meat and making preserved meat; two of them, the while, ascending a rise in the land which they saw, to reconnoitre.
label: literal
rationale: The sentence literally details roasting meat and two men ascending a rise; the footnote provides no figurative commentary.
footnote_en: [1] LB on itohtêwak :  The Cree are the third person, subject of this last verb; hence the sentence should properly read ... ayahciyiniwah ês ê-kîh-nipahâyit ... , with the Blackfoot in the obviative form.

text_cree: mosci wâpamêwak ayahciyiniwa ê-pâ-pasahkâpiyit, osâm kisiwâk ê-kapêsimostawâcik.
text_en: Plainly they could see even when a Blackfoot blinked his eyes, so close had they camped to them.
label: literal
rationale: The footnote provides a variant form of 'mosci' and does not indicate figurative language.
footnote_en: [2] LB on moscis :  For moscih or moscih isih .

text_cree: êkwa misatimwa kêkâc pâh-pistiskâkwak, ê-wî-minihkwêyit.
text_en: And they nearly were stepped on by the horses that came to drink.
label: literal
rationale: No footnote applies, and the sentence is literal.
footnote_en: [2] LB on moscis :  For moscih or moscih isih .

text_cree: aspapiwina kikiskamwak misatimwak; pîsâkanâpiy otâpêwak ê-sakikwêpisocik.
text_en: The horses had saddles on; they were dragging reins, being all bridled.
label: literal
rationale: No footnote applies, and the sentence is literal.
footnote_en: [2] LB on moscis :  For moscih or moscih isih .

text_cree: êkwa ê-pôn-âpihtâwi-kîsikâk, kîtahtawê ômisi itwêw sâyiman: "âta niwî-kawacin; âta wiya niya nika-pimâtisin," itwêw, "kiya mâka?" itêw manitowi-kihiwa.
text_en: When noon had passed, Solomon spoke: “I am almost frozen to death; yet I shall live,” he said; “But as for you?” he said to Spirit-Eagle.
label: idiom
rationale: Bloomfield's footnote explains that 'nika-pimâtisin' means 'I feel sufficient mystic power in me to know that I shall live,' which is a non-literal, conventional expression, thus an idiom.
footnote_en: [4] LB on nikah-pimâtisin :  I.e. “I feel sufficient mystic power in me to know that I shall live.”

text_cree: "ômisi nika-itâw," itwêw awa iskwêw.
text_en: “Thus I shall speak to him,” said the woman.
label: literal
rationale: The footnote explains that the woman's words were not dictated, indicating a literal statement of intent; no figurative language is described.
footnote_en: [1] LB:  What she would say was not dictated.

footnote_en: [2] CHECK ka -> kâ

text_en: The youth could not strike him.

footnote_en: [2] CHECK ka -> kâ

text_cree: êkosi awa nâpêw kwâskwêpayihôw; wâskikaniyihk êkota ta-tahkiskawêw; piyisk otinam ocîkahikanisiyiw, êwako ohci ê-câ-cîkahwât.

rationale: Plain narration of physical combat actions, no non-literal language.

text_cree: kîtahtawê asiniy kâ-mihkosit isiyîhkâsôw; nama wîhkâc wâpahtam nôtinitôwin, osâm ê-sâkihikot ôhtâwiya awa oskinîkiw.
text_en: Once upon a time there was a man called Red-Stone; never had he seen fighting, for his father too much cherished this young man.
label: literal
rationale: The footnote only comments on hyphenation and does not describe figurative language; the sentence is a straightforward narrative statement with no non-literal expressions.
footnote_en: [1] KR: asiniy-kâ-mihkosit is a hyphenated in Bloomfield's text.

text_en: Then these others, the Assiniboine, made ready to fight.

rationale: The footnote concerns a morphological uncertainty, not figurative language. The sentence is a plain statement of the Assiniboine preparing to fight.
footnote_en: [2] CHECK kâ-nôtinâyicik - HCW unsure. probably conflation, ?sub nôtinâyit .

text_en: Very many were the people who were coming to fight against them; and they fought.
label: literal
rationale: The footnote concerns the word form 'kâ-nôtinâyicik', which relates to sentence 4, not figurative language. This sentence describes the number of enemies and the fight, using no metaphors or idioms.
footnote_en: [2] CHECK kâ-nôtinâyicik - HCW unsure. probably conflation, ?sub nôtinâyit .

text_en: Presently the young man whose father loved him, looked upon them; he watched his people fighting.
label: literal
rationale: The footnote does not mention figurative language. The sentence literally narrates the young man watching his people fight.
footnote_en: [2] CHECK kâ-nôtinâyicik - HCW unsure. probably conflation, ?sub nôtinâyit .

text_en: Soon he saw his comrades being attacked, four of them fighting a brave who attacked here, there, and everywhere.

text_en: The plight of his companions angered him.

footnote_en: [2] CHECK kâ-nôtinâyicik - HCW unsure. probably conflation, ?sub nôtinâyit .

text_en: A white horse he rode who was slaying them.

text_en: As to the rider of the white horse who was so sorely besetting them, “If he is brave, when I come to attack him, he too will come to attack me. If he is brave, he will dismount. Then I shall kill him; I shall stab him with this knife,” he thought.
label: literal
rationale: The footnote mentions a possible error in a verb direction, not any figurative language. The sentence itself consists of straightforward literal statements of intent and action.
footnote_en: [3] Probably an erroneous direction in one of these verbs.

text_en: Presently they set out for that place, and where that Blackfoot lay who had been slain, they put him up on something.

text_cree: êkwa ôma ita kâ-kî-pimisihk asiskiy ê-manisahkik, tâpiskôc ayîsiyiniw ê-pimisihk êkosi ê-isi-manisahkik; êkwa awa opwâsîmôw ita kâ-ôh-wâpamât ôhi ayahciyiniwa, êkota mîna asiskiy ê-ati-manisahkik, tâpiskôc ita ê-pimohtêt ayîsiyiniw ê-isi-manisahkik asiskiy.
text_en: Then they cut away some of the ground where he had lain, cutting it like a man lying there; and there whence that Assiniboine had seen that Blackfoot, there too they went cutting the ground, carving it out like a man walking.
label: simile
rationale: The phrase 'tâpiskôc ayîsiyiniw ê-pimisihk' explicitly compares the cutting to a man lying, using the simile marker 'tâpiskôc'.
footnote_en: [1] LB on kîkwa :  Word-avoidance, têsipicikan : “scaffold”.

footnote_en: [1] LB:  I suspect that there is a tabu, - except for certain special circumstances, cf. below in this story, - against saying, “whome I (or we) have killed.”  Certainly some of my Plains Cree friends have killed their man, but I have never heard them, even in telling of war, mention such a fact.

text_cree: pêyak opwâsîmôw, mistahi ê-miyosit oskinîkiw, sihkosiwayâna ê-kikamoyit oskotâkâhk mîna otâsihk, kahkiyaw ê-mîkisiwiyiki otayôwinisa, mîna otastotin sihkosiwayâna ê-kikamoyit, êskana ê-kikamoyit otastotinihk, êwako êkota ê-ayât ôma ê-nôtinitôwiht, namôya nôtinikêw, ê-pêhât ôhtâwiya, câpihcikanis ê-tahkonahk, êkwa cîkahikani-pakamâkan ê-tahkonahk, êkwa napakihkomân, âsay nîso ê-pê-tahkamât câpihcikanis ohci ayahciyiniwa, êkwa pêyak ê-cîkahwât ôma ohci ocîkahikanis, êkosi nisto ê-nipahât, ostikwâniyiwa ôhi pâh-pahki ê-pahkwêkisamwât, "pita nika-miyâw nôhtâwiy," ê-itêyihtahk, otêmiyiwa nîso ê-otinât mîna.
text_en: A certain Assiniboine, a very handsome youth, with weaselskins on his coat and on his breeches, with beads on all his clothes, and weaselskins also on his toque, and horns, beside, on his headgear, he, staying tight close to the fight, took yet no active part in it, for he was awaiting his father, holding in hand a lance and a tomahawk and a bowie knife; with his lance he had already transfixed two Blackfoot on the way hither, and had tomahawked one, so that he had slain three: taking a part of each one's scalp, in the thought, “Later I shall give them to my father,” and taking also two of their horses.
label: literal
rationale: Sentence describes a person's appearance and actions literally; no figurative language detected.
footnote_en: [3] LB:  A typical Central Algonquian sentence, such as for obvious reasons is not often obtained in dictation or in the laborious process fo syllabic writing.  In length and suppleness of subordination it resembled earlier Indo-European, e.g. Latin.

text_en: Soon many of his companions had arrived.
label: literal

footnote_en: [3] LB:  A typical Central Algonquian sentence, such as for obvious reasons is not often obtained in dictation or in the laborious process fo syllabic writing.  In length and suppleness of subordination it resembled earlier Indo-European, e.g. Latin.

text_cree: kîtahtawê kâ-wâpamât ôhtâwiya ita ê-apit ê-pê-itohtêyit.
text_en: Presently he saw his father coming to where he sat.
label: literal
rationale: The footnote (Bloomfield's note 3) applies, commenting on the sentence's structure and rarity, but it contains no figurative expression. Sentence is literal.
footnote_en: [3] LB:  A typical Central Algonquian sentence, such as for obvious reasons is not often obtained in dictation or in the laborious process fo syllabic writing.  In length and suppleness of subordination it resembled earlier Indo-European, e.g. Latin.

text_cree: "â, nîso nipê-tahkamâwak;" "otêmiwâwa nitôtinimâwa; mîna ostikwâniwâwa nitôtinên."
text_en: “Oh, two I stabbed on the way; I took their horses; and I took their heads.”
label: idiom
rationale: Bloomfield notes that 'ostikwâniwâwa' literally means 'their heads' but is used here for 'scalps,' a conventional non-literal substitution, fitting the idiom class.
footnote_en: [4] LB on ostikwâniwâwa : “Head” for “scalp”, as often; I do not know whether this locution dates back to the antecedents of the custom.

text_cree: ômisi itwêw: "hahahêy, tâpwê nipakwâtên ê-pistahowêyân!" itwêw, ê-pasikôt, êkota ê-nitawi-nahapit ôhi oskinîkiwa kâ-nipahât.
text_en: Thus he spoke: “Alas, truly I am grieved at having made a fatal error!” he cried, rising to his feet, and went and sat by the youth he had killed.

rationale: The sentence describes actions and speech in a straightforward manner without non-literal expression.

text_cree: namwâc kinwêsk apiw âsay ostikwânihk ê-tawahokot ayahciyiniwa; kîpiwêpahok.
