label: literal
rationale: The sentence narrates events literally, with no figurative language present.
footnote_en: [5] LB on omê :  Probably error for ôma .

text_cree: êkosi otinâw, âkawâyihk ê-itohtahiht awa mîna oskinîkiw.
text_en: So he was taken up and brought to a sheltered spot, and the body of the youth as well.
label: literal
rationale: Plain description of actions; no metaphor, simile, or idiom.
footnote_en: [5] LB on omê :  Probably error for ôma .

text_cree: âhci piko yêhyêw awa ayahciyiniwa ostikwânihk kâ-pâskisokot.
text_en: He who had been shot in the head by the Blackfoot was still breathing.
label: literal
rationale: A literal statement about someone still breathing after being shot.
footnote_en: [5] LB on omê :  Probably error for ôma .

text_cree: nicawâc nipiy ita ê-ayâyik, êkota itohtahâw, êkota ê-pimisihk, ê-akwanahiht wâpowayân.
text_en: He was taken to where there was water, and there he lay, covered with a blanket.
label: literal
rationale: The footnote only comments on a probable textual error, not on figurative language; the sentence itself is a literal account.
footnote_en: [5] LB on omê :  Probably error for ôma .

text_cree: êkosi isi ohpimê itohtêwak ôki ayisiyiniwak, ôma ê-nôtinitocik kêyâpic.
text_en: Then the people went off, to fight again.
label: literal
rationale: A direct statement about people leaving to fight again, without figurative embellishment.
footnote_en: [5] LB on omê :  Probably error for ôma .

text_cree: êkwa ê-miyikot, êkwa itohtêw.
text_en: When the other gave it him, he went there.
label: literal
rationale: No figurative language detected; the statement is a straightforward narrative.
footnote_en: [1] LB on nîso :  Evidently I here missed the word pêyak : “one (of them)”.

text_cree: êkwa ê-pônamiyit, pîhcâyihk ê-apiyit, nâciyôstawêw.
text_en: The others had made a fire and were sitting indoors; he crept up to them.
label: literal
rationale: Describes actions literally.
footnote_en: [1] LB on nîso :  Evidently I here missed the word pêyak : “one (of them)”.

text_cree: êkwa ê-otihtât, isi-niyânaniyiwa, ê-nâh-nawaciyit.
text_en: When he got near them, they were five, a-roasting of meat.
label: literal
rationale: Plain description of approaching and the number of people.
footnote_en: [1] LB on nîso :  Evidently I here missed the word pêyak : “one (of them)”.

text_cree: nawasawâpamôw; tânihi ê-miyohoyit, êwakoni pâskiswêw, ê-sâkowêt.
text_en: He took careful aim; he shot at those who wore the best clothes, and gave a whoop.
label: literal
rationale: Literal account of aiming, shooting, and giving a war whoop.
footnote_en: [1] LB on nîso :  Evidently I here missed the word pêyak : “one (of them)”.

text_cree: ê-tapasîyit nîso, ê-tâh-tâwikisiniyit mistikohk, osâm ê-sêkihât, êwakoni mîna pimwêw; nipahêw mîna.
text_en: While two fled, one kept bumping into things, so much had he frightened him; this one too he shot; he killed him too.
label: literal
rationale: Although the footnote notes a likely mishearing of 'nîso' for 'pêyak', it does not indicate figurative language; the sentence describes actions literally.
footnote_en: [1] LB on nîso :  Evidently I here missed the word pêyak : “one (of them)”.

text_cree: êkosi nisto nipahêw.
text_en: So he had killed three.
label: literal
rationale: Simple statement of the number killed.
footnote_en: [1] LB on nîso :  Evidently I here missed the word pêyak : “one (of them)”.

text_cree: ê-kiskêyihtahk ê-tapasîyit; pîhtokêw, otayiwinisiyiwa ê-otinahk, mîna pâskisikan pêyak, pêyak acosisa, pêyak cîkahikani-pakamâkan, êkwa pêyak câpihcicikanis, môhkomâna nêwo, mîna ostikwâniyihk ôta ôma ê-manisamwât.
text_en: When he saw that they had fled, he went inside and took their garments, and a gun, a set of arrows, a tomahawk, and a lance, and four knives, and he cut off this, on their heads here.
label: literal
rationale: Lists items taken and the act of cutting off, likely scalping, in a literal manner.
footnote_en: [1] LB on nîso :  Evidently I here missed the word pêyak : “one (of them)”.

text_cree: kahkiyaw omaskisiniyiwa otinam, êkwa ê-kîwêhtatât, ôhi kâ-kaskatahomiht wîcêwâkana, ê-pîhtokatât, ê-miyât.
text_en: He took all their moccasins, and took it all back with him and gave it, when he brought it into their hut, to his wounded companion.
label: literal
rationale: Describes taking moccasins and sharing spoils; no figurative language.
footnote_en: [1] LB on nîso :  Evidently I here missed the word pêyak : “one (of them)”.

text_cree: mistahi miywêyihtam awa oskinîkiw, êkwa ê-sipwê-têhtapit, ê-pê-sîhkitisahwâyit ôhi nâpêsisa misatimwa.
text_en: The young man was very glad, and rode away, while the boy drove on the horses.
label: literal
rationale: The sentence describes literal actions and emotions with no figurative language.
footnote_en: [2] CHECK tipiskwah

text_cree: kapê-tipisk pimipayiwak.
text_en: They rode all night.
label: literal
rationale: The footnote '[2] CHECK tipiskwah' flags a word form but does not indicate any figurative language; the sentence itself is a literal statement.
footnote_en: [2] CHECK tipiskwah

text_cree: ê-kîsikâyik, ê-wâpamât awa oskinîkiw misatimwa, "tâpwê miyosiwak!" itêyihtam.
text_en: When day came and the young man saw the horses, “Really, they are fine ones!” he thought.
label: literal
rationale: It reports a character's thought literally, with no metaphor, simile, or idiom.
footnote_en: [2] CHECK tipiskwah

text_cree: kapê-kîsik pimâmôwak, mîna kapê-tipisk.
text_en: They fled all day, and again all night.
label: literal
rationale: The sentence literally describes the duration of their flight.
footnote_en: [2] CHECK tipiskwah

text_cree: nîsotipiskwa namôya nipâwak.
text_en: For two nights they did not sleep.
label: literal
rationale: It is a straightforward literal statement about not sleeping.
footnote_en: [2] CHECK tipiskwah

text_cree: êkoyikohk ê-wâpamâcik mostoswa, nawaswêw awa nâpêsis.
text_en: Then, as they saw some buffalos, the boy gave chase.
label: literal
rationale: The sentence recounts a literal action of giving chase.
footnote_en: [2] CHECK tipiskwah

text_cree: miywêyihtam awa oskinîkiw, êkota ê-nîhtakosît, ê-wî-wiyanihtâkêcik, ê-wî-mîcisocik.
text_en: The young man was glad; he dismounted, and they skinned it and cut it up and made ready to eat.
label: literal
rationale: It describes literal actions of dismounting, skinning, and preparing to eat.
footnote_en: [2] CHECK tipiskwah

text_cree: êkwa wiyawâw ê-kîsi-wiyanihtâkêcik, êkwa ê-kîsitêpocik, ê-paminawasocik, iyikohk ê-kîsi-mîcisocik, mîna sipwêhtêwak.
text_en: But, as for them, when they had cleaned their game, and cooked their meal, and eaten, they went on.
label: literal
rationale: Plain description of actions (cleaning game, cooking, eating, departing); no figurative language.
footnote_en: [3] LB on kâ-kîh-itwêt :  Probably read as kâ-kîh-itwêhk : “it was so reported”, as in translation.

text_cree: nîswâw ê-nipâcik, kîtahtawê kâ-wâpahtahkik wîkiwâwa.
text_en: After two nights on the way, presently they came in sight of their camp.
label: literal
rationale: Literal statement of travel duration and sighting the camp; no non-literal expression.
footnote_en: [3] LB on kâ-kîh-itwêt :  Probably read as kâ-kîh-itwêhk : “it was so reported”, as in translation.

text_cree: miywêyihtam awa kâ-kî-kaskatahoht.
text_en: The one who had been wounded was glad.
label: literal
rationale: Direct statement of the wounded person's gladness; no figurative language.
footnote_en: [3] LB on kâ-kîh-itwêt :  Probably read as kâ-kîh-itwêhk : “it was so reported”, as in translation.

text_cree: ispî ê-wâpamihcik, ê-pê-sipwêpayit pêyak oskinîkiw, awîniki ôki êyakonik, "nipahâwak," kâ-kî-itwêt.
text_en: When they were seen, a young man came to them from the camp; whom did he see, but those of whom it had been said that they were killed!
label: literal
rationale: Bloomfield's footnote only clarifies the verb form as 'it was so reported'; the expression is a literal report of speech, not figurative.
footnote_en: [3] LB on kâ-kîh-itwêt :  Probably read as kâ-kîh-itwêhk : “it was so reported”, as in translation.

text_cree: êkota ohci kîwêpayiw awa, ê-nitawi-wîhtamawât ôhi okimâwa ê-takosiniyit okosisiyiwa mîna ôhi kâ-kî-kaskatahomiht, ê-isi-pêhtahkik, ê-nitawi-nakiskawâcik.
text_en: Then this man rode back to tell the chief that his son had come home, as well as the man who had been wounded; and when they heard this, they went to meet them.
label: literal
rationale: Straightforward narrative of riding back, telling the chief, and going to meet them; no figurative language.
footnote_en: [3] LB on kâ-kîh-itwêt :  Probably read as kâ-kîh-itwêhk : “it was so reported”, as in translation.

text_cree: ê-pêtastimwêyit awa okosisa, okimâwa, awa nâpêsis ôhi kâ-kaskatahomiht niyânan miyêw misatimwa; wiya mîna niyânan ayâwêw misatimwa.
text_en: That boy, the chief's son, who brought the horses, gave five of them to the man who had been wounded; five horses he kept.
label: literal
rationale: Factual account of the gift of horses; no metaphor or idiom.
footnote_en: [3] LB on kâ-kîh-itwêt :  Probably read as kâ-kîh-itwêhk : “it was so reported”, as in translation.

text_cree: mistahi miywêyihtam awa okimâw.
text_en: The chief was very glad.
label: literal
rationale: Simple statement of the chief's gladness; no figurative language.
footnote_en: [3] LB on kâ-kîh-itwêt :  Probably read as kâ-kîh-itwêhk : “it was so reported”, as in translation.

text_cree: piyisk kahkiyaw awiyak miywêyihtamwak; mîna ayahciyiniwa nisto ê-nipahât awa nâpêsis, miywêyihtamwak ôki ayisiyiniwak, ê-miyawâtahkik, ê-nîmihitocik, awa ohci nâpêsis osâm ê-sôhkêyimiht, "tâpwê nâpêhkâsôw!" ê-itêyimiht, ôhi mîna nâpêwa ê-kaskatahomiht êkâ kâ-wî-nakatât, osâm namôya cêskwa mitoni ê-oskinîkit.
text_en: Then everyone was glad; also because the boy had slain three Blackfoot those people were glad, and celebrated the outcome with a dance, thinking that boy very brave, thinking of him, “Truly, he is a brave warrior!” especially because he had refused to abandon the wounded man, even though he was not yet full-grown.
label: literal
rationale: Describes gladness, reasons, celebration, and thoughts; the quoted praise 'nâpêhkâsôw' is a direct literal statement ('he is a brave warrior') within the narrative.
footnote_en: [3] LB on kâ-kîh-itwêt :  Probably read as kâ-kîh-itwêhk : “it was so reported”, as in translation.

text_cree: êwako anima ohci kâ-ôh-miywêyihtahkik ayîsiyiniwak.
text_en: That was why those people were glad.
label: literal
rationale: Summarizing reason for gladness; no figurative expression.
footnote_en: [3] LB on kâ-kîh-itwêt :  Probably read as kâ-kîh-itwêhk : “it was so reported”, as in translation.

text_cree: nama isko ê-takosihkik wîkiwâhk, mostoswa wâpamêwak.
text_en: Before they reached their camp, they came in sight of some buffalos.
label: literal
rationale: The sentence is a plain description of reaching camp and seeing buffalo; no figurative language. The footnote discusses a different sentence.
footnote_en: [1] LB on êh-wayawîhtamâtot :  A particle, wayawîhtah “going outside,” is here compounded with the verb; if correctly recorded, it is of unusual formation.

text_cree: pêyak nipahêwak, êkota ê-nâh-nawacîcik, ê-mîcisocik.
text_en: They killed one and stopped to preserve the meat and to eat.
label: literal
rationale: Literal description of killing, stopping, and eating; no figurative language. The footnote does not apply.
footnote_en: [1] LB on êh-wayawîhtamâtot :  A particle, wayawîhtah “going outside,” is here compounded with the verb; if correctly recorded, it is of unusual formation.

text_cree: ê-kîsi-mîcisocik, awa kâ-kî-nipahât owîkimâkana pasikôw; sipwêhtêw, ohpimê ê-nitawi-nahapit, ê-wayawîhtamâtot, ê-tapahtiskwêyit.
text_en: When they had eaten, he who had slain his wife arose; he went and sat down somewhere, weeping alone, with his head bowed in grief.
label: literal
rationale: The sentence describes actions literally. The footnote comments on the unusual formation of 'ê-wayawîhtamâtot', but this is grammatical, not figurative.
footnote_en: [1] LB on êh-wayawîhtamâtot :  A particle, wayawîhtah “going outside,” is here compounded with the verb; if correctly recorded, it is of unusual formation.

text_cree: êkosi awa kotak oskinîkiw kâ-kî-itât, "mâtoyini, ka-nipahitin", kâ-kî-itwêt, wâpamêw ê-tapahtiskwêyiyit, ê-mâtoyit, ê-itêyimât.
text_en: Then that youth who had said to him, “If you weep, I will kill you,” saw him with bowed head and, as he thought, weeping.
label: literal
rationale: Literal recounting of the youth's thought and sight; no figurative language. The footnote does not apply.
footnote_en: [1] LB on êh-wayawîhtamâtot :  A particle, wayawîhtah “going outside,” is here compounded with the verb; if correctly recorded, it is of unusual formation.

text_cree: otinam pâskisikan, ê-nitawâpamât.
text_en: He took his gun and went to look at him.
label: literal
rationale: Literal action of taking a gun and going to see; no figurative language. The footnote does not apply.
footnote_en: [1] LB on êh-wayawîhtamâtot :  A particle, wayawîhtah “going outside,” is here compounded with the verb; if correctly recorded, it is of unusual formation.

text_cree: ê-wâpamât, tâpwê mâtoyiwa.
text_en: When he saw him, he was really weeping.
label: literal
rationale: Literal statement of seeing and weeping; no figurative language. The footnote does not apply.
footnote_en: [1] LB on êh-wayawîhtamâtot :  A particle, wayawîhtah “going outside,” is here compounded with the verb; if correctly recorded, it is of unusual formation.

text_cree: kayâs mostoswak, paskwâwi-mostoswak, nânitaw mitâtaht tipahikan, êkoyikohk askiy nama kêkway nôkwan, ê-akoskahkik paskwâwi-mostoswak.
text_en: The old-time buffalos, for a distance of some ten miles the earth was not visible, as the buffalos covered it.
label: literal
rationale: The footnote only comments on the morphology of 'ê-tawitisahwâcik' and does not indicate any figurative language; the sentence is purely literal.
footnote_en: [1] LB on êh-tawocahwâcik : Probably the normal form is êh-tawitisahwâcik , initial stem taw- : “open”, transitive verb final -tisahw- : “drive” (cf. pimitisahwêw : “he drives him on”).

text_cree: êwako âcimôwin namôya kayâs, mâskôc niyânano-mitanaw askiy êkospî ôma iyikohk ê-mihcêticik mostoswak.
text_en: This story is not old, perhaps fifty years ago it was, when the buffalos were so many.
label: literal
rationale: The footnote does not apply; the sentence is a straightforward statement about the story's age and the buffalo's abundance, with no figurative elements.
footnote_en: [1] LB on êh-tawocahwâcik : Probably the normal form is êh-tawitisahwâcik , initial stem taw- : “open”, transitive verb final -tisahw- : “drive” (cf. pimitisahwêw : “he drives him on”).

text_cree: nâpêwak niyânan êwakonik ê-âcimocik ê-wâpamâcik, piko ê-pimohtêcik ôki nêhiyawak, akohpa ômisi ê-wêpinahkik, ê-tawitisahwâcik mostoswa; êkwa ôtê nâway kâwi ômisi ê-pê-tipwayâyit ê-misihtawayâyit.
text_en: Five men they were who told of it, having seen it when they were out for a walk, these Cree.
label: literal
rationale: The footnote concerns verb morphology and does not indicate figurative usage; the description of men walking and shaking blankets is literal.
footnote_en: [1] LB on êh-tawocahwâcik : Probably the normal form is êh-tawitisahwâcik , initial stem taw- : “open”, transitive verb final -tisahw- : “drive” (cf. pimitisahwêw : “he drives him on”).

text_cree: êkwa mitâtaht tipahikan êkoyikohk isko ê-ayâcik paskwâwi-mostoswak, iyikohk ê-mihcêticik, êkâ ê-tawâyik ita kâ-pimohtêcik.
text_en: They shook their blankets like this, to drive the buffalos apart, and behind them the herd closed in again.
label: literal
rationale: The footnote is unrelated; the sentence describes the extent of the buffalo herds without any non-literal language.
footnote_en: [1] LB on êh-tawocahwâcik : Probably the normal form is êh-tawitisahwâcik , initial stem taw- : “open”, transitive verb final -tisahw- : “drive” (cf. pimitisahwêw : “he drives him on”).

text_cree: êkoyikohk isko, mitâtaht tipahikan isko mihcêtiyit mostoswa, ê-wâpamâcik nêhiyawak kayâs, nânitaw niyânano-mitanaw askiy.
text_en: And for a distance of ten miles there were buffalos so numerous that there was no opening where they walked.
label: literal
rationale: No figurative language is present; the footnote's morphological note does not apply to this literal description of the herd's size.
footnote_en: [1] LB on êh-tawocahwâcik : Probably the normal form is êh-tawitisahwâcik , initial stem taw- : “open”, transitive verb final -tisahw- : “drive” (cf. pimitisahwêw : “he drives him on”).

text_cree: êwako pêyak âcimowin.
text_en: Ten miles in length was the herd of buffalos which these Cree saw of old, some fifty years ago.
label: literal
rationale: The sentence is a simple statement identifying a story, with no figurative language; the footnote is irrelevant.
footnote_en: [1] LB on êh-tawocahwâcik : Probably the normal form is êh-tawitisahwâcik , initial stem taw- : “open”, transitive verb final -tisahw- : “drive” (cf. pimitisahwêw : “he drives him on”).

text_cree: pêyak nâpêw powâmêkan isiyîhkâsôw; êwako kâ-wâpamât ôhi mostoswa.
text_en: One man was called Powamekan; he saw these buffalos.
label: literal
rationale: Plain statement of a man's name and action; no figurative language.
footnote_en: [4] LB on tâmpêsin :  So recorded;  is this the tawipîsin who occurs in text 10?

text_cree: êkwa pêyak nâpêw tâmpêsin isiyîhkâsôw.
text_en: And one man was called Tampesin.
label: literal
rationale: Plain statement of a man's name; footnote only questions a name variant, not figurative language.
footnote_en: [4] LB on tâmpêsin :  So recorded;  is this the tawipîsin who occurs in text 10?

text_cree: êkwa pêyak wataniy isiyîhkâsôw.
text_en: And one was called Bird-Tail.
label: literal
rationale: Plain statement of a man's name ('Bird-Tail'); no figurative language.
footnote_en: [4] LB on tâmpêsin :  So recorded;  is this the tawipîsin who occurs in text 10?

text_cree: êkonik ê-wâpamâcik iyikohk ê-mihcêtiyit paskwâwi-mostoswa.
text_en: They saw the herd of buffalos that was so great.
label: literal
rationale: Literal description of seeing a large herd; no figurative language.
footnote_en: [4] LB on tâmpêsin :  So recorded;  is this the tawipîsin who occurs in text 10?

text_cree: "nah ôhi kanawêyihta," itêw.
text_en: “Take these things and save them up,” he told her.
label: literal
rationale: The footnote is an editorial note about the word 'nah' and does not indicate figurative language; the sentence is a literal directive.
footnote_en: [1] CHECK nah

text_cree: osîhêw atimo-otâpânâskwa, ê-pasahwât mistikwa, napakitâpânâskwa ê-osîhât.
text_en: He built a dog-sled with split trees, a flat dog-sled.
label: literal
rationale: No figurative language detected; the sentence describes building a sled literally.
footnote_en: [2] LB on tahpotêw :  Probably takohtêw : “he came back to the house.”

text_cree: ê-kî-kîsihât, takohtêw.
text_en: When he had finished it, he tied it up.
label: literal
rationale: The footnote suggests a variant reading 'takohtêw' but identifies no figurative language; the sentence is a literal statement about finishing and tying up the sled.
footnote_en: [2] LB on tahpotêw :  Probably takohtêw : “he came back to the house.”

text_cree: êkota napakâhtikohk ahêw mostoswayâna mîna mahîhkaniwayâna, nanâtohk atâwâkana.
text_en: On the boards of it he put buffalo-robes, wolfskins, and all kinds of furs.
label: literal
rationale: No figurative language detected; the sentence literally describes placing furs on the sled.
footnote_en: [2] LB on tahpotêw :  Probably takohtêw : “he came back to the house.”

text_cree: sipwêhtêw, ê-itohtêt wâskahikanihk, otatâwêwa ê-nitawâpamât.
text_en: He went off to see the trader in his house.
label: literal
rationale: No figurative language detected; the sentence literally describes going to see the trader.
footnote_en: [2] LB on tahpotêw :  Probably takohtêw : “he came back to the house.”

text_cree: ê-kîsi-postayôwinisêt awa iskwêw, êkwa awa nâpêw postayôwinisêw, wêmistikôsiwi-ayôwinisa; astotin, postastotinêw.
text_en: When the woman had dressed up, the man also dressed up in white-man's clothes, and put on his hat.
label: literal
rationale: No figurative language detected; the sentence literally describes dressing up in white-man's clothes and putting on a hat. The footnote does not apply to this sentence.
footnote_en: [3] LB's translation merged into first sentence of next paragraph.

text_cree: âsay namôya kitimâkisiwak.
text_en: Now they were no longer poor.
label: literal
rationale: Straightforward literal statement that they were no longer poor. No metaphor, simile, or idiom. The footnote does not apply.
footnote_en: [3] LB's translation merged into first sentence of next paragraph.

text_cree: otinam; oyâkanihk iskotêwâpoy sîkinam, êkwa êwako ê-minihkwêcik.
text_en: He took the whiskey and poured it into a bowl and then they drank it.
label: literal
rationale: The sentence literally describes taking whiskey, pouring it, and drinking. The footnote notes that the translation was merged into the next paragraph, but it indicates no figurative language.
footnote_en: [3] LB's translation merged into first sentence of next paragraph.

text_cree: "kahkiyaw pêtâyiw pôsihtâyêko ta-pê-sipwêhtêwak." "mahti nika-wâpamimâwa owîkimâkana mistahi kâ-atoskêyit."
text_en: “When you have loaded it all, let them set out and come here. I should like to see his wife who does so much work.”
label: literal
rationale: The footnote suggests a probable error in 'pêtâyiw' but does not indicate any figurative language; the sentence is a literal instruction to load and set out.
footnote_en: [4] LB on pêtâyiw : Probably an error.

text_cree: âcimostawêw tânisi kâ-tôtahk.
text_en: He told them how he had done.
label: literal
rationale: The sentence is a plain statement of telling someone about actions; no figurative language is present.
footnote_en: [5] LB on kîh-kîsihtâwâw : Wrongly recorded; probably I overheard the prefix ni- : “I”.

text_cree: "anohc kâ-piponiyik kî-kîsihtâwâw êwako ôma kê-wâpahtamêk ôhi êkwa kâ-miyitakok." "êkosi nititik, 'okimâw.'"
text_en: “This winter I have paid him for all this which you see here, and these things which I have given you. He called me 'Chief.'”
label: literal
rationale: The sentence contains direct speech stating facts (payment, giving, being called Chief); no metaphor, simile, or idiom. The footnote comments only on a recording error, not on figurative language.
footnote_en: [5] LB on kîh-kîsihtâwâw : Wrongly recorded; probably I overheard the prefix ni- : “I”.

text_cree: mitoni ninikotwâsinân, ê-sipwêhtêyâhk.
text_en: There were six of us who set out.
label: literal
rationale: The sentence is a literal statement of number and departure, with no figurative language.
footnote_en: [1] CHECK ?? kâsow VTA - RELATIONAL -wânân 1eAIrel3

text_cree: wiyâpahtamâhko mîkiwâhpa, nikâsowânân, êkâ ta-wâpamikoyâhkok ayahciyiniwak, ê-pimohtatâyâhk ôtê ohci ayiwinisa, ê-nitawi-wîtaskiyâhk wâhyaw awasâpisk.
text_en: When we saw any tipis, we hid from the people, lest the Blackfoot see us. We were carrying garments with us, from here, for we were bound on an embassy far beyond the Rocky Mountains.
label: literal
rationale: The sentence describes actions literally; the footnote provides a grammatical gloss for 'nikâsowânân' and does not indicate figurative language.
footnote_en: [1] CHECK ?? kâsow VTA - RELATIONAL -wânân 1eAIrel3

text_cree: piyisk nôtihtênân asinîwaciy, têpiskâki piko ê-pimohtêyâhk, êkâ awiyak ta-nôtinikoyâhk, ê-wî-kakwê-takohtêyâhk itê kâ-itohtêyâhk.
text_en: At last we came to the Rocky Mountains, walking the while only at night, lest anyone fight with us, for we meant to reach our destination.
label: literal
rationale: The sentence is a plain narrative of travel and intent, with no figurative language.
footnote_en: [1] CHECK ?? kâsow VTA - RELATIONAL -wânân 1eAIrel3

text_cree: piyisk awasâpisk nitakohtânân.
text_en: At last we arrived beyond the Rockies.
label: literal
rationale: The sentence states arrival in a straightforward, literal manner.
footnote_en: [1] CHECK ?? kâsow VTA - RELATIONAL -wânân 1eAIrel3

text_cree: êkosi êkwa, "wâpamaci ayahciyiniw, wî-nipahiski, wêpinâhkanik ôki misatimwak kâ-miyikawiyêk." "mistahi mâh-mîhkawikiwak êkonik." "piko kîwê- tapasîhkêk." "êkosi ta-miywâsin, takosiniyani kitaskîhk."
text_en: And so then, “If you see Blackfoot and they want to kill you, give rein to these horses that have been given to you. They are very swift. Simply flee for home. In this way you will easily reach your country.”
label: literal
rationale: The footnote merely clarifies the meaning of 'kîwê-' as 'homeward', with no indication of figurative language; the text is a literal command.
footnote_en: [2] LB on kihîh :  Probably kîwêh- : “homeward”.

text_cree: "tâpwê nisâkihikwak kinêpikoyiniwak," kî-itwêw êwako kisêyiniw: "'pitanê êkâ wîhkâc maci-wîcêhtocik, wiyâpahtotwâwi,' nikî-itwân mâna, ispî ê-okimâwiyân." "êwako ohci nanâtohk ayîsiyiniwak kâ-ôh-kî-sâkihicik: namôya wîhkâc n-ôh-nipahtâkân." "kâkikê nikî-ayân ayahciyiniwak otaskîwâhk." "êkosi kiyîwêyâni nitaskîhk isi, nikî-mâna-pîkiskâtâwak ayahciyiniwak." "êwako ohci, kwayask ê-itâtisiyân, kâ-ôh-kisêyinîwiyân." "'êwako ani kakwê-ayâk, nitawâsimisitik, êwako.'" "'kahkiyaw ayîsiyiniw ka-miyo-wîcêwâwâw,' nikî-itâwak mâna nitawâsimisak."
text_en: “Truly, the Snake people were fond of me,” said that old man; “'Would they might never deal wrongly with each other, when they see one another,' I used to say, when I was chief. That is why all kinds of people loved me: I never killed people. All the time I was in the Blackfoots' country. And when I went home, they would always regret my departure, the Blackfoot. Because I was of decent and righteous character, is why I reached old age. 'That is the way you must try to be, my children, even thus. You must deal rightly with every human being,' I always told my children.”
label: literal
rationale: The footnote comments on a possible mistranslation of direction in the verb 'pikiskatawak', which is not about figurative language; the paragraph contains no metaphors, similes, idioms, or other non-literal expressions.
footnote_en: [3] pikiskatawak Direction possibly mistranslated.

text_cree: êkwa mâh-mâsihêw iskwêw.
text_en: Then the woman lay with him.
label: idiom
rationale: The footnote explains that mâh-mâsihêw literally means 'wrestle' but is a common euphemism for 'lay with', making it a conventional non-literal idiom.
footnote_en: [1] LB on mâh-mâsihêw :  Literally, “wrestle”; in the present sense a common and, strangely enough, euphemistic expression.

text_cree: âhci piko mâsihêw nâpêwa ôhi.
text_en: Still she lay with that man.
label: literal
rationale: The sentence is a plain, literal description of the woman still lying with the man; no figurative language is present.
footnote_en: [2] LB:  Our narratress forgets to develop this motif.

text_cree: kêtahtawê êkwa ocihcîyiw otinam; ocâhcanisiyiwa otinimêw.
text_en: Presently she took his hand; she took a ring from his finger.
label: literal
rationale: The sentence is a straightforward, literal account of her taking his hand and ring; Bloomfield's footnote comments on narrative structure ('forgets to develop this motif'), not on figurative language.
footnote_en: [2] LB:  Our narratress forgets to develop this motif.

text_cree: "namôya." "konita ê-kî-mâtôhkâsoyân, ê-kotêsi-miywêyihtamân ê-sipwêhtêt," itêw.
text_en: “No. I only pretended to weep, but I was really glad when he went,” she told him.
label: literal
rationale: Bloomfield's footnote merely notes an unknown particle and does not indicate any figurative language; the meaning is straightforward.
footnote_en: [3] LB on êh-kotêsi-miywêyihtamân :  The particle kotêsi here compounded with the verb is otherwise unknown to me and may be wrongly recorded.

text_cree: êkwa ê-wâpaniyik sipwêhtêw; tapasîw êkwa.
text_en: Then in the morning she went away; she fled.
label: literal
rationale: No figurative language present; straightforward description of departure and flight.
footnote_en: [4] Book has no space between êk and êh-wâpamât .

text_cree: tahto-kîsikâw pimohtêw, wayawîtimihk ê-nipât.
text_en: She walked every day and slept out of doors.
label: literal
rationale: No figurative language; literal description of daily walking and sleeping outdoors.
footnote_en: [4] Book has no space between êk and êh-wâpamât .

text_cree: kêtahtawê sâkêwêw, ispatinâhk kâ-wâpamât ayîsiyiniwa ê-pâpayiyit.
text_en: Presently she came out upon a place where she saw a man riding that way over a hill.
label: literal
rationale: No figurative language; literal description of coming out and seeing a man riding.
footnote_en: [4] Book has no space between êk and êh-wâpamât .

text_cree: iyikohk êkâ ê-wâpamât sipwêhtêw.
text_en: When she saw him no longer, she went on.
label: literal
rationale: The footnote notes an orthographic detail, not figurative language; the sentence is literal.
footnote_en: [4] Book has no space between êk and êh-wâpamât .

text_cree: âsay mîna ê-sâkêwêt, kâ-wâpamât âsay mîna ê-pâpayiyit; kâsôhtawêw.
text_en: When she came out over the next hill, she saw him again riding toward her; she hid from him.
label: literal
rationale: No figurative language; literal description of seeing the man again and hiding.
footnote_en: [4] Book has no space between êk and êh-wâpamât .

text_cree: sipwêhtêw êkâ ê-wâpamât.
text_en: She set out when she saw him no longer.
label: literal
rationale: No figurative language; literal description of setting out after losing sight.
footnote_en: [4] Book has no space between êk and êh-wâpamât .

text_cree: otihtam mîkiwâhpa mistahi ê-mihcêniyiki.
text_en: She reached a place where there were many tipis.
label: literal
rationale: No figurative language; literal description of reaching a place with many tipis.
footnote_en: [4] Book has no space between êk and êh-wâpamât .

text_cree: âsay mîna êkota otihtêw ocîmisima.
text_en: This time too she came to where her lover was.
label: literal
rationale: No figurative language; literal statement of arriving where her lover was.
footnote_en: [4] Book has no space between êk and êh-wâpamât .

text_cree: takosiniyiwa êkota owîkimâkana ê-pê-nitonâkot; mâka kotaka nâpêwa papâ-kwâsihik.
text_en: Her husband came there, looking for her; but the other man kept her away from her husband.
label: literal
rationale: No figurative language; literal description of the husband's arrival and the other man's actions.
footnote_en: [4] Book has no space between êk and êh-wâpamât .

text_cree: "êha," itêw; "ê-pê-tapasiyân."
text_en: “No,” she answered her; “I ran away and came here.”
label: literal
rationale: Footnote [5] explains the literal discourse function of 'êha' as a negative agreeing answer, not any figurative usage.
footnote_en: [5] This is the agreeing answer to a yes-or-no question;  if the question, as here, is put negatively, êhag corresponds to our “No.”

text_cree: kêtahtawê âsay mîna ê-âh-ihkihk, mîna kotak ayahciyiniw kâ-âsitêyimât kotaka nâpêwa.
text_en: Another thing which used to happen, was when some Blackfoot became suspicious about another man.
label: literal
rationale: The footnote comments on the phonetic heaviness of 'ây', not on any figurative language; the sentence is a plain statement.
footnote_en: [1] CHECK heaviness of ây

text_cree: acosisa tahkonam awa ayahciyiniw.
text_en: That Blackfoot took some arrows.
label: literal
rationale: Simple literal statement of taking arrows.
footnote_en: [1] NB weird reduplication

text_cree: ê-nakiskawât owîkimâkana êkwa pêyak nâpêsisa ê-wîcêwâyit, nîkân owîkimâkana pa-pî-pimwêw.
text_en: When he encountered his wife and a boy who was with her, first he shot arrow after arrow into his wife.
label: literal
rationale: Contains the reduplicated form 'pa-pî-pimwêw' noted in the footnote, but the expression remains literal.
footnote_en: [1] NB weird reduplication

text_cree: êkwa nâpêsisa mîna, mîna êwakoni pimwêw; nipahêw.
text_en: Then the boy, too, him too he shot; he killed him.
label: literal
rationale: Literal description of shooting and killing.
footnote_en: [1] NB weird reduplication

text_cree: êkwa oskinîkiwa nitonawêw; papâ-têhtapiw sakâhk.
text_en: Then he looked for the young man; he rode about in the woods.
label: literal
rationale: Literal description of searching and riding about.
footnote_en: [1] NB weird reduplication

text_cree: êwako mîna pêyak ayahciyiniw otôtamôwin; maywês ihtakohk wiyasôwêwin êwako kâ-kî-ispayik; mêkwâc paskwâwi-mostoswa ê-ohtâpanihocik ayîsiyiniwak, ayahciyiniwak, mîna pwâsîmowak, sasîwak, kinêpikoyiniwak, kâ-otaskîwikamikowak, nahkawiyiniwak, êwako anima kâ-kî-ihkihk.
text_en: This too was a custom of the Blackfoot; before there was any law was when this took place; when the people were still living on buffalo-flesh, - the Blackfoot and the Assiniboine, the Sarsi, the Snakes, the Earth-Lodge People, the Salteaux, - that was when this took place.
label: literal
rationale: The sentence lists historical facts about the Blackfoot custom and other tribes, with no non-literal expression. Bloomfield's footnote comments on an unidentified tribal name but does not describe any figurative usage.
footnote_en: [2] LB on k-ôtaskîwikamikowak :  I have not been able to identify this tribe.

text_cree: wâhyaw ê-ihtâcik, kîtahtawê pêtisâpahtamwak ê-mâyi-kîsikâyik; sakamo pê-kitoyiwa, kâh-kitoyiwa piyêsiwa.
text_en: When they had gone a long way, at one time they saw a storm coming; unceasingly the Thunderers were coming with repeated noise.
label: literal
rationale: The sentence describes seeing a storm and hearing the Thunderers in literal terms; Bloomfield's footnote does not refer to this sentence.
footnote_en: [1] LB on asê-takosinomakaniyiw :  The sandstorm is viewed as though the Thunderers were presenting themselves backwards; hence solid rain instead of liquid.

text_cree: êkwa kisiwâk ê-pê-mâyi-kîsikâyik, ocistikosiwak.
text_en: When the storm came near, they made a shelter.
label: literal
rationale: The sentence states they made a shelter when the storm approached; no figurative language is indicated, and the footnote does not apply.
footnote_en: [1] LB on asê-takosinomakaniyiw :  The sandstorm is viewed as though the Thunderers were presenting themselves backwards; hence solid rain instead of liquid.

text_cree: apiwak, opâskisikaniwâwa ê-cimatâcik; êkwa akotâwak otakohpiwâwa; êkota pîhcâyihk ayâwak.
text_en: They stayed in one place, fixing their guns upright in the ground; over them they hung their blankets; they stayed underneath there.
label: literal
rationale: The sentence details their actions of fixing guns and hanging blankets; it is a plain description, and the footnote is not relevant.
footnote_en: [1] LB on asê-takosinomakaniyiw :  The sandstorm is viewed as though the Thunderers were presenting themselves backwards; hence solid rain instead of liquid.

text_cree: asê-takosinomakaniyiw, yêkaw pisisik êkotowahk ohci kâ-kimiwaniyik.
text_en: It came backwards; a downpour of sand was the rain.
label: metaphor
rationale: Bloomfield's footnote explains that the sandstorm is metaphorically viewed as the Thunderers presenting themselves backwards, causing solid sand rain instead of liquid rain.
footnote_en: [1] LB on asê-takosinomakaniyiw :  The sandstorm is viewed as though the Thunderers were presenting themselves backwards; hence solid rain instead of liquid.

text_cree: êkosi pasikôwak; sipwêhtêwak âsay mîna.
text_en: Then they arose; they set out again.
label: literal
rationale: The sentence simply states they arose and set out again; there is no figurative language, and the footnote does not apply.
footnote_en: [1] LB on asê-takosinomakaniyiw :  The sandstorm is viewed as though the Thunderers were presenting themselves backwards; hence solid rain instead of liquid.

text_cree: pêyak oskinîkiw: "nitawi-nipa; mîcisôhâhkahk nipahaci."
text_en: One youth was told, “Go kill it; let us eat, when you have killed it.”
label: literal
rationale: Bloomfield's footnote only says to check the word 'micisowahkahk', giving no indication of figurative language. The sentence is a straightforward command to kill something and eat it.
footnote_en: [2] CHECK micisowahkahk

text_cree: êkwa ê-mêkwâ-pimohtêcik kisâstêyiw; nôhtêyâpâkwêwak.
text_en: Then, as they marched along, the weather grew hot; they became thirsty.
label: literal
rationale: The footnote is a textual note about 'eh-mekwac' and does not indicate figurative language. The sentence is literal.
footnote_en: [3] CHECK eh-mekwac - HCW:  REPAIR

text_cree: nama kêkway nipiy kî-miskamwak.
text_en: They could not find any water.
label: literal
rationale: No figurative language detected; the statement is literal.
footnote_en: [3] CHECK eh-mekwac - HCW:  REPAIR

text_cree: êkwa atimwa pêyak wîcêwêwak, omaskisiniwâwa ê-otâpêyit; paskêpahtâw awa atim, ê-nôhtêyâpâkwêt.
text_en: They had a dog with them to carry their moccasins; this dog left the trail in its thirst.
label: literal
rationale: No figurative language detected; the description is literal.
footnote_en: [3] CHECK eh-mekwac - HCW:  REPAIR

text_cree: kîtahtawê ê-itâpicik, kî-minihkwêyiwa.
text_en: Soon when they looked, it had drunk.
label: literal
rationale: No figurative language detected; the statement is literal.
footnote_en: [3] CHECK eh-mekwac - HCW:  REPAIR

text_cree: êkwa kotak nâpêw mâmaskâc êsa kî-miywêyihtam ê-mihkosihot.
text_en: Now, there was another man, the story goes, who greatly liked to wear red clothes.
label: literal
rationale: The footnote is empty, and the sentence is a plain, literal statement about a man who liked red clothes.
footnote_en: [1] LB has a footnote number on nisto-pipon , but no footnote.

text_cree: pêyakwâw ê-wawêsît, mihkosiyiwa opakwahtêhona; êkwa asikanêyâpiy opîhtasinânêyâpîw; êkwa mihkwêkinwêtâsa kikitâsêw; êkwa mihkokwana otastotinihk itamoyiwa.
text_en: Once when he dressed up, his belt was red, and red yarn he had for his ammunition-bag; he wore red flannel breeches; a red feather was on his hat.
label: literal
rationale: The footnote is empty, and the sentence is a literal list of red clothing items.
footnote_en: [1] LB has a footnote number on nisto-pipon , but no footnote.

text_cree: êkwa nisto-pipon isiyîhkâtêwa kayâs ayîsiyiniwak ê-kî-wiyâhtâcik; êkotôwa mîna ê-kikiskahk ê-mâcît.
text_en: And 'three-year' were called some things which the old-time people wore; one of these also he had on, as he hunted.
label: literal
rationale: The footnote marker is on 'nisto-pipon' but no footnote content exists; the term 'three-year' is a literal compound name for certain worn items, not figurative.
footnote_en: [1] LB has a footnote number on nisto-pipon , but no footnote.

text_cree: "ka-kakwêcimik," itêw osîma, "'awîna kâ-mîcisot?' kika-itik." "'wiya awa nisîm,' kika-ititin." "'cî?' ititâni, "êha," kika-itwân." "êkây êkosi wî-itwêyini, ka-nipahitin."
text_en: “He will ask you,” she told her sister, “'Who has been eating here?' he will ask you. 'Why, my sister here,' I will say of you. When I ask you, 'Isn't that so?' you will answer, 'Yes.' If you do not speak thus, I will kill you.”
label: literal
rationale: The footnote discusses the interrogative particle 'cî', which is a grammatical note with no indication of figurative language; the sentence is literal.
footnote_en: [1] LB on cî :  This particle, the regular sign of a yes-or-no question, is not ordinarily used along; one says tâpwê cî?

text_cree: êkwa kêtayôwinisêw oskinîkiw.
text_en: Then the youth took off his clothes.
label: literal
rationale: Plain narration of the youth undressing, with no figurative language.
footnote_en: [1] LB on kakêtihk : Unknown word

text_cree: pîhtokêwak êkwa matotisânihk, pimiy mîna ôma, masko-pimiy.
text_en: Then they entered the sweat-lodge, with that fat, that bear's-grease.
label: literal
rationale: Literal description of entering the sweat-lodge with bear's grease.
footnote_en: [1] LB on kakêtihk : Unknown word

text_cree: akwanahamwân omatotisâniwâw.
text_en: Their companions covered their sweatlodge for them.
label: literal
rationale: Straightforward statement about companions covering the sweatlodge.
footnote_en: [1] LB on kakêtihk : Unknown word

text_cree: êkwa êkosi ê-sîkahasiniyêt kisêyiniw, ê-pôh-pôtâtât oskinîkiwa, piyis namôya ta-ihtakoniyiw ôma kâ-ocikisiyit.
text_en: Thereupon, when the old man poured the fat on the stone, and kept blowing on the youth, at last the pock-marks on his face began to disappear.
label: literal
rationale: Describes ritual actions (pouring fat, blowing) and the gradual disappearance of pock-marks without figurative comparison.
footnote_en: [1] LB on kakêtihk : Unknown word

text_cree: piyis ê-mêstinahk pimiy ôma, mîna kîhtwâm pîhtokatâwân.
text_en: When he had used up that fat, some more was handed in to them.
label: literal
rationale: Narrative of using up the fat and receiving more, no figurative language.
footnote_en: [1] LB on kakêtihk : Unknown word

text_cree: êwako ê-mêstinahk, âsay nama kêkway ihtakoniyiw ocikisiwin.
text_en: When he had used this up, his pock-marks were gone.
label: literal
rationale: States the completion of the process: pock-marks are gone, a literal outcome.
footnote_en: [1] LB on kakêtihk : Unknown word

text_cree: êkwa ê-pâskît, namôya kakêtihk ta-kahkâpêwiw oskinîkiw.
text_en: And when he opened the lodge, whole and without flaw in body was the youth.
label: literal
rationale: Bloomfield's footnote on 'kakêtihk' calls it an unknown word, but the sentence as a whole is a literal description of the youth's healed state; no figurative language is indicated.
footnote_en: [1] LB on kakêtihk : Unknown word

text_cree: otinêw asiniya ê-pakamahwât, ê-nipahât.
text_en: She took a stone and struck it so as to kill it.
label: literal
rationale: Literal description of taking a stone and striking; neither the footnote nor the sentence indicates non-literal language.
footnote_en: [1] LB on êh-otihciyit :  Meaning unknown; probably error.

text_cree: êkosi mistik otinam, ê-itohtêt ê-pakamahwât; nipahêw, kâ-wâpamât tâwayihk oskahtikoyihk otêskana ê-kikamoyit, ê-pêyakoyit.
text_en: Then she took a stick and went up to it and beat it; she killed it; and then she saw that in the middle of its forehead it had a single horn.
label: literal
rationale: Literal narrative of the killing and observation of the horn; no figurative expression present.
footnote_en: [1] LB on êh-otihciyit :  Meaning unknown; probably error.

text_cree: êkwa ê-otihciyit kinêpikwa, tâpiskôc sôniyâw ostikwân êsinâkwaniyik.
text_en: And the serpent's head looked like bright metal.
label: simile
rationale: The footnote concerns the unknown word 'êh-otihciyit' and does not describe figurative language, but the sentence directly contains an explicit comparison with 'tâpiskôc' ('like'), making it a simile.
footnote_en: [1] LB on êh-otihciyit :  Meaning unknown; probably error.

text_cree: namôya wâpamêw tâni iyikohk ê-iskosiyit ôhi kinêpikwa kâ-nipahât.
text_en: She could not see how long this serpent was which she had killed.
label: literal
rationale: Literal statement about not seeing the serpent's length; no figurative language.
footnote_en: [1] LB on êh-otihciyit :  Meaning unknown; probably error.

text_cree: mitoni ê-sôhkêyimot awa iskwêw, kâ-nipahât ôhi kinêpikwa.
text_en: Very brave was this woman, to have slain that serpent.
label: literal
rationale: Literal appraisal of the woman's bravery; no metaphor or idiom.
footnote_en: [1] LB on êh-otihciyit :  Meaning unknown; probably error.

text_cree: êkosi sipwêhtêw, ê-âmaciwêt.
text_en: So she went from there, up the bank.
label: literal
rationale: Plain description of leaving and going up the bank.
footnote_en: [1] LB on êh-otihciyit :  Meaning unknown; probably error.

text_cree: êkota kâ-wâpahtahk ê-misâyik wâti.
text_en: There she saw a great cave.
label: literal
rationale: Simple statement of seeing a cave; no figurative elements.
footnote_en: [1] LB on êh-otihciyit :  Meaning unknown; probably error.

text_cree: ômisi itwêw awa ostêsimâw: "hahâw, nimosô, piyêsiw, 'kîspin kêkway sêkihikoyani, kisiwâk kika-osâpamitin,' kikî-itwân; êwako ohci nama kêkway kâ-ôh-kostamân," itwêw awa ostêsimâw.
text_en: Thus spoke the elder brother: “Now then, 0 my grandfather, Thunderer, 'If by anything you should be frightened, from close by I shall be looking at you,' you said; that is why I fear nothing,” said the elder brother.
label: literal
rationale: The footnote only expresses uncertainty about the word 'osâpamâtn' and does not indicate any figurative language; the sentence is direct speech with no idiom, metaphor, or simile.
footnote_en: [1] CHECK osâpamâtn - HCW unsure

text_cree: "mâka pita wâskahikanihk ka-itohtânânaw, kika-atâwêyahk môsw-asiniya êkwa kaskitêw êkwa ayiwinisa, êkâ kita-isi-nôhtêpayiyahk kêkway, pêyak askiy ka-kakwê-ayâyahk," itêw.
text_en: “But first we shall go to the fort, to buy bullets and powder and clothes, so that we may not run short of anything, as we plan to stay a year,” he told him.
label: literal
rationale: The footnote only suggests a spelling correction and does not describe figurative language; the sentence is a straightforward plan with no non-literal expressions.

text_en: When they spoke, one of those who were sleeping there, heard that it was their fellow-tribesmen speaking, and shouted, saying, “It is we!”

label: simile
rationale: Contains the simile marker 'tâpiskôc' ('as if') in 'as if it saw something'.

text_en: It seemed to him as if it wanted to flee, the way the bear kept looking at him.
label: simile
rationale: The footnote notes a probable transcription error in 'ê-kitâpamikot', but the sentence still uses 'tâpiskôc' ('as if') to express a simile.
footnote_en: [4] LB on êh-kiti-kitâpamikot : -kiti- is probably my error.

footnote_en: [4] LB on êh-kiti-kitâpamikot : -kiti- is probably my error.

label: literal
rationale: Literal description of the bear's movement along the woods.
footnote_en: [4] LB on êh-kiti-kitâpamikot : -kiti- is probably my error.

text_cree: piyis ê-otihtahk mistahi ê-sakâyik, êkota sêskisiyiwa.

label: literal
rationale: Literal statement of the bear entering dense brush.
footnote_en: [4] LB on êh-kiti-kitâpamikot : -kiti- is probably my error.

text_cree: wîsta sêskisiw; piyis ita ê-kaski-sakâyik, êkota kâ-nahapiyit.
text_en: He too went among the trees; finally, where the woods were densest, it sat down.
label: literal
rationale: Literal account of the man entering the woods and the bear sitting down.
footnote_en: [4] LB on êh-kiti-kitâpamikot : -kiti- is probably my error.

text_cree: wîsta êkota nahapiw.

label: literal
rationale: Literal action of the man sitting down.
footnote_en: [4] LB on êh-kiti-kitâpamikot : -kiti- is probably my error.

text_cree: kîtahtawê êkotê kâ-ohtohtêcik tahki âh-itâpiyiwa ôhi wâkayôsa.

label: literal
rationale: Literal description of the bear looking back.
footnote_en: [4] LB on êh-kiti-kitâpamikot : -kiti- is probably my error.

footnote_en: [4] LB on êh-kiti-kitâpamikot : -kiti- is probably my error.

label: literal
rationale: Quoted speech relaying a story; no figurative expression present.
footnote_en: [6] LB on ê-wîh-pôsit : Word avoidance: mihtos “raft”, freely used in Text 36.

footnote_en: [6] LB on ê-wîh-pôsit : Word avoidance: mihtos “raft”, freely used in Text 36.

text_en: When he had finished it, and embarked, and paddled across, as he looked back, just as he was in the middle of the stream, into the water went the bear.
label: literal
rationale: Narrative sequence describing actions; no non-literal language.
footnote_en: [6] LB on ê-wîh-pôsit : Word avoidance: mihtos “raft”, freely used in Text 36.

text_cree: ita ê-kapât, êkota cîki kapâyiwa.
text_en: Close by where he landed, it came ashore.
label: literal
rationale: Literal description of the bear coming ashore.
footnote_en: [6] LB on ê-wîh-pôsit : Word avoidance: mihtos “raft”, freely used in Text 36.

footnote_en: [6] LB on ê-wîh-pôsit : Word avoidance: mihtos “raft”, freely used in Text 36.

label: literal

footnote_en: [6] LB on ê-wîh-pôsit : Word avoidance: mihtos “raft”, freely used in Text 36.

footnote_en: [6] LB on ê-wîh-pôsit : Word avoidance: mihtos “raft”, freely used in Text 36.

text_cree: êkosi êkota tahkohcâyihk namôya wâhyaw kâ-ayâyit ôhi wîstâwa.
text_en: And not far from there, at the top of the bank, was where his brother-in-law lived.
label: literal
rationale: Factual statement about the brother-in-law's location.
footnote_en: [6] LB on ê-wîh-pôsit : Word avoidance: mihtos “raft”, freely used in Text 36.

text_cree: êkwa sakâhk êkota apiw mîna awa wâkayôs.
text_en: He stayed there in the woods, with the bear.
label: literal
rationale: Literal description of staying in the woods with the bear.
footnote_en: [6] LB on ê-wîh-pôsit : Word avoidance: mihtos “raft”, freely used in Text 36.

text_cree: "hâ, nikwêmê, nisâkwêyimon!" "ôki wêmistikôsiw awa kâ-wî-otihtak kika-nipahik." "êkwa mîna nitôtêmak otihtakwâwi, kîskwêwak oskinîkiwak; kika-nipahikwak." "namôya nika-kî-kostikwak oskinîkiwak; kika-nipahikwak." "namôya kinôhtê-tako-wîcêtin," itêw.
text_en: “Oh, Brother, I cannot do that! These people, this Frenchman to whom I am going, will kill you. And when I reach my fellow-tribesmen, the young men are reckless; they will kill you. It is unlikely that I can bring the young men to respect my wishes; they will kill you. I do not want to have you with me when I arrive where the others are,” he told it.
label: literal
rationale: The footnote comments on the conduct of white men compared to reckless Indian adolescents, but it does not point to any figurative language in the Cree text. The text consists of literal statements and a refusal.
footnote_en: [7] LB: In such a matter, the conduct to be expected of a white man is on a level with that of the most reckless Indian adolescent.

rationale: The sentence contains no figurative language; the footnote does not apply to this sentence.

text_en: When, they had eaten, at once his brother-in-law gave him a blanket, a shirt, a pipe, tobacco, and matches, and said to him, “These things here I cannot give you; you would not like them; your sister will sew something into leggings for you,” he told him.
label: literal
rationale: The footnote explains the literal use of 'ômatôwahk' to refer to the items, which is a conventional distinction rather than figurative language.

rationale: The statement that the old man had many wives because he was of manitou nature is a literal description within the story's worldview.
footnote_en: [1] LB on wêmistikôsiwak :  Really “Frenchman”, but the term is often used for “white man” in general; this is here the case, if my understanding of wîcihôwin as “Hudson's Bay Company” is correct.  I have tried to analyze the incidents in this story in _Atti del XXII Congresso degli Americanisti_ (Rome, 1928) II, 23 ff.

text_cree: kostik sakâw-iyinîsa, osâm ê-manitôwit, mêyosiyici iskwêwa, sôskwâc ê-otinât.
text_en: The Bush People feared him because he was of manitou nature: whenever there was a pretty woman, at once he would take her for himself.
label: literal
rationale: The sentence explains why he was feared and his actions toward women; no figurative language is evident.
footnote_en: [1] LB on wêmistikôsiwak :  Really “Frenchman”, but the term is often used for “white man” in general; this is here the case, if my understanding of wîcihôwin as “Hudson's Bay Company” is correct.  I have tried to analyze the incidents in this story in _Atti del XXII Congresso degli Americanisti_ (Rome, 1928) II, 23 ff.

text_cree: êkâ tiyâpwêhtâkoci, sêmâk nipahêw.
text_en: If people resisted him, at once he would kill them.
label: literal
rationale: This is a plain statement that killing immediately followed resistance.
footnote_en: [1] LB on wêmistikôsiwak :  Really “Frenchman”, but the term is often used for “white man” in general; this is here the case, if my understanding of wîcihôwin as “Hudson's Bay Company” is correct.  I have tried to analyze the incidents in this story in _Atti del XXII Congresso degli Americanisti_ (Rome, 1928) II, 23 ff.

text_cree: piyisk êkota ohci kostâw.
text_en: In time thus, he came to be feared.
label: literal
rationale: The sentence concludes that he came to be feared, with no figurative elements.
footnote_en: [1] LB on wêmistikôsiwak :  Really “Frenchman”, but the term is often used for “white man” in general; this is here the case, if my understanding of wîcihôwin as “Hudson's Bay Company” is correct.  I have tried to analyze the incidents in this story in _Atti del XXII Congresso degli Americanisti_ (Rome, 1928) II, 23 ff.

text_cree: "nîsta iskwêw kikî-nihtâwikihik!" "piko wâh-tôtaman kâ-tôtaman!" itêw.
text_en: “You too were born of a woman! It seems that you do anything that comes into your head!” he said to the other.
label: literal
rationale: Bloomfield's footnote suggests a possible slip of the tongue or error of record, not a figurative use; the translation follows the recorded text literally.
footnote_en: [2] The translation follows the text; probably however, the last word is a slip of the tongue or an error of record for ka-tôtên , giving the meaning: “You will do whatever you want,” i.e., “I shall have to take the consequences of interfering with you; I cannot do other than I am doing.”

text_cree: êkwa ômisi itwêw: "haw, sipwêhtêk!" "konita awa tômaskatihkway ka-kostâwâw," itwêw.
text_en: So he said, “Now, go away from here! Like fools you will be fearing this greasy old scab,” he said.
label: simile
rationale: The footnote discusses the cultural interpretation of the white man's words as bravado, not figurative language. The sentence contains the explicit comparison 'Like fools', which is a simile.
footnote_en: [3] LB:  The white man's words are no doubt correctly quoted; but the Indians take them for mere bravado, and assume that the white man shares their fear of the old sorceror.  Else, why does he give him presents?

text_cree: êkoyikohk kâ-kiskisopayit awa mac-ôhôw opawâkana.
text_en: Only then did Bad-Owl remember his dream guardian.
label: literal
rationale: The sentence is a straightforward narrative statement with no figurative language; the footnote describes a different context not relevant to this sentence.
footnote_en: [4] A pair of moose is the Bony Spectre's characteristic gift.

text_cree: piyisk misiwê wâpatonisk astêw.
text_en: Then he put the white clay all over his body.
label: literal
rationale: The footnote discusses kinship terms and does not describe any figurative usage; the sentence is a plain statement of action.
footnote_en: [1] LB:  “Their son”: father's brother and mother's sister use the terms, “my son” and “my daughter” more often than the specific nikosim , nitôsim ; the distinction between these is unknown to me; Lacombe's statement (Dict. 669f.) is confused.

text_cree: âta ê-âhkosiyit okosisiwâwa, otinêw, ê-wayawîhtahât awa oskinîkiw.
text_en: Although their son was ill, the youth took him up, and carried him out of the tent.
label: literal
rationale: The footnote does not apply; this is a straightforward narrative of taking up an ill son.
footnote_en: [1] LB:  “Their son”: father's brother and mother's sister use the terms, “my son” and “my daughter” more often than the specific nikosim , nitôsim ; the distinction between these is unknown to me; Lacombe's statement (Dict. 669f.) is confused.

text_cree: ê-pîhtokahât ôhi awâsisa, miyw-âyâyiwa.
text_en: When he brought the child in again, he was well.
label: literal
rationale: The footnote is irrelevant; the sentence literally describes the child being brought back and being well.
footnote_en: [1] LB:  “Their son”: father's brother and mother's sister use the terms, “my son” and “my daughter” more often than the specific nikosim , nitôsim ; the distinction between these is unknown to me; Lacombe's statement (Dict. 669f.) is confused.

text_cree: êkosi kîtahtawê wîwiw; tâpiskôc wîwiwak ostêsa.
text_en: Then, in the course of time, he took a wife; he took his wife from the same family as had his elder brother.
label: simile
rationale: Bloomfield's footnote gives a literal translation 'they had wives in the same way' and notes the text's interpretation is a surmise, pointing to figurative language; the Cree uses the simile marker 'tâpiskôc' ('like'), making this a simile.
footnote_en: [2] LB:  Literally, “they had wives in the same way”; the interpretation in the text is a surmise.

text_cree: "hây, nitawâsimisak kî-nîpawîstâtowak." "âta nôton, 'êkâ wiya êkotôwahk iyinito-ayisiyiniw ohtin iskwêw,' nikî-itâw awa nikosis; "manitôwiwak iyini-ayisiyiniw," nikî-itâw mâna, wiyîhtamawaki kêkway, âhci piko kâ-tôtahk, kâ-katâc ê-onâpêmiyit kâ-maskahtwêt awa nikakêpâtisîm, êkâ ê-tâpwêhtawit." "- nikosis, êkosi awa ê-tâpwêt, awa kikosâk kâ-isi-wîhtamâsk." "kapê-tipisk ka-nikamohitinân, tânisi ta-tôtaman." "kiyâm niya kitimâkihtawin." "mistahi nisâkihtânân nipâskisikaninâna." "êwako awa ostêsimâw kiciwâm ninahihtâk;" "tânisi ê-itak tôtam, awa kikosâk ê-kakêpâtisit, kâ-nitawi-kimotamâsk kiwîkimâkana." "êkosi anihi ê-tâpwêt, ôma kâ-itisk."
text_en: “Alas, my children have stood facing each other! Although often, 'Do not take a woman of the common, mortal men,' I said to my son; 'Of manitou nature are real men,' though I told him more than once, when I instructed him, yet none the less he did so, robbing, as if none other would serve, one who had a husband, this stubborn fool of mine, who does not heed my words. - My son, even thus he speaks true, this thy fellow-husband, in what he has told thee. All night we will teach thee songs and how to do. Pray, hear me with pity. We greatly prize our guns. This one here, your kinsman now, obeys my word; as I tell him, he does, while he, your fellow-husband is foolish and stubborn, and thus has gone and stolen your wife from you. But in this he spoke true which he told you.”
label: idiom
rationale: Footnote [3] indicates that 'kî-nîpawîstâtowak' has a literal meaning of 'they have stood in relation to each other, by each other' but an unknown actual meaning, suggesting it is a conventional non-literal expression (idiom).
footnote_en:
[3] LB:  Literally, “they have stood in relation to each other, by each other”, but the actual meaning is unknown to me.
[4] LB on nôton :  Unknown word.
[6] LB on kiciwâm :  Thus it appears that niciwâm : “my brother (man speaking(” has, among its many uses that of “my fellow-husband's brother.”

text_cree: "pêyakotipiskwa piko ôta nika-ayânân; wâpahki nika-kîwânân awa kistim."
text_en: “One night only we shall stay here; tomorrow your daughter-in-law here and I shall go home.”
label: literal
rationale: The footnote explains the morphological division of 'pêyakotipiskwa', not figurative language; the sentence is straightforwardly literal.
footnote_en: [7] LB on pêyakotipiskwa :  Not to be divided by hyphen; -tipiskwa (particle) and -tipiskwê- (verb) are the non-initial (suffixal) forms corresponding to tipisk and tipiskwâw .  Similarly, kîsikâw : “it is day” has the odd non-initial verb-forming suffix -kîsihkwê- .

text_cree: êkosi osîhtâwân têsipicikan.
text_en: Accordingly a scaffold was built for him.
label: literal
rationale: The sentence describes the construction of a scaffold in plain, non-figurative language; the footnote does not concern this sentence.
footnote_en: [8] LB on kâ-matwêwêyit :  If correctly recorded, an animate form, my impression is, however, that -wêwê- : “noise” forms only inanimate verbs; if so, we should read matwêwêyik .

text_cree: êkwa ê-tipiskâyik, êkotê itohtahâw awa iskwêw kâ-âhkosit.
text_en: Then, at nightfall, the sick woman was taken there.
label: literal
rationale: This is a straightforward statement about taking the sick woman at nightfall, with no figurative elements; the footnote is not relevant here.
footnote_en: [8] LB on kâ-matwêwêyit :  If correctly recorded, an animate form, my impression is, however, that -wêwê- : “noise” forms only inanimate verbs; if so, we should read matwêwêyik .

text_cree: ê-kîwêcik, namwâc cêskwa otihtam awa wîkiwâw, awa oskinîkiw, awa mîna ostêsimâw, âsay ita wîtimwa kâ-akociniyit, êkota âsay kâ-matwêwêyik, ê-sâkowêwiht.
text_en: When they went back home, that youth with his elder brother had not yet reached their dwelling-place, when already, from where the latter's sister-in-law lay high on the scaffold, there came the report of a gun, and they heard shouting.
label: literal
rationale: The sentence narrates events literally; the footnote comments on a possible grammatical mis-recording of 'kâ-matwêwêyit' but does not indicate any figurative language.
footnote_en: [8] LB on kâ-matwêwêyit :  If correctly recorded, an animate form, my impression is, however, that -wêwê- : “noise” forms only inanimate verbs; if so, we should read matwêwêyik .

text_cree: "hâw, kotokwaskisin, nîswâw kêtisk ayîsiyinîwiwin kôtahon ôta ohci." "âsay niyânanwâw kêtisk ayîsiyiniwak pê-ayâwak ôta askîhk." "êkosi nîswâw kâ-itwêyân." "awa nakatamani askiy, kotak âniskê kita-ayisiyinîwiw." "êwako nipahikêhkâci: kotak mîna êkota ohci kita-ayisiyinîwiw."
text_en: “There, Crooked-Moccasin, twice a full span of human life you have here won from me. Already five times the full span have mortal men so far stayed on this earth. Thus it is that I say twice. When you in your present person leave the earth, another will take up mortal life where you leave off. When he dies of old age, still another will from that point on live a human life.”
label: literal
rationale: The footnote discusses the particle 'kêtisk' and notes uncertainty in translation, but does not describe any figurative language; the passage describes lifespans in literal terms.
footnote_en: [1] LB on kêtisk :  On the meaning of this particle (given by Lacombe as “juste ce qu'il faut”) hinges the whole passage.  It is not made clearer by the explanation at the end of the text.  In both places, my translation is guess-work.

text_cree: "ôma mîna pêyak ê-otahoyan, miyêtawêyini kita-âpacihtâyan." "namôya wiya ayîsiyiniw ka-kakwê-kitimahâw, têpiyâhk êkâ kêkway ta-mêskoskaman, kînikâw ohtiskawinamâski ana kê-wîci-mêtawêmat." "êkwa ôma nipâskisikan." "awa kêtiskâwi-kêtiski-ayisiyinîwit, âpihtaw âpihtâwi-ayisiyinîwici êwako awa, kiyi-otihtikoyêk wêmistikôsiw." "êwako awa kita-wâpamêw ta-mihcêtiyit wêmistikôsiwa." "êkospî ôma kika-âpacihtân."
text_en: “Here is another thing which you have won from me, to use when you engage in contests. You will not, indeed, try to destroy people, but, only so that you need fear nothing, if he draw a sharp weapon against you, with whom you are playing. And here is my gun. When he who lives the full span of mortal life is halfway through his human course, then the Frenchman will come to where you are. He will see the Frenchmen grow many. At that time you will use this thing.”
label: literal
rationale: The sentence is a straightforward statement about an object to be used in contests, with no figurative language.
footnote_en: [2] LB on ta-mêskoskaman :  Another word I do not know; perhaps wrongly recorded.  I translate as though it read ta-kostaman : “that thou fear it.”

text_cree: "nanâtohk kita-isi-mêtawêw; êkota kîsta kika-âpacihtân." "êkwa kîwêyani, ôta ohci ka-kîwân." "kâ-wîkiyan âstamita kâ-sakâk, kotak âscam-itahîs apisîs sakâsin." "êkota kika-ohtinên kita-asamiyan." "êkota ayâwak môswak; êyakonik kimiyitin." "osâm mistahi kikitimâkisin; kikitimâkisinâwâw kâ-ayisiyinîwiyêk." "pimiy asamîhkan," itik ôhi pâkahkosa; "hâ, ôma ita kîwêhtatâ nipâskisikan; ayisk k-ôtahon."
text_en: “He will play all kinds of games; that is where you too will use it. Now, when you go home, go directly home from here. In the wood that is this side of where you dwell, a bit to this side is a small clump of trees. From there you will get that with which to feed me. In that place are moose; I give them to you. You are too pitiable; you all are too pitiable who are mortal men. Give me an offering of fat,” the Bony Spectre told him; “And yes, take home this gun of mine; for you have won it from me.”
label: literal
rationale: Literal instruction about playing games and using something; no figurative language.
footnote_en: [3] LB on sakâsin :  Probably for sakâsiw .

text_cree: êwako âcimowin kayâs.
text_en: This is an ancient tale.
label: literal
rationale: The sentence states plainly that the tale is ancient; no figurative language is present, and the footnote provides no relevant information.

text_cree: êwako kisêyiniw nipahikêhkâw.
text_en: This old man died of age.
label: literal
rationale: The sentence literally reports the old man's death of old age; no metaphor or idiom is involved, and the footnote says nothing about it.

text_cree: êkota, ôma niya, kisêyinîwici ayîsiyiniw, êwako pêyak kêtisk ayisiyiniw; kotak ta-nihtâwikiw.
text_en: Here, when even as I, a man grows old, that is one full span of life; another will be born.
label: literal
rationale: The description of a full span of life and the birth of another is straightforward, with no indication of figurative language; the footnote offers no commentary.

text_cree: êkoyikohk isko kêtisk ayisiyiniwiwin; nama êskwa ihtâw êwako.
text_en: So long is a full span of life; not yet does he exist.
label: literal
rationale: The statement about the length of a full span of life is literal; the footnote is void and does not suggest any non-literal reading.

text_cree: kêyâpic kinwêsk kitayân askiy; kêyâpic nama mayaw ta-pêkopayiw.
text_en: Still for a long time the earth will be; not yet for a while will it go to pieces.
label: literal
rationale: Although 'go to pieces' could be read idiomatically in English, the Cree is taken literally as the earth physically breaking apart; no figurative language is indicated, and the footnote is silent.

text_cree: nika-kakwêcihkêmon pita," itwêyiwa; "ê, kikitimâkêyimitin mâka, nikosis, piko ta-atâwêyân," itêw.
text_en: Let me first inquire,” said his father; “But I love and cherish you, my son, and there is nothing for me to do but buy her,” he told him.
label: literal
rationale: Bloomfield's footnote on t-âtâwêyân discusses the semantic range of atâwêw ('trades') and expresses uncertainty about the translation 'buy her', but it does not indicate any figurative language; the sentence is a literal statement of the father's intention to trade/buy.
footnote_en: [1] LB on t-âtâwêyân : The word is atâwêw : “he trades (especially furs against White Man's products)”; I do not know whether it can bear the meaning I have given in the translation, or how else it may fit here.

text_cree: ê-pîhtokêyit, ômisi itêw, ê-kîsi-mîcisocik: "hâw, nitôtêm, kâ-ôh-natomitân, pêyak oskinîkiskwêw ê-akâwâtamâtân." "nisto êtokê kitayâwâwak oskinîkiskwêwak," itêw; "niyanân wiya ôtê paskwâhk kâ-ayâwâyâhk,- êkoyikohk miyo-atimêw mostoswa, iyikohk ê-ispisît,- êwako kimiyitin, miyiyini kitânis." "namôya niya ê-wî-wîcêwak, nikosis ê-wî-wîcêwât." "namôya apiw; kî-wayawîw." "mâka ê-nôhtê-wîcêwât, 'mahti kakwêcim,' kâ-ôh-isit," itêw.
text_en: When the latter came to the tent, he spoke thus to him, after they had eaten: “Now, Fellow-Tribesman, the reason I have invited you is because I want one of the young women. It appears that you have three young women,” he said to him; “That creature which we have here in the Plains Country, - then does he well pursue the buffalo, when he has his growth, - such a one I give you, if you give me your daughter. It is not I that wish to consort with her, but my son wishes to consort with her. He is not here; he has gone out. But, wishing to be married to her, 'Do ask him,' he has said to me,” he told him.
label: idiom
rationale: Bloomfield's footnote describes a circumlocution for 'horse', which is a conventional non-literal expression indicating an idiom.
footnote_en: [2] LB on êwako :  He makes a circumlocution, instead of using the word “horse.”  This may be the same word-avoidance as that which I met; the old man is talking, if not to a foreigner, at least to a member of a different branch of the Cree tribe, of a markedly different dialect.

text_cree: "yahô, nitôtêm, niya ani wiya nika-miywêyihtên, paskwâw-iyiniw tita-otêmiyân." "tâpwê mâka niyanân itê kâ-otaskiyâhk ma-manêpayiwak misatimwak," itêw; "namôya anohc nânitaw ka-kî-ititin, nitôtêm." "wiya tipêyimêw otawâsimisa ninôtokwêm; wiya kî-âyimihik ê-wî-ohpikihât," itêw; "mahti kiyi-itêyihtahk; nika-wîhtamawâw," itêw.
text_en: “Hoho, Fellow-Tribesman, as for me, I shall be glad to have an animal like the Plains Cree. Truly there where we others dwell, there is a lack of horses,” he told him; “I cannot at this time tell you anything, Fellow-Tribesman. It is my wife who has decision over her children; it is to her they gave trouble when she labored to bring them up,” he told him; “Let us see what she thinks; I shall tell her of this,” he told him.
label: literal
rationale: The footnote discusses a possible error in the word 'tita-otêmiyân' and suggests it should mean 'to have a Plains Cree in my family'; this is a literal statement, not figurative language.
footnote_en: [3] LB on tit-ôtêmiyân :  The word here is otêmiw : “he has a horse, dog, or other familiar animal”.  Probably the form in the text is an error of speech or record for tit-otôtêmiyân , from otôtêmiw : “he has a kinsman,” and the sentence should be translated, “to have a Plains Cree in my family.” Cf. the next note.

text_cree: "nâh, êkosi mâna mâka kê-mêkiyahk!" "wiyâyêpac wiya otôtêmiyahk!" itwêw awa nôtokêsiw.
text_en: “Goodness, do let us give her, then! We ought to be glad to have him in our family!” said the old woman.
label: literal
rationale: The footnote comments on 'otôtêmiyahk' as a possible error for 'otêmiyahk' or 'tit-ôtêmiyahk', meaning 'to have such an animal', which is a literal expression; no figurative language is indicated.
footnote_en: [4] LB on otôtêmiyahk :  Perhaps the reverse of the preceding error, for otêmiyahk or tit-ôtêmiyahk : “to have such an animal”.

text_cree: êkosi êkwa êkota ayâwak, iyikohk ê-mâwacîhitocik, ê-mihcêtisicik, nanâtohk ê-âh-isi-wîhkohtocik, mîna ê-nîmihitocik.
text_en: So there they stayed, when the band had assembled in great number, inviting one another to all manner of feasts, and dancing religious dances.
label: literal
rationale: The footnote [5] concerns a textual variant of a word, not figurative language. The sentence describes actions literally.
footnote_en: [5] CHECK wîhkayimik - ? cîhkêyimik  PROBABLY

text_cree: wiya oskinîkiw kîtahtawê pêyak cîhkêyimik oskinîkiwa, pisisik ê-kiyokâkot.
text_en: In time a certain other young man became fond of this youth and constantly visited him.
label: literal
rationale: The footnote does not indicate figurative language; the sentence is a straightforward statement about a young man's behavior.
footnote_en: [5] CHECK wîhkayimik - ? cîhkêyimik  PROBABLY

text_cree: mâka ôhi wîtimwa tahki mawinêhok, ê-pakêsêcik.
text_en: His sisters-in-law kept bothering him to play the cup-game with them.
label: literal
rationale: No figurative language is noted; the sentence literally reports the sisters-in-law's bothering.
footnote_en: [5] CHECK wîhkayimik - ? cîhkêyimik  PROBABLY

text_cree: ayis namôya mâcîwak: ôma ê-otami-wa-wîhkohtowiht.
text_en: For they did no hunting, but were busy with feasting one another.
label: literal
rationale: The clause is a plain explanation: they did not hunt but feasted. No figurative expression.
footnote_en: [5] CHECK wîhkayimik - ? cîhkêyimik  PROBABLY

text_cree: piyisk awa oskinîkiw kâ-ôh-kâ-ka-kiyokêt, êwako mîna kiskêyihtam ê-mêtawêt, piyisk ê-wîhtamawât kotaka oskinîkiwa ê-ayât awa paskwâw-iyiniw pakêsêwiyâkan.
text_en: After a time that young man who kept visiting them had, he too, learned the game, and in time told the other young men that the Plains Cree had a bowl for the cup-game.
label: literal
rationale: Although the footnote is attached to this sentence, it only questions a word form (cîhkêyimik), not figurative usage. The content is literal.
footnote_en: [5] CHECK wîhkayimik - ? cîhkêyimik  PROBABLY

text_cree: kîtahtawê mâna pîhtokêyiwa oskinîkiwa, ê-wî-kiskinawâpahtamiyit ôma omêtawêwin, ê-kiskinôhamawât; piyisk kiskêyihtamiyiwa; piyis mâna nitomâw êkotê ê-mêtawêcik, ê-kiskinôhamawât oskinîkiwa; piyisk kâ-kapê-kîsik mêtawêw, nêtê kâ-kîsi-miywêyihtahk pisisik kâ-kî-mêtawêt.
text_en: Presently some young man would always be coming into the tipi, to learn that game of his by looking on, and he would teach it to him; in time the other would learn it; in time he would be invited to come where they were playing and teach it to the young men; presently he was playing all day and every day, with the same addiction that had kept him always a-playing in his home off yonder.
label: literal
rationale: The description of learning and teaching the game is literal; 'addiction' translates a Cree term for pleasure/enjoyment without non-literal meaning.
footnote_en: [5] CHECK wîhkayimik - ? cîhkêyimik  PROBABLY

text_cree: êkosi êkwa tôtam, pisisik ê-mêtawêt.
text_en: That was what he did, he played all the time.
label: literal
rationale: The closing summary is a literal statement of his constant playing.
footnote_en: [5] CHECK wîhkayimik - ? cîhkêyimik  PROBABLY

text_cree: "piciwân êkwa wîkiwâw paskwâw-iyiniw," itâw.
text_en: “The Plains Cree's people are moving their camp,” he was told.
label: literal
rationale: The footnote only flags 'piciwânan' as weird, without indicating any figurative meaning; the sentence is a literal statement about moving camp.
footnote_en: [6] CHECK piciwânan WEIRD

text_cree: "êhêhêy haha" itwêyiwa ôhi sakâw-iyiniwa; "nitôtêm, âyimisiw ana; namôya ani okisêwâtisiwiniw." "kîspin kêkway kâ-kisiwâhikot, âyimisiw." "namôya kisêwâtotam kîkwaya." "âsay ani ê-kisiwâhat, êkâ kâ-ôh-pê-wîhtamâkawiyan ê-wî-picit." "sôskwâc, kîspin kêkway kikiskêyihtên, kakwê-âhkamêyimo." "manitôwiw ani!" itik ôhi nâpêwa.
text_en: “Dear me!” said that Bush Cree; “Fellow-Tribesman, he is a dangerous person; he has no kindliness at all. If anything angers him, he is dangerous. He has no kindliness toward anything. You have already incurred his displeasure: that is why you were not sent the message that he is about to break camp. Without delay, if you have any knowledge beyond the common, try to gather your energies. He is a manitou person, I tell you!” that man said to him.
label: literal
rationale: The footnote only discusses a textual variant reading; the sentence contains no explicit figurative language and is interpreted literally.
footnote_en: [7] LB on oh-pih-wîhtamâkawiyin :  Probably read k-ôh-pêh-

text_cree: "êhâ, êkosi ana kê-nipahit kôhtâwiy!
text_en: “Oh, if that is so, then your father will kill me!
label: literal
rationale: The sentence is a plain statement expressing a condition with no figurative language; the footnote discusses a later phrase and does not apply here.
footnote_en: [8] LB on namoya :  The normal combination is nama kêkway : “nothing”; here the more general negative namoya is used, probably because kêkway kiskêyihtam : “he knows something” has here the specialized sense of “he has mystic knowledge.”

text_cree: namôya kêkway nikiskêyihtên," itêw.
text_en: I have no mystic knowledge,” he told her.
label: idiom
rationale: The footnote explains that 'kêkway kiskêyihtam' has a specialized non-literal sense 'he has mystic knowledge', making it a conventional idiom.
footnote_en: [8] LB on namoya :  The normal combination is nama kêkway : “nothing”; here the more general negative namoya is used, probably because kêkway kiskêyihtam : “he knows something” has here the specialized sense of “he has mystic knowledge.”

text_cree: êkosi kiyipa mîna âsay kâ-pê-matwêwêyik, ê-pê-sâkowêyit.
text_en: Then quickly again came the report of a shot, as that person came a-whooping.
label: literal
rationale: The footnote only says 'CHECK - add verb HCW' and does not describe figurative language. The sentence describes a shot report and whooping literally.
footnote_en: [9] CHECK - add verb HCW

text_en: But a wind blew; as that one arrived, he blew the flame into a leaping flare, striking it as with a gust of wind.
label: literal
rationale: The footnote does not mention figurative language. The Cree describes the wind and blowing literally; the English 'as with a gust of wind' is a translator's addition, not an explicit simile in the source.
footnote_en: [9] CHECK - add verb HCW

text_cree: êyiwêhk ê-itâpit, akâmiskotêw mihti ê-astêyik, êkota kî-apiyiwa ayîsiyiniwa, mitoni ê-kawâhkatosoyit, wîstêpahkwaya ê-wiyâhtamiyit.
text_en: When the youth at last looked, across the fire, where lay a log of firewood, there sat a man, very lean and clad in bits of smoky leather.
label: literal
rationale: Footnote not about figurative language. The sentence is a literal description of a man sitting by the fire.
footnote_en: [9] CHECK - add verb HCW
