text_en: As he looked upon him, the other did not move his eyes from him.
label: literal
rationale: Footnote not about figurative language. The sentence literally describes mutual looking.
footnote_en: [9] CHECK - add verb HCW

text_cree: "êhê êy, ha ha, nôsisê!
text_en: “Alas, alas, my grandchild!
label: literal
rationale: The footnote comments on 'âhcih', not present in this sentence; the exclamation contains no figurative language.
footnote_en: [10] LB on âhcih : âhcih : “from one place to another; continuing, in spite”; probably read ohci : “thence, therefore, by means of that.”

text_cree: âta ani nîsta nikî-kitimâkêyimâw, tâpwê ana ê-kitimâkêyihtâkosit, mâka pêyak kêkway nikî-mihtawamâw, ôma kâ-tôtâsk âhci." "namôya kika-nipin; âta wiya, 'ninipin,' kitêyihtên." "mâka kika-papâ-wa-wîcêtin." "pimiya kika-omîciwininânaw, êkotôwahk anihi ê-omîciwiniyân," itik; êkwa, "hâ, nôsisê, kakwê-waniskâ!
text_en: The fact is, to be sure, that I have blessed him, for truly he was in a piteous state, but one thing I regret having given him, that with which he is doing this to you. You will not die; even though, 'I shall die,' is your thought. But you will go about with me.
label: literal
rationale: The footnote glosses 'âhcih' as 'from one place to another; continuing, in spite' but identifies no figurative language; the sentence is literal speech with no metaphor, simile, or idiom.
footnote_en: [10] LB on âhcih : âhcih : “from one place to another; continuing, in spite”; probably read ohci : “thence, therefore, by means of that.”

text_cree: êkwa nâha kisêyiniw miywêyihtam, "ê-nipahâhkatosot ninahâhkisîm," ê-itêyihtahk. êkwa awa oskinîkiskwêw namôya mâna wî-mîcisôw, ê-ati-asamiht; piyis mâna tâpwêhtawêw ôhtâwiya, ê-kâ-kakwê-sîhkimikot.
text_en: Then that old man off yonder rejoiced, thinking, “My son-in-law has starved to death.” And that young woman was always unwilling to eat, when she was given food; but in the end she always obeyed her father, who kept urging her.
label: literal
rationale: The footnote only notes a likely typo in 'tâpwêhtawêw'; no figurative language is described. The sentence is literal (rejoicing, obedience, urging).
footnote_en: [11] tâpwêhtawêw probably typo

text_cree: mistahi kwatakihtâw, pisisik ê-mâtot, ê-sâkihât onâpêma, tahki ê-sîhkimiht, kwayask ta-mîcisot, mâka mayaw ohpimê kâ-itohtêt, âsay ê-mâtot.
text_en: She was very unhappy, weeping all the time, for love of her husband, as she was being constantly urged to eat well; but as soon as she could go off alone, already she was in tears.
label: literal
rationale: No footnote applies; the sentence conveys literal emotional states and actions (unhappy, weeping, love, urged, alone, tears).
footnote_en: [11] tâpwêhtawêw probably typo

text_cree: otakohpiwâwa pimiwitâwak, ayis ê-wî-katikonicik.
text_en: They took their blankets with them, for they were going to stay out all night.
label: literal
rationale: Straightforward action described plainly without metaphor, simile, or idiom.
footnote_en: [12] LB on kâ-pêh-sâkôwêwiht :  Probably read kâ-pêh-sâkôwêyit : “the other came a-whooping.”

text_cree: êkwa kîtahtawê ê-pa-pimohtêcik, mâtâhêwak wâwâskêsiwa.
text_en: Presently, as they walked along, they came upon the track of an elk.
label: literal
rationale: Literal description of finding animal tracks; no figurative language.
footnote_en: [12] LB on kâ-pêh-sâkôwêwiht :  Probably read kâ-pêh-sâkôwêyit : “the other came a-whooping.”

text_cree: êwakoni ma-mitihtêwak.
text_en: They followed its trail.
label: literal
rationale: Plainly states they followed the trail; non-figurative.
footnote_en: [12] LB on kâ-pêh-sâkôwêwiht :  Probably read kâ-pêh-sâkôwêyit : “the other came a-whooping.”

text_cree: iyikohk ê-otâkosik, êkoyikohk wâpamêwak.
text_en: Toward evening they came in sight of it.
label: literal
rationale: Literal temporal and visual detail; 'came in sight of it' is ordinary language.
footnote_en: [12] LB on kâ-pêh-sâkôwêwiht :  Probably read kâ-pêh-sâkôwêyit : “the other came a-whooping.”

text_cree: êkwa êkota pânahikêwak, ê-wî-kotawêcik, "wâpahki itâp ka-kîwânânaw," ê-itwêcik ôki oskinîkiwak.
text_en: Right where they were, they cleared away the snow, to make a fire for “Tomorrow we shall go home,” said those youths.
label: literal
rationale: Describes actions of clearing snow and making a fire, with no figurative element.
footnote_en: [12] LB on kâ-pêh-sâkôwêwiht :  Probably read kâ-pêh-sâkôwêyit : “the other came a-whooping.”

text_cree: tâpwê ê-kî-kotawêcik, ê-nawacîcik, êkosi ati-ta-tipiskâyiw.
text_en: When then they had built their fire and were making their roasts, night came on.
label: literal
rationale: Narrative of fire-building and nightfall; straightforward and literal.
footnote_en: [12] LB on kâ-pêh-sâkôwêwiht :  Probably read kâ-pêh-sâkôwêyit : “the other came a-whooping.”

text_cree: êkwa mistahi nikohtêwak, êkâ ta-kawacicik, ê-itêyihtahkik.
text_en: Then they prepared a great amount of firewood, so as not to suffer from the cold.
label: literal
rationale: Literal account of gathering firewood to avoid cold; no non-literal expression.
footnote_en: [12] LB on kâ-pêh-sâkôwêwiht :  Probably read kâ-pêh-sâkôwêyit : “the other came a-whooping.”

text_cree: piyisk pa-pimisinwak; namôya ê-wî-nipâcik.
text_en: In due time they lay down; but they did not mean to sleep.
label: literal
rationale: Describes lying down without intent to sleep; plain, non-figurative.
footnote_en: [12] LB on kâ-pêh-sâkôwêwiht :  Probably read kâ-pêh-sâkôwêyit : “the other came a-whooping.”

text_cree: kîtahtawê kêkway kâ-pêhtahkik ê-pê-matwêwêyik, kâ-pê-sâkôwêwiht.
text_en: Presently they heard the report of a gun and someone coming a-whooping.
label: literal
rationale: The footnote concerns a textual variant of 'kâ-pê-sâkôwêwiht' but does not indicate figurative language; 'a-whooping' is a literal description of a sound.
footnote_en: [12] LB on kâ-pêh-sâkôwêwiht :  Probably read kâ-pêh-sâkôwêyit : “the other came a-whooping.”

text_cree: pita ta-mâsihkêw!" "pisisik mâna kâ-âcimihcik êkosi ê-wî-tôtahkik, ôma kâ-wî-tôtâsk!" itêw osîma.
text_en: Let us give him a fight! That which they are said always to be wanting to do, he is now about to do to you!” he told his brother.
label: literal
rationale: The footnote discusses 'bony spectres' which is not present; the sentence is a literal call to fight and a statement about expected actions.
footnote_en: [13] LB:  I do not know what the bony spectres do, beyond wrestling.

text_cree: "hâh, nisîm, êkâya pakitinâtân!" "iyây-ihkinokwê, awa pâkahkos kâ-kanawêyihtahk kîscâsinawa opakêsêwiyâkan!" itêwak.
text_en: “Come, Brother, let us not lose hold of him! What strange thing may it be, that this bony spectre is possessed of our cousin's gaming-bowl!” they said of it.
label: literal
rationale: Bloomfield's footnote discusses the grammatical form of 'iyây' and makes no mention of figurative language; the sentence is a straightforward statement without idiom, metaphor, or simile.
footnote_en: [14] CHECK iyây (IC of heavy reduplication?) YUP and (VII) dubitative.

text_cree: tâpwê nitawi-sîhkimêw ôhtâwiya.
text_en: So he went to make the request of his father.
label: literal
rationale: The sentence is plain literal description of an action. The footnote discusses a morphological variant in sentence 3, not figurative language, so it does not apply here.
footnote_en: [15] LB on oscâsiwâwa :  The normal form is wîstsâsiwâwa , but cf., a few lines below, ostâsah for wîstâsah ; perhaps a neologism.

text_cree: tâpwê pakâhtâw maskihkiya awa kisêyiniw.
text_en: Accordingly, the old man set the medicines to boil.
label: literal
rationale: The sentence literally describes the old man boiling medicines. The footnote does not mention this sentence or any figurative language.
footnote_en: [15] LB on oscâsiwâwa :  The normal form is wîstsâsiwâwa , but cf., a few lines below, ostâsah for wîstâsah ; perhaps a neologism.

text_cree: ê-kîsihtât, êwako ôma ohci mîna ê-minahâcik wîscâsiwâwa, êkosi tâpwê pimâtisiyiwa.
text_en: When he had finished this, again, they gave to their cousin to drink, and now truly he lived.
label: literal
rationale: The sentence literally states that they gave the cousin a drink and he lived. The footnote notes a variant form of 'wîscâsiwâwa' but does not describe any figurative language.
footnote_en: [15] LB on oscâsiwâwa :  The normal form is wîstsâsiwâwa , but cf., a few lines below, ostâsah for wîstâsah ; perhaps a neologism.

text_cree: êkwa asamêwak, êkwa wîstawâw ê-mîcisocik.
text_en: Then they gave him food, and they, too, ate.
label: literal
rationale: The sentence literally describes giving food and eating. No figurative expression is present, and the footnote is not concerned with this sentence.
footnote_en: [15] LB on oscâsiwâwa :  The normal form is wîstsâsiwâwa , but cf., a few lines below, ostâsah for wîstâsah ; perhaps a neologism.

text_cree: "nîscâs, niwâpamânân nitawêmânân." "kêyâpic namôya nânapâcihow." "tâpwê êsa kikî-mihtâtik." "mayaw ê-nisitawêyimikoyâhk sêmâk pahpahkikawâpiw," itêw.
text_en: “Cousin, we have seen our kinswoman. Even now she wears no finery. It seems that truly she has been grieving for you. As soon as she recognized us, she shed tears,” he told him.
label: literal
rationale: The footnote discusses the kinship term 'nitawêmânân' but does not suggest figurative language; the statement is literal.
footnote_en: [16] LB on ntawêmânân : nitawêmâw : “my sister (man speaking); my brother (woman speaking)” is widely used between persons of the opposite sex; whether the use here, in the sense of “my cross-cousin's wife (man speaking)” is specialized or not, I cannot say.

text_cree: âsay mîna namôya mîcisôw ê-âpihtâ-kîsikâyik.
text_en: At noon again he did not eat.
label: literal
rationale: The footnote is about punctuation, not figurative language, and the sentence is a plain literal statement.
footnote_en: [1] No period in book.

text_cree: piyisk ê-tipiskâyik namôya mîcisôw.
text_en: Then, in the evening, he did not eat.
label: literal
rationale: The footnote is about punctuation, not figurative language, and the sentence is a plain literal statement.
footnote_en: [1] No period in book.

text_cree: êkwa mistahi pakwâtam awa iskwêw ê-wâpaniyik mîna ê-asamât, namôya wî-mîcisoyiwa.
text_en: The woman greatly disliked this. In the morning, when again she gave him food, he would not eat.
label: literal
rationale: The footnote is about punctuation, not figurative language, and the sentence is a plain literal statement.
footnote_en: [1] No period in book.

text_cree: piyisk mîna tipiskâyiw, êkâ ê-wî-mîcisot.
text_en: Night came, and still he would not eat.
label: literal
rationale: The footnote is about punctuation, not figurative language, and the sentence is a plain literal statement.
footnote_en: [1] No period in book.

text_cree: tâpwê awa iskwêw wêpinêw atimwa.
text_en: So the woman turned the dogs loose.
label: literal
rationale: The sentence describes a literal action of turning dogs loose, with no figurative language. Bloomfield's footnote does not apply to this sentence.
footnote_en: [2] LB on nayêw :  The last word is almost certainly an error; probably read nayômêw : “he carried her on his back”; the sentence is somewhat tangled.

text_cree: êkwa wîtimwa nayômêw êkwa ocawâsimisa.
text_en: Then he took his sister-in-law and the children on his back.
label: literal
rationale: Bloomfield's footnote [2] corrects 'nayêw' to 'nayômêw' meaning 'carried on his back', a literal action. The note addresses a textual error, not figurative language, so the sentence remains literal.
footnote_en: [2] LB on nayêw :  The last word is almost certainly an error; probably read nayômêw : “he carried her on his back”; the sentence is somewhat tangled.

text_cree: pêyak awa iskwêw nayômêw; êkwa awa nâpêw tahkonêw wîtimwa mîna nayômêw.
text_en: The woman took one on her back; the man took hold of his sister-in-law, and bore her on his back.
label: literal
rationale: Both clauses describe literal actions: taking on one's back and taking hold of someone. No figurative language is present.
footnote_en: [2] LB on nayêw :  The last word is almost certainly an error; probably read nayômêw : “he carried her on his back”; the sentence is somewhat tangled.

text_cree: êkwa kâ-pêtisâpamâcik miskwamîhk ê-pê-pmohtêyit ôhi iskwêwa.
text_en: And then they saw that woman come walking toward them over the ice.
label: literal
rationale: The sentence depicts a literal observation of a woman walking on ice. It contains no figurative expressions.
footnote_en: [2] LB on nayêw :  The last word is almost certainly an error; probably read nayômêw : “he carried her on his back”; the sentence is somewhat tangled.

text_cree: "kipê-nitomitin, nicâhkos!" itêw êsa awa kâ-nitawi-nipahât.
text_en: “I have come to invite you, my gossip,” he who had come to kill her said to her.
label: literal
rationale: The footnote explains that 'nicâhkos' literally means 'my sister-in-law' used between women, with no figurative extension; the term is used literally in a deceptive context.
footnote_en: [3] LB on nicâhkos :  he addresses her as “my sister-in-law”, with a word used by woman to woman.  He throws off the disguise a few lines below, when he addressed his real sister-in-law as nîtim , a word used only between persons of opposite sex.

text_cree: "tâpwê kikitimahin, nîtim, êkâ wîkimiyin," itwêw êsa awa iskwêw; "'tâpwê êtokê ê-kitimâkêyimât ôhi otawâsimisa?' kititêyimitih!" itêw êsa wîtimwa.
text_en: “Truly, you cause me sorrow, Brother-in-Law, by not marrying me,” said that woman; “'I wonder if he really loves the children!' I have been thinking of you!” she said to her brother-in-law.
label: idiom
rationale: The footnote explains that 'otawâsimisah' literally means 'his children' but is conventionally used for 'his brother's children', a fixed non-literal expression.
footnote_en: [4] LB on otawâsimisah :  Literally, “his children”, instead of “his brother's children”; so usually of straight nephews and nieces, rather than the specific terms, nikosim and nicôsim .

text_cree: nêwiwak êsa, mistahi ê-manitôwicik.
text_en: They were four, who had great manitou power.
label: literal
rationale: Literal statement about the number of people and their spiritual power; no figurative language.
footnote_en: [5] LB on ê-wîh-kosâpahtahkik :  This is the Ojibwa tcîsâhkân , Menomini tsî?sâhkyan , cf. Skinner, _Anthropological Papers of the American Museum of Natural History_, XIII, 192.

text_cree: tâpwê mâci-osîhtâwak êsa, ê-wî-kosâpahtahkik, ê-wî-kakwê-nipahâcik.
text_en: And so they set about building that which they would use for the medium's work, meaning to try to kill him.
label: literal
rationale: Footnote provides cognate forms for 'ê-wî-kosâpahtahkik' but does not indicate figurative usage; sentence is literal description of building the medium's tent.
footnote_en: [5] LB on ê-wîh-kosâpahtahkik :  This is the Ojibwa tcîsâhkân , Menomini tsî?sâhkyan , cf. Skinner, _Anthropological Papers of the American Museum of Natural History_, XIII, 192.

text_cree: tâpwê âta ê-pê-nitomiht, opawâkaniyiwa ê-nitomikot, namôya tâpwêhtam.
text_en: Truly, though he was summoned from his home, though their dream spirit summoned him, he gave no heed.
label: literal
rationale: Literal description of summons and disregard; no figurative language.
footnote_en: [5] LB on ê-wîh-kosâpahtahkik :  This is the Ojibwa tcîsâhkân , Menomini tsî?sâhkyan , cf. Skinner, _Anthropological Papers of the American Museum of Natural History_, XIII, 192.

text_cree: nêwo-tipiskâw tahto-tipiskâw ê-kosâpahtahkik ôki maci-ayîsiyiniwak, namôya kî-itohtêyiwa.
text_en: For four nights every night those evil men used the medium's tent, but he did not go there.
label: literal
rationale: Contains 'ê-kosâpahtahkik'; footnote is on the same root but does not describe figurative language; sentence is literal about using the tent.
footnote_en: [5] LB on ê-wîh-kosâpahtahkik :  This is the Ojibwa tcîsâhkân , Menomini tsî?sâhkyan , cf. Skinner, _Anthropological Papers of the American Museum of Natural History_, XIII, 192.

text_cree: "nika-wîcêwâwak," itwêw êsa kaspwân; "anohc ôma kâ-pipohk, êkwa kâ-wî-takohtêt wîhtikôw," itwêw êsa; "âta wiya namôya nikêhcinâhon ta-kî-nipahak." "nawac piko nikostâw," itwêw êsa kaspwâl.
text_en: “I shall go with them,” said Gaspard; “This winter is when the Windigo will come,” he said; “To be sure, I am not certain that I shall be able to kill him. Rather, in fact, I fear him,” said Gaspard.
label: literal
rationale: The footnote comments only on the pronunciation of 'kaspwâl' and does not indicate any figurative language; the passage is a literal statement of intent and belief.
footnote_en: [6] LB on kaspwâl :  Plainly so pronounced: l exists in neighboring dialects, while r is quite impossible.  But I cannot accout for the w in the Cree form.

text_cree: ômisi êsa itêw: "anohc êkwa kâ-wî-tipiskâk wîhtikôw kâ-wî-takosihk." "kîstanaw nitawâpitân," itêw êsa wîwa.
text_en: He said to her, “In this very night that is now at hand, is when the Windigo will arrive. Let us too be on the lookout,” he told his wife.
label: literal
rationale: The sentence reports speech and a straightforward suggestion to be on the lookout; there is no metaphor, simile, or idiom apparent. The footnote checks a word form but indicates no figurative meaning.
footnote_en: [7] CHECK ntawâpahtân.  HCW: probably best

text_cree: "tânisi êtokê ka-kî-isi-nipahânaw?" "ômisi kakwê-isi-nipahâtân," itwêwak êsa ôki oskinîkiwak; "'mahti wâh-wîhtamâtotân kêkway kita-isi-kî-ohci-nipahikawiyahk,' kika-itânaw," itwêwak êsa oskinîkiwak.
text_en: “How do you suppose we shall be able to kill him? Let us try to kill him in this way,” said those young men; “'Let us tell one another by what means each of us can be killed,' we will say to him,” said the young men.
label: literal
rationale: The sentence is a direct report of speech with no figurative language; its meaning is literal. The footnote does not mention any figurative expression.
footnote_en: [8] CHECK kiy-si...

text_cree: "kinâpêm-mihko!" itêw awa owîkimâkana.
text_en: “Your husband's blood!” he said to his wife.
label: literal
rationale: The footnote explains the morphological formation as a nonce-compound, but does not describe any non-literal meaning; without evidence of figurative usage, the phrase is taken literally.
footnote_en: [1] LB on kinâpêm-mihkoh :  “Your husbands blood” would be kinâpêmak omihkowâw ; what we have here is a nonce-formation on the model of the normal type kinêpiko-mihkoh : “snake-blood”, in which the first member is a species of animal.

text_cree: "nâ, mâkw awa nika-kakwâhyakihikoh!" itwêw awa iskwêw, ê-ati-wayawît, ê-itohtêt ôhi mistikwa.
text_en: “Heavens, but he has frightened me!” cried the woman, as she left the tent and went to that tree.
label: literal
rationale: The footnote discusses a phonological/grammatical contraction (mâkw âwa for mâkah awa), not figurative language; the sentence contains a routine exclamation.
footnote_en: [2] LB on mâkw âwa :  For mâk âwa, mâkah awa ; so often, on the model of êwakw âwa, êwakoh awah and similar combinations, where the first word ends in -o .

footnote_en: [4] LB:  Slip of the informant's tongue, or of my hand, for wâkayôs : “the bear,” and so translated.

text_cree: ohtiskawapîstawêw ômisi ê-itinât êskana, ê-wî-nipahatâhtamiyit, mayaw kâ-itâpamikoci, "whw!" ê-nimisîwihât.
text_en: He sat down facing him, holding out the horn at him, like this, while the other was almost dead, puffing for want of breath, and every time the other looked at him, he threatened him, going “Hwoo!”
label: literal
rationale: The footnote does not pertain to this sentence and mentions no figurative language; the actions described are literal.
footnote_en: [4] LB:  Slip of the informant's tongue, or of my hand, for wâkayôs : “the bear,” and so translated.

text_cree: tâwatiw wâkayôs, ispî ê-pê-itisinimiht ôhi êskana, wîpita ê-sâmahamoht.
text_en: The bear had his mouth gaping, and the horn was stuck out at him till it touched his teeth.
label: literal
rationale: The footnote addresses a grammatical possibility (relational verb form) and does not indicate any figurative language; the sentence is a literal description of a bear with its mouth open and a horn touching its teeth.
footnote_en: [5] CHECK Last verb may be a relational instead.  HCW:  Indefinite agent relational.

text_cree: iyikohk ta-pôni-askîwik, êkoyikohk nikî-itik kôhtâwînaw ta-kîskowêyân," itik.
text_en: When the green earth ceases to be, only then did Our Father tell me to cease from my noise,” it told him.
label: idiom
rationale: The phrase 'when the green earth ceases to be' is a conventional adynaton meaning 'never'; Bloomfield's footnote highlights the wordplay on askiy ('earth','summer','year'), confirming its non-literal, idiomatic character.
footnote_en: [1] LB on ta-pôn-âskîwik :  As askiy means not only “earth,” but also “summer” and “year,” double meaning and misunderstanding are probably essential to the story.

text_cree: êkota nahapiw êkwa wîsahkêcâhk, ôma ê-pêhtâkwaniyik.
text_en: Then Wisahketchahk sat down there where its sound was heard.
label: literal
rationale: Literal description of Wisahketchahk sitting where a sound is heard; no figurative language.
footnote_en: [2] LB on blblblbl :  Sound made by pulling tongue back and forth between rounded lips, with voicing.

text_cree: êkwa ômisi itwêw wîsahkêcâhk: "blblblbl!"
text_en: And Wisahketchahk said, “Blblblbl!”
label: literal
rationale: The footnote explains the sound 'blblblbl' as an onomatopoeic representation, which is not figurative.
footnote_en: [2] LB on blblblbl :  Sound made by pulling tongue back and forth between rounded lips, with voicing.

text_cree: êkwa kôna kahkiyaw nama kêkway.
text_en: Then all the snow disappeared.
label: literal
rationale: Plain factual statement about the snow's disappearance, no figurative language.
footnote_en: [3] LB on omayikohk :  Gesture to chest.

text_cree: êkwa mistahi nipiy ôta pê-ayâyiw, ita ê-apit.
text_en: Then much water came and was where he sat.
label: literal
rationale: Literal description of water arriving and its location.
footnote_en: [3] LB on omayikohk :  Gesture to chest.

text_cree: piyisk ômayikohk iskopêw nipiy.
text_en: At last he was up to here in the water.
label: literal
rationale: The footnote describes a gesture accompanying 'ômayikohk', but the phrase itself is a literal spatial indication ('up to here') rather than a metaphor, simile, or idiom.
footnote_en: [3] LB on omayikohk :  Gesture to chest.

text_cree: êkoyikohk pasikôw, pêyak askiy, "blblblbl!" ê-itwêt.
text_en: Only then he arose to his feet, having said, “Blblblbl!” for a whole year.
label: literal
rationale: Narrative of standing and making a sound for a year; no non-literal expression.
footnote_en: [3] LB on omayikohk :  Gesture to chest.

text_cree: tâpwê otinam, ê-nitawi-manisahk otêyaniy.
text_en: So he took it, and went out and cut out the tongue.
label: literal
rationale: The footnote only discusses a possible omitted word and does not describe any figurative language; the sentence appears to be a literal description of actions.
footnote_en: [1] LB on tâpwêh otinam :  Probably the word môhkomân : “knife” has dropped out in record.

text_cree: "yahô, nisîm, êkosi êsi-kîskwêhkwasiskiyân!" "awa êtokê ka-otinamân kiwîskwêpitâkan!" itêw, ê-kêtôwatêt, kâwi ê-tahkopitahk.
text_en: “Dear me, little brother, I am afflicted with sleep-walking like this! And here it seems I have taken your sacred bundle!” he told him, removing his burden and tying it back in its place.
label: literal
rationale: The footnote only discusses a grammatical error (animate 'awah' used with inanimate verb) and does not describe figurative language; reading the sentence directly reveals no metaphors, similes, or idioms.
footnote_en: [2] LB on awah :  The animate form awah : “this” is a slip of record or speech, since the following verb has inanimate form of object.

text_cree: mîna ê-tipiskâyik, âsay mîna ê-nipâyit, otinam, ê-wîwahot, mîna ê-tapasît, ê-sôhki- ê-tapasît.
text_en: The next night, as soon as the other slept, again he took the thing slung the bundle across his shoulder, and again made off, fleeing with all his might.
label: literal
rationale: The sentence describes actions plainly; the footnote queries the form êh-sôhkih but does not indicate any figurative usage.
footnote_en: [3] CHECK êh-sôhkih.  HCW: fragment

text_cree: iyikohk mîna ê-wî-wâpahk, âsay mîna wî-nipâw.
text_en: When dawn again was near, again he meant to sleep.
label: literal
rationale: The sentence simply states that dawn was near and he intended to sleep, with no figurative language.
footnote_en: [3] CHECK êh-sôhkih.  HCW: fragment

text_cree: kîhcêkosîw ispimihk.
text_en: He climbed high up on a tree.
label: literal
rationale: The sentence literally says he climbed high into a tree, with no metaphor or simile.
footnote_en: [3] CHECK êh-sôhkih.  HCW: fragment

text_cree: êkota êkwa nipâw, mîna ê-asitahpisot.
text_en: There he went to sleep, after again tying himself fast.
label: literal
rationale: The sentence plainly states he slept there after tying himself, no figurative meaning.
footnote_en: [3] CHECK êh-sôhkih.  HCW: fragment

text_cree: cîki ê-ihtât wîkihk, kâ-wâpahtahk mistahi ê-astêyiki mihta wîkihk.
text_en: When he was near his dwelling-place, he saw a great pile of firewood by his tent.
label: literal
rationale: Describes a literal scene of approaching a dwelling and seeing firewood.
footnote_en: [1] LB on awiyak ê-kîh-takohtêt :  Short, simple speeches are often conjunct.

text_cree: ay-itêyihtam; "awiyak ê-kî-takohtêt," êkosi itêyihtam.
text_en: He wondered about it; “It must be that someone has come,” he thought. He was glad.
label: literal
rationale: The footnote notes that the reported speech uses a conjunct form, which is a grammatical observation, not figurative language. The sentence is literal.
footnote_en: [1] LB on awiyak ê-kîh-takohtêt :  Short, simple speeches are often conjunct.

text_cree: miywêyihtam. ê-pîhtokêt, nama awiya wâpamêw, êsa kâ-wêpâhtakahikêwihk.
text_en: When he entered, he saw nobody, though it was plain that someone had swept the place.
label: literal
rationale: Describes entering and seeing no one, noting cleaned area, all literal.
footnote_en: [1] LB on awiyak ê-kîh-takohtêt :  Short, simple speeches are often conjunct.

text_cree: mihtâtam êkâ ê-wâpamât awiya.
text_en: He was sorry that he saw no one.
label: literal
rationale: Expresses his feeling of sorrow at seeing no one, literal.
footnote_en: [1] LB on awiyak ê-kîh-takohtêt :  Short, simple speeches are often conjunct.

text_cree: "tânêhki ôma êkâ kâ-ôh-apit awiyak?" itêyihtam.
text_en: “How is it that there is no one here?” he thought.
label: literal
rationale: A direct question expressing his thought, literal.
footnote_en: [1] LB on awiyak ê-kîh-takohtêt :  Short, simple speeches are often conjunct.

text_cree: pôti ita kâ-apit maskisina miskam.
text_en: Lo, there where he sat, he found some moccasins.
label: literal
rationale: Exclamation at finding moccasins, literal.
footnote_en: [1] LB on awiyak ê-kîh-takohtêt :  Short, simple speeches are often conjunct.

text_cree: mistahi miywêyihtam, "iskwêw mâskôc kâ-kî-takohtêt," ê-itêyihtahk; "kîkisêpâ nika-mâcîn;" "nika-kakwê-kêsiskawâw, mîna takohtêci," ê-itêyihtahk.
text_en: He was very glad, thinking, “A woman perhaps is the one who came here. In the morning I shall hunt; I shall try to come upon her while she is here, if she comes again,” he thought.
label: literal
rationale: Relays his gladness and detailed thoughts about a possible female visitor and hunting plans, all literal.
footnote_en: [1] LB on awiyak ê-kîh-takohtêt :  Short, simple speeches are often conjunct.

text_cree: "wîcôhkamawin," itwêw awa iskwêw; "'tânisi ê-tôtahk?' kâ-itêyihtaman, ka-kiskêyihtên tânisi ê-tôtamân," itwêw awa iskwêw.
text_en: “Help me,” said the woman; “Since you have been thinking, ‘How does she do it?’ you shall now know how I do,” she said.
label: literal
rationale: The footnote concerns a possible variant spelling and does not indicate figurative language; the sentence itself is a straightforward request and statement with no metaphors, similes, or idioms.
footnote_en: [2] LB on wîciwôhkamawin :  Error or real variant?  The usual form would be wîcôhkamawin .

text_cree: êkwa kisiwâk wîkiwâhk kâ-pê-nipahihtwâwi ôki maskosisak, sêmâk awa iskwêw kisiwâsiw êsa.
text_en: Then when, close to the lodge those bear-cubs were killed, at once that woman grew angry.
label: literal
rationale: The footnote only asks about the iterative form; the sentence is a literal statement of the woman growing angry.
footnote_en: [1] LB on kâ-pih-nipahihtwâwi :  Why iterative?

text_cree: onâpêma kîhkâmêw; wayawî-kwâskohtiw; nitawi-otinêw ôhi kâ-kî-osihât oskotâkaya, ôhi maskwayâna.
text_en: She upbraided her husband; she sprang out of the lodge; she went and took that mystic dress she had made, that bear-skin robe.
label: literal
rationale: The sentence describes a sequence of literal actions.
footnote_en: [1] LB on kâ-pih-nipahihtwâwi :  Why iterative?

text_cree: êkosi isi ati-isi-kwêskîmôw.
text_en: At once she thus changed her bodily form.
label: literal
rationale: The transformation is a literal magical event in the story.
footnote_en: [1] LB on kâ-pih-nipahihtwâwi :  Why iterative?

text_cree: pîhtikwê-kwâskohtiw kêhciwâk wîkiwâhk; onâpêma ati-nipahêw.
text_en: She came bounding right into the lodge; she killed her husband.
label: literal
rationale: The bounding and killing are literal actions.
footnote_en: [1] LB on kâ-pih-nipahihtwâwi :  Why iterative?

text_cree: êkota ohci mitoni kahkiyaw ayîsiyiniwa mêscihêw.
text_en: Then she killed off all the people.
label: literal
rationale: Literal statement of killing all people.
footnote_en: [1] LB on kâ-pih-nipahihtwâwi :  Why iterative?

text_cree: mitoni êsa ê-mihcêtihk, êwakoni kahkiyaw mitoni nipahêw.
text_en: Although there were many of then, she killed them all. Only her mother she spared.
label: literal
rationale: Literal narration of killing despite many people.
footnote_en: [1] LB on kâ-pih-nipahihtwâwi :  Why iterative?

text_cree: okâwiya piko iskohêw. âta ê-pâ-pâskisoht, namôya êsa kî-sâkôcihâw; namôya kî-nipahâw, piyisk êkosi isi kahkiyaw ayîsiyiniwa kâ-kîsi-mêscihât.
text_en: Although she was shot at again and again, she could not be overcome; it was impossible to kill her, so that at last she thus had exterminated those people.
label: literal
rationale: Literal description of her invulnerability and extermination.
footnote_en: [1] LB on kâ-pih-nipahihtwâwi :  Why iterative?

text_cree: êkwa awa oskinîkiw kîwôtêw, êwako awa omisa kâ-wâkayôsiwiyit.
text_en: Then that young man went visiting, whose elder sister was the woman who had turned into a bear.
label: literal
rationale: Literal statement about the young man and his transformed sister.
footnote_en: [1] LB on kâ-pih-nipahihtwâwi :  Why iterative?

text_cree: êkwa awa iskwêw ôhtâwiya iskohêw. ôhcitaw ê-wî-kakwâtakihât.
text_en: And that woman had spared her father, only so as to torture him.
label: literal
rationale: Literal explanation of sparing to torture.
footnote_en: [1] LB on kâ-pih-nipahihtwâwi :  Why iterative?

text_cree: tâpwê pêyak mistahi kwâtakihêw okâwiya, mîna osîmisa pêyak, êwakoni piko ê-iskohât.
text_en: Truly, she tormented her mother and her little sister, having spared only them.
label: literal
rationale: Literal account of tormenting specific relatives.
footnote_en: [1] LB on kâ-pih-nipahihtwâwi :  Why iterative?

text_cree: êkwa mâna piko itê ê-papâmâcihot, piyê-takohtêci piko nayêstaw ê-kîhkâmât, nanâtohk ê-isi-kwâtakihât, kiyikaw ê-saskahwât, misiwê êsa omikîwak ôki kêhtê-ayak mîna awa iskwêsis. mistahi êsa kitimahêw.
text_en: When she had been going about here and there, when she came back, she would do nothing but scold them, and torment them in various ways, burning them pell-mell, so that those old people and that little girl were all covered with scars.
label: literal
rationale: Literal description of wandering and mistreatment.
footnote_en: [1] LB on kâ-pih-nipahihtwâwi :  Why iterative?

text_cree: kîtahtawê awa oskinîkiw kâ-takohtêt, "tânêhki ôma?" itêyihtam, ita ôma kâ-kî-mihcêtiyit ayîsiyiniwa kahkiyaw ê-mêscihimiht.
text_en: She kept them in a grievous state. Presently, when that young man arrived, “What can be the matter?” he thought, since all the many people there had been killed.
label: literal
rationale: Literal thought and situation of the young man.
footnote_en: [1] LB on kâ-pih-nipahihtwâwi :  Why iterative?

text_cree: pêyak piko mîkiwâhp wâpahtam, ohpimê ê-cimatêyik.
text_en: He saw only one tipi, standing off to one side.
label: literal
rationale: Literal observation of a tipi; 'standing' is a conventional descriptor.
footnote_en: [1] LB on kâ-pih-nipahihtwâwi :  Why iterative?

text_cree: êkwa kîtahtawê osîmisa kâ-wâpamât, ê-nitawi-tâpakwêyit, wâposwa ê-wî-kakwê-nipahâyit.
text_en: Then presently he saw his little sister going out to snare rabbits.
label: literal
rationale: Literal sighting of the sister snaring rabbits.
footnote_en: [1] LB on kâ-pih-nipahihtwâwi :  Why iterative?

text_cree: "hâ, namôya, nitânis!" "'mâskôc mistahi manitôwiw,' ê-itêyimitân, kâ-ôh-nôhtê-kiskêyihtamân tânimatôwihk ta-onipiwiniyan."
text_en: “Oh, no, my daughter! Because I thought of you, ‘Doubtless she is greatly endowed with spirit power,’ is why I wish to know in what part you have your vital spot.”
label: literal
rationale: The footnote discusses morphology of 'onipôwiniyan' without indicating any figurative language, and the sentence is a direct statement about wanting to know the location of the vital spot.
footnote_en: [2] LB on t-ônipôwiniyan :  The regular formation from nipiw : “he dies” would be nipiwin : “death” (cf. onipiwin : “his death” earlier in this text) and onipiwiniw : “he has his death.”  But the form here in the text is probably recorded right: nipôwin : “death” and onipôwiniw : “he has his death” are probably relics of the time when “to die” was an irregular verb, cf. Fox nepwa , Menomini nepoah : “he dies,” Fox nepôweni : “death”.

text_cree: kîtahtawê ê-pipohk mihcêt awâsisak mâ-mêtawêwak mistikwa; sôsimêwak, mitâtaht nîsosâp.
text_en: At one time, in winter, many children were playing with sticks; they were throwing snow-darts, twelve of them.
label: literal
rationale: Footnote explains the literal object 'sôsimêwak' (snow-dart), no figurative language described.
footnote_en: [1] LB on sôsimêwak :  Throwing the snow-dart, sôsimân , animate gender.  A Cree friend later made me a pair:  the dart consists of a cigar-shaped piece of light wood, about 5 inches long and about 1 inch in diameter, ornamented with a burnt pattern, and fixed on a slender reed.  These are thrown so as to speed along the ice or hard snow.  The sport has gone out of use.

text_cree: êkwa sôsimâna êkoni mitihtêwak.
text_en: They followed the snow-darts.
label: literal
rationale: Literal description of following snow-darts, footnote does not address this sentence.
footnote_en: [1] LB on sôsimêwak :  Throwing the snow-dart, sôsimân , animate gender.  A Cree friend later made me a pair:  the dart consists of a cigar-shaped piece of light wood, about 5 inches long and about 1 inch in diameter, ornamented with a burnt pattern, and fixed on a slender reed.  These are thrown so as to speed along the ice or hard snow.  The sport has gone out of use.

text_cree: awiyak itê poyoyici osôsimâna, êkotê ta-ôh-pê-kîwêcik.
text_en: From wherever anyone's snow-dart stopped in its course they would go home.
label: literal
rationale: Literal condition about going home from where dart stopped, no figurative language.
footnote_en: [1] LB on sôsimêwak :  Throwing the snow-dart, sôsimân , animate gender.  A Cree friend later made me a pair:  the dart consists of a cigar-shaped piece of light wood, about 5 inches long and about 1 inch in diameter, ornamented with a burnt pattern, and fixed on a slender reed.  These are thrown so as to speed along the ice or hard snow.  The sport has gone out of use.

text_cree: piyis nîso piko ayisiyiniwak.
text_en: At last only two were left.
label: literal
rationale: The footnote comments on the word 'ayêsinwak' as a probable error, not figurative language, and the sentence is a plain statement of fact.
footnote_en: [2] LB on ayêsinwak :  Probably an error.

text_cree: piyisk nêwâw na-nipâwak; ê-otâkosihk êkwêyâk otihtêwak osôsimâna, êwako ê-apisîsisit osîmimâw, êwako nâpêsis osôsimâna.
text_en: Four nights they slept on the way; not till the next morning did they reach the snow-dart of the smallest one, the youngest brother, that boy's snow-dart.
label: literal
rationale: The footnote does not relate to this sentence; the description of nights slept and reaching the snow-dart is literal narrative.
footnote_en: [2] LB on ayêsinwak :  Probably an error.

text_cree: êkosi êwako iskwêyâc otihtêwak nêwâw mwêhci ê-nipâcik.
text_en: This one they reached last, after four nights.
label: literal
rationale: A straightforward statement about the order of arrival, with no figurative elements.
footnote_en: [2] LB on ayêsinwak :  Probably an error.

text_cree: êkosi osîhtâwak mistikwa ohci wîkiwâw.
text_en: Thereupon they built a tent for themselves out of sticks.
label: literal
rationale: Directly describes building a tent from sticks, with no non-literal meaning.
footnote_en: [2] LB on ayêsinwak :  Probably an error.

text_cree: kîtahtawê ê-nîsicik awâsisak mâka mîna sôsimêwak. ma-mitihtêwak.
text_en: Then again, at another time the two children threw snow-darts and followed them.
label: literal
rationale: The sentence describes literal actions of throwing and following snow-darts; footnote [3] only notes merged sentences, no figurative language.
footnote_en: [3] Merged three sentences

text_cree: êkoni. nikotwâsik ê-nipâcik otihtêwak osôsimâniwâwa.
text_en: After six nights on the way they reached their snow-darts.
label: literal
rationale: The sentence literally states they reached their snow-darts after six nights; footnote is not about figurative language.
footnote_en: [3] Merged three sentences

text_cree: kotaka mîkiwâhpa êkotê kiyôtêwak.
text_en: There they visited some other lodges.
label: literal
rationale: The sentence literally says they visited other lodges; no figurative meaning.
footnote_en: [3] Merged three sentences

text_cree: tâpwê pêhtâkwan ê-takohtêcik.
text_en: The report went round that they had come.
label: literal
rationale: The Cree 'pêhtâkwan' means 'it is heard', a literal expression for news spreading; not idiomatic, no metaphor.
footnote_en: [3] Merged three sentences

text_cree: kîtahtawê wîkiwak ayîsiyiniwak, nîso okimâwak, pêyak macihkiwis ôhtâwiya.
text_en: Once upon a time some people dwelt in a place, and there were two chiefs, and one of them was Silly-Fellow's father.
label: literal
rationale: Plain narrative statement; the footnote comments on the character but does not indicate figurative language.
footnote_en: [2] LB on macihkiwis :  In this tale the position of this person is much like that of Wisahketchahk. On Star-Blanket Reserve one of my informants identified the two.

text_cree: kîtahtawê awâsisak mihcêt sôsimêwak.
text_en: Then at one time many of the children played at throwing snow-darts.
label: literal
rationale: Straightforward description of children playing; no figurative language indicated by the footnote.
footnote_en: [2] LB on macihkiwis :  In this tale the position of this person is much like that of Wisahketchahk. On Star-Blanket Reserve one of my informants identified the two.

text_cree: kîtahtawê ê-otâkosiniyik, awîna ôma, kî-mihtiskâyiw.
text_en: Presently, as evening came on, they were deep in the woods.
label: literal
rationale: The footnote [3] comments on the unknown word kî-mihtiskâyiw, stating the translation is a guess, with no mention of figurative language.
footnote_en: [3] LB on kî-mihtiskâyiw :  Unknown word; translation a guess.

text_cree: kêkâc pahkisimoyiw; kwayask ômisi isi cimasoyiwa osôsimâna.
text_en: It was near sunset; there, standing straight upright in the snow, like this, was the boy's snow-dart.
label: literal
rationale: The sentence describes a physical scene literally; the footnote does not refer to this sentence.
footnote_en: [3] LB on kî-mihtiskâyiw :  Unknown word; translation a guess.

text_cree: êkoyikohk yôtiniyiw; misponiyiw.
text_en: Just then the wind began to blow; it snowed.
label: literal
rationale: The sentence states weather conditions plainly; the footnote does not refer to this sentence.
footnote_en: [3] LB on kî-mihtiskâyiw :  Unknown word; translation a guess.

text_cree: kitâpamêw awa macihkiwis.
text_en: Silly-Fellow watched them.
label: literal
rationale: The sentence 'Silly-Fellow watched them' is a straightforward narrative statement with no figurative language.
footnote_en: [4] LB on k-ôyâtamiyit :  Unknown word; translation a guess.

text_cree: tâpwê pîhtokêpayiyiwa sôsimâna, konita kâ-oyâtamiyit awâsisa, ê-miywêyihtamiyit, ê-wiyanihtâkêyit.
text_en: Really, the snow-darts came flying into the house, and boys cheered loudly with joy, and set about cleaning the game.
label: literal
rationale: Footnote [4] notes the word 'oyâtamiyit' is unknown and the translation a guess, but this does not indicate figurative language; the rest of the sentence describes events literally.
footnote_en: [4] LB on k-ôyâtamiyit :  Unknown word; translation a guess.

text_cree: "â, nisîmitik, ka-wîcêtinâwâw." "osâm ninôhtêhkatân itê kâ-ohtohtêyân, êkâ awiyak ê-kî-minahot, ê-nôhtêhkatêhk, piko ê-mêtawêhk, êkosi ê-isi-mîcisohk," itwêw.
text_en: “Oh, little brothers, let me stay with you. I go hungry too much in the place whence I come, because no one there can kill any game, and all go hungry and eat only as one eats after a contest,” he said.
label: literal
rationale: The footnote explains the cultural practice behind the phrase 'eat only as one eats after a contest,' indicating it is a literal description of a real event, not figurative language.

text_en: So, when he entered their tipi, “My brother, Little Snow-Dart, has a store of meat. I have taken him up, adopted him, father,” he told his father; “This grandmother of ours who lives right here, it is her grandson has the store of meat. But I am going to tell my grandmother about it,” he said; “‘Tomorrow let our father move his camp here, and my grandmother, too. All the people are to move camp to this place,” says my brother, Little Snow-Dart,” he told his father.
label: literal
rationale: The footnote discusses the morphology of 'kita-pê-piciw' (preverb particle/initial stem) and makes no mention of figurative language; the sentence is a literal instruction to move camp.
footnote_en: [8] LB on kita-pê-piciw :  A preverb particle, such as pêh : “hither” is freely added to any verb, e.g., pêhitohtêw : “he walks hither.”  An initial stem, such as pê- : “hither” is never added to a word, but appears only before non-initial elements, as in pêpahtâw : “he runs hither,” where -pahtâ- : “run” is an element that never occurs in word-initial.  Thus: particle: initial stem: papêh papâm- : “around, about” isih it- : “thither, thus” ohcih, ôh oht- : “thence, therefore” and many others. There is overlapping of two kinds.  In central Algonquian certain initials and non-initial stems are alike (except for the difference implied by these names), e.g. Cree pici- and -pici- : “move camp,” whence pêh-piciw and pêpiciw : “he moves camp hither,” probably with some difference of meaning. The other kind of overlapping is peculiar to Cree, and probably due to phonetic alterations which shifted the boundary between t (which occurs at the end of many initial stems) and c (which occurs as the penult of many particles).  Thus pêcâstam- : “facing hither,” as, e.g. in pêcâsamohtêw : “he walks facing hither” looks as though it contained a preverb particle * pêcih : “hither,” which otherwise is unknown in Plains Cree, or else an initial stem pêc- , a form unparalleled in Cree and in the related languages.  The initial stem here was really * pêt- ; Cree pêcâstam- is a phonetic or analogic modification of * pêcâstam- , cf. Menomini pîtâ'namôhnew : “he walks facing hither.”  Similarly Cree mistatim : “horse” for * mistastim (or * misc-astim , or * mis-astim ).  Cf. Introduction.

You, my brother, when mortal men grow forth and flourish, ‘Lynx,’ they will call you; you will find your sustenance in the woods; and so you, my brother, have found your place. And you, my father, ‘Mink,’ mortal man will call you; by the water you will have your domain; but all kinds of things you will eat, the flesh of little snakes; from whatever creature has flesh you will get your life. So now in different directions, into the form of different animals you will all go. When mortal men come into being, they will overcome you all. As for me, ‘Great White Loon,’ I shall be called. text_en: “Hey, grandson, wait a moment! You have defeated me,” she said to him; “Now, grandson, in future time mortal man will live in successive generations. They will gather crumbly wood. There I shall keep warm the child that is to grow up, so that I too shall have part in bringing him up. But in the place of the setting sun I shall have my home. ‘I have dreamt of the old woman,’ when a mortal being speaks thus, he will speak truly. So now, my grandson, touch me with it.”

That is what your son-in-law said.”

text_en: The elder sister, who had scorned him, saw him; now that he was handsome, she liked him, as she saw her younger sister climbing up to give him the berries, saying to him, “Here, take these.” The youth took them.

rationale: No figurative language detected; 'ashamed' and 'carrying on his back' are used literally.

text_cree: piyisk ômisi ôta wî-kipihkitonênik.
text_en: But in time, here, like this, she had him almost strangled.
label: literal
rationale: Describes being almost strangled; no simile, metaphor, or idiom present.

text_cree: ômisi itwêw: "hâ, nôtokêsiw, cêskwa ôtê nîkân ayîsiyiniwak tita-ayâwak;" "ômisi tita-itwêwak,"- pakamisimêw; osit piko ôma nôkwaniyiw awa nôtokêsiw,- "'kôhkôhk-ôyaman' tita-itwêwak!"

rationale: Bloomfield's footnote [22] comments on the unknown substance 'kôhkôhk-ôyaman' but does not describe it as figurative; the sentence simply narrates a prediction without metaphor, simile, or idiom.

This, in fact, was our father's thought, when he came and left my sisters here, for ‘Perhaps some man or men will not disdain them and marry them, and then kill something in the way of game,’ was what our father thought,” said those youths; “He will be very glad, when he sees the way things are,” the one told him.

text_en: When she stopped weeping, she said to them, “My children, he is your mother's brother; he is my younger brother; he was very handsome, and beaded was his head, but his fellow Wampum-Head challenged him to a contest and carried off his head. Is he still breathing!”

rationale: Bloomfield's footnote describes this speech as an instance of 'bravado', a rhetorical stance rather than a figurative expression; no metaphor, simile, or idiom is identified, so the language is treated as literal.

One man who ran by here said, ‘Wisahketchahk is too hot on my trail; he wants to kill me.’ So do you at least hear us with pity. If you like, the two of us will marry you!” they told him.

There stayed that youth. Then, in time, he would go away and sit on a hilltop and look at all the tipis. After a while his wife would come to him there on the hilltop. text_en: “Come, brothers, wash your faces; when you have washed your faces, tidy yourselves; put on your good clothes; I am bringing women, the sisters of your sister-in-law who went away. As many as you are, so many are the women. In the order of our ages they will take their seat by your sides, when they enter,” he said.
label: literal

text_cree: "ômisi," itwêw awa nôtokwêw; "cîkahikan kika-otinên;" "nistikwânihk ka-pakamahên," itwêw awa nôtokwêw; "ôtê êkâ ê-pîsimôwik nêwo osêtinawa, ôma ôta nistam osêhcâw kika-âmaciwân." "êkota ohci mîna kotak ispatinâw ka-têpâpahtên." "nêwo ispatinâwa miyâskamani, êkotê kakwê-takwâmôhkan pîwâpisko-wâskahikan." "êwakoni êkotê ê-sâkôcihikot." "kîspin êkotê takwâmoyani, êkosi kika-pimâtisin," itik êsa; "takwâmoyani êkotê, ômisi itwêhkan: 'nistêsê, niwî-nipahik âyîtawihkwâkan wîhtikôw!' kika-itwân." "itâp ana kika-yôhtênamâkwak."
text_en: Thus spoke the old woman: “You will take an ax; you will strike a blow on my head,” said the old woman; “Yonder, in the direction where there is no sun, are four hills, the first and nearest of which you will climb. From there you will see the second hill. When you have crossed four hills, there try to reach in your flight an iron house. The one who dwells there will overcome him. If you manage to get there in your flight, then you will live,” she told her; “When you reach the place in your flight, speak thus: “Big brother, the both-side-faced Windigo wants to kill me!' you will say. Then they will open the door for you.”
label: literal
rationale: The footnote offers an alternative translation for 'ômisi' but does not describe any figurative language; the sentence contains straightforward narrative and instructions with no non-literal predication, simile marker, or conventional idiom.

text_cree: kîtahtawê nanâtohk piyisk, "namôya tâpwê niya ayîsiyiniw," itwêw êsa awa oskinîkiskwêw; "ninitawêyimik êkwa nôhtâwiy." "nitawâc êkwa niwî-wâwâskêsiwin." "êkoyikohk kahkiyaw kimiyo-tôtâtinâwâw, oskinîkiskwêwak ê-miyitakok."
text_en: Then at one time, “I am not really a human being,” said the young woman; “And now my father wants me. So I shall turn into a deer. I have completed my benefaction to all of you, in giving you young women.”
label: literal
rationale: The text contains statements about identity and transformation that appear literal in context; the footnote only comments on a misreading and does not indicate figurative language.
footnote_en: [4] LB on nanâtohk pîsk :  These two words have no place here.  Perhaps the informant was going to say nanâtohk pisiskiwah : “various animals.”

text_cree: â, âsay mîna mayaw ê-wâpaniyik, sipwêhtêwak, ê-kî-mîcisocik.

label: literal

text_cree: tâpwê êkosi isi isi-wêpinêw ôhi otawâsimisa, namôya kayâs ê-kî-nôkohât.
text_en: And so in this wise she abandoned her child which not long before she had borne.
label: literal
rationale: Footnote [2] discusses the morphological breakdown and homonymy of isi-wêpinêw, with no suggestion of figurative meaning; the sentence literally describes abandonment.
footnote_en:
[2] LB on isi-wêpinêw :  Hyphen is used, because the meaning is here isi : “thither, thus” plus wêpinêw : “she abandons him.”  By contrast, the very common unit word isiwêpinêw : “he throws him that way or there” has -wêp- : “throw” as a non-initial stem.  This illustrates the difficulty of drawing a clear line between simple words and compounds;  for a native speaker it would be easy. The repetition of isi is worth noting; it is perhaps due to the existence of the much commoner homonym;  as homonymy is rare in Cree, the combination isi-wêpinêw is inadequate and disturbs the speaker.
[3] CHECK wewepitot, CHECK reduplication length

footnote_en: [4] LB on maskosîwakân :  Normal form doubtless maskosîwikân , and below, the diminutive, normal: maskosîwikânis .

label: literal
rationale: The sentence describes having human form and being aided by Higher Powers, which, though possibly a conventional religious reference, is not a metaphor, simile, or idiom. The footnote's instruction to 'CHECK kekwayi' does not point to figurative usage.
footnote_en: [5] CHECK kekwayi

text_cree: tâpwê awa nâpêw ê-wî-mâcît, "âstam, wêskinîkiyin!" "iskêkâni nahâhkapiyani," itâw awa awâsis.
text_en: So, when that man was ready to go hunting, “Come here, young fellow! It would seem you are staying with people,” the child was told.
label: metaphor
rationale: Bloomfield's footnote describes 'nahâhkapiyani' as ironic, drawing a comparison between the addressee and a son-in-law expected to be a good worker while staying with his wife's people, which constitutes an implicit metaphorical use.
footnote_en: [6] LB on nahâhkapiyani : The verb nahâhkapiw : “he is staying, as son-in-law, with his wife's people”; it applied here only in so far as during this stay a son-in-law is supposed to show himself a good worker. Irony.

text_cree: "kakwêyâho!" itik; "pasikô!" itik: "mâ ani âta ê-manitowakêyimoyan, ita wiya ati-atimitâni, kika-nipahitin;" "kika-ati-patakwâtimâtitin."
text_en: “Look lively!” he told him; “Get up!” he told him; “Believe it or not, though you think yourself of manitou kind, if I overtake you on the way, I will kill you; I will stamp you under my snowshoes.”
label: literal
rationale: The footnote discusses the verb 'patakwâkimatitin' meaning 'stamp under snowshoes' as a literal action, with no figurative interpretation indicated.
footnote_en: [7] LB on kik-âti-patakwâkimatitin :  The medial stem is -âkimê- : “snowshoe” (verbal), cf. Ojibwa âgim , Menomini âkim (animate): “snowshoe.”  The word used in Cree is asâm (animate): “snowshoe.” I did not catch the word when dictated, but succeeded in making informant repeat it.  As a result it is not used in the recurrence of the incident, below.

text_cree: kayâs ayîsiyiniwak ômisi kî-pakitinikôwisiwak: kahkiyaw kêkway kî-kitimâkêyimikwak, tahto kêkway kâ-wâpahtamihk, mîna êkâ kâ-wâpahtamoht.

text_cree: "nôhtâ, ôma piko kita-isi-nayômiyan," itwêw êsa awa oskinîkiw.
text_en: “Father, there is only this, that you must carry me on your back,” said the youth. So the old man took his son on his back and carried him.
label: literal
rationale: The footnote only discusses a grammatical correction and morphological breakdown, with no indication of figurative language; the sentence is a straightforward request with no implicit comparison or non-literal expression.
footnote_en: [2] LB on pîci-nayômiyin :  The prefixed particle is doubtless wrong; perhaps read kitsi- , which seems to be an allegro variant of (a) kitah-isi-, kit-êsi , i.e., kitah-, tah- : “that, in order that,” plus isih- : “thither, thus,” and (b) kitisi- , i.e., isih- with personal prefix ki-, kit- of second person.

text_cree: tâpwê awa kisêyiniw nêyawiskosoci ayiwêpiw ê-nayôhcikêt.
text_en: So whenever the old man wearied under his burden, he rested, with his load on his back.
label: literal
rationale: The footnote discusses verb morphology for ê-nayôhcikêt, not figurative language; sentence literally describes resting with a load.
footnote_en: [4] LB on ê-nayôhcikêt : The normal form seems to be nayômâw : “he carries him on back,” nayahtam : “he carries it on back,” and, derived from the latter, nayahcikêw : “he carries on back”; but we find also nayôhtam, nayôhcikêw . Menomini has nayômêw, nayôhtam , but for the former also nayâhêw .

text_cree: mitoni mistahi kosikwatiyiwa, pâskac êsa ostikwânihk ê-tahkopisot, iyikohk ê-miywêyihtahk okosisa ê-wâpamât.
text_en: The latter was very heavy, the more so, as the old man had tied the strap round his head, so glad was he to see his son.
label: literal
rationale: The footnote is purely morphological; sentence describes physical weight and emotional state straightforwardly.
footnote_en: [4] LB on ê-nayôhcikêt : The normal form seems to be nayômâw : “he carries him on back,” nayahtam : “he carries it on back,” and, derived from the latter, nayahcikêw : “he carries on back”; but we find also nayôhtam, nayôhcikêw . Menomini has nayômêw, nayôhtam , but for the former also nayâhêw .

text_cree: ohpimê wâhyaw mânokêw êsa.
text_en: Then far off to one side he set up a tipi.
label: literal
rationale: The footnote does not address figurative meaning; sentence is a literal action of setting up a tipi.
footnote_en: [4] LB on ê-nayôhcikêt : The normal form seems to be nayômâw : “he carries him on back,” nayahtam : “he carries it on back,” and, derived from the latter, nayahcikêw : “he carries on back”; but we find also nayôhtam, nayôhcikêw . Menomini has nayômêw, nayôhtam , but for the former also nayâhêw .

text_cree: mâka wiya awa iskwêw namôya êsa ohci wâpamêw okosisa, êkosi ê-isi-nipiyit.
text_en: But as for the woman, she never again saw her son, who in this wise now had died.
label: literal
rationale: The footnote clarifies the reference of 'the woman' and the narrative context, but does not indicate any figurative language; the sentence is a plain statement.
footnote_en: [5] LB on mâka wiya awa iskwêw :  i.e., it was his mother who had violated the command; either the tale is laconically told or I missed a sentence above.

text_cree: ê-pîhtokêyit owîkimâkana, ômisi itêw: "niwîkimâkan, namôya êkosi ê-kî-itêyihtamân, kisîm kâ-ôh-kitimâkêyimak." "anohc ê-pîhtokêt, nikakwêcimik ta-nôcîhkawit," itêw; "mitoni nimâmaskâtên ê-isi-kitosit, kâ-ôh-wîhtamâtân." "êkosi namôya êkwa nika-kî-kitimâkêyimâw kisîm," itêw.
text_en: When her husband came into the tent, she told him thus: “My husband, it was not in this way that I meant it, when from the first I showed affection to your younger brother. [no translation] she told him, “I was greatly surprised when he spoke in this way to me; that is why I am telling you of it. And so now I shall no longer be able to feel any fondness for your younger brother,” she told him.
label: literal
rationale: The footnote is a grammatical note ('kîh with negative?') and does not describe figurative language; the sentence is a straightforward narrative and direct speech with no metaphors, similes, or idioms.
footnote_en: [1] kîh with negative?

"êkota ki-ka-itohtân; êkota ka-nahapin." "kî-nahapiyini, êkota cîki sâkahikanihk ka-wâpamâw ta-pê-sâkêwêt ayîsiyiniw ê-misikitit." "tâpiskôc iskwêw tita-isîhow." "namôya ka-wâpahtên osita." "êkâya tâpwêhtawâhkan." "ômisi itâhkan: 'namôya êwako kâ-nitawêyimak,' kika-itâw." "êkosi, 'yâh, tâpwê êkwa, nôsisê!' kika-itik." "itê kâ-ohtohtêt kika-isi-kîwêhtahik." "êkoyikohk kê-pê-pêkopêt kotak misatim;" "êwako ana ka-misi-wanâcihisk," itik; "êkâ tâpwêhtawâhkan," itik; "nêwo-tipiskâw êkota kika-ayân." "ispî sâkôcimaci, wî-pîhtokêci, ati-pîhtokêci, ôma ohci miscikos kika-ohpâskwahamwân oskotâkay." "ka-wâpahtên osita." "tâpiskôc misatim osita ka-isi-wâpahtamwân." "'wêy! tânisi awa nimosôm ê-isinâkwaniyiki osita!' kika-itâw." "'tânisi êsinâkwahki, nôsisê?'" "'ê-cî-wâpahtaman?' kika-itik." "'êha! tâpiskôc misatimoskasiya êsinâkwahki kisita,' kika-itâw." "nôsisê, mêyâkwâm kakwê-wâpahtam osita." "kîspin wâpahtamwaci, êkosi ani ka-sâkôcihâw." "mâka êkâ wâpahtamani, kika-sâkôcihik," itik; "mâka wâpahtamani osita, êkosi ani ka-sâkôcihâw." "mîna ôhi wêstakaya kêkâc ta-sâmaskêhtiniyiwa." "pê-kapâci, 'nahi, nôsisê, otin!' kika-itik." "êkâya tâpwêhtawâhkan." "'otinamawin!' kika-itâw." "kî-otinâci, 'wiyahpitamawin,' kika-itâw." "mâka maywês têhtahiski otinaci, kika-misi-wanâcihik êwako ana misatim; kika-môwik," itik; "mâka têhtahiski, êkosi ani ta-pê-kîwêyan." "misahkamik oskinîkiwak êkâ kâ-ôh-pê-kîwêcik, ê-ati-misi-wanâcihikocik," itik; "mistahi kaskêyihtam kôhtâwiy kikâwiy kistês kîtimwak aniki kâ-kitimâkêyimiskik," itik.
text_en: His grandmother told him as follows: “My grandson, even though I have taught young men in this same way, they did not follow my instructions, and therefore, went, one after another, to their ruin. If you heed my words, you will fare well; but if he dissuades you to whom you will come, he will destroy you,” she told him; “At any rate, carry this on your person,” she told him, giving him the skin of a beaver-owl; “This thing, my grandson, you will keep for four nights. If he does not destroy you, when you are sleepy, ‘Grandfather, let me lie down a while!’ you will say to him. If he says ‘Yes,’ you will place this thing on your chest. ‘Now then, if my grandfather speaks to you, answer him! I shall sleep. When daylight is near, then wake me!’ you will say to this thing. And this,” she told him, “You will spread under you as you lie,” his grandmother told him, as she gave him her breech-clout; “Only by doing thus will you be able to overcome that old man. And when you are near there, as you go along you will pick up a stick, a stick that is not large. When you have slept twice on the way, you will see water. Not at all will you be able to see where that body of water has its end,” she told him; “And so, after the day is past noon, then you will have come near that lake. It will be level land. You will see a very small rise in the land. To it you will go; there you will seat yourself. When you have seated yourself, there close to the lake you will see a tall man come into view. He will be dressed like a woman. You will not see his feet. When he comes to where you are, ‘Ha, grandson, go back home! The one you have come to fetch you may take home with you,’ he will say to you. At that a handsome white horse will come forth into view. ‘There, this one I give to you. Go home!’ he will say to you. Do you not heed his words. Say this to him: ‘It is not this one I desire,’ you will say to him. Then, ‘Oh, yes, that is true, grandson!’ he will say to you. He will take you back with him to the place from which he came. ‘Go bring the saddle, that you may ride home,’ he will say to you, when you reach his dwelling; ‘Go, grandon, and take it! Go right in! It is a beaded saddle,’ he will tell you. If you take it, persuaded by his speech, that horse will indeed come there. ‘Take him; saddle him’ he will say to you. When you have saddled him, ‘Mount!’ he will tell you; ‘Go home!’ he will tell you. If he persuades you, and you mount, try as you may to depart, that horse will take you off straight to the lake. You will not be able to manage him. In the end he will go under the water. You must wait for a different horse to come up from the water; that one will destroy you,” she told him; “Do not heed his words,” she told him; “Four nights you will stay there. If you heed this which I tell you, you will overcome him, if you stay there four nights. But when you are sitting on that little mound, and he comes walking to where you are, if them you do not heed this which I have told you, he will talk you into acting against your will. ‘Go ahead, walk right in!’ he will tell you. ‘Do you enter first!’ you will say to him. If you persuade him, as he is about to go in, just as he enters the dwelling, with that little stick you will lift up his skirt. You will see his feet. You will see that his feet are like a horse's. ‘Heavens! What do my grandfather's feet look like!’ you will say to him. ‘What do they look like, grandson? Do you mean to say that you see them?’ he will ask you. ‘Yes! Your feet look like horses' hoofs,’ you will answer him. My grandchild, be sure, by all means, to try to see his feet. If you see them, then indeed you will overcome him. But if you do not see them, if you do not do as I now am teaching you, he will overcome you,” she told him; “But if you see his feet, then indeed you will overcome him. Then if you succeed in staying there four nights, then every day he will give you one horse. ‘Go home!’ he will tell you. You will not obey him. It is really only if you defeat him that he will give you those horses. When the fourth night of your stay has passed, ‘Now, grandfather, it is your own horse, the stallion, that I have come to fetch,’ you will say to him. ‘Very well,’ he will answer you. By the door there will be lying an ugly saddle; and the rawhide bridle, strung together of small ends, will be ugly. For these you will ask him. ‘It is those other saddles that are good, and those bridles,’ he will say to you. Do not heed his words. He will defeat you with this one thing, even though you go unharmed through the four nights,” she told him; “If you persuade him this time too, ‘Very well then, grandson; now for my own horse which you have come to fetch!’ he will say to you. Then he will go out of the lodge. He will take that very same ugly saddle and bridle. Then you will follow him. He will stand beside the lake. ‘My horse, come to land!’ he will call. At once the water will rise up high; it will look as if it were boiling. At last a stallion with a bay coat will come out of the water. It will come to the land. It will drag its tail on the ground. And its mane, here, too, will almost reach the ground. When it comes to land, ‘There, grandson, take him!’ he will say to you. Do not obey him. ‘Take him for me!’ you will say to him. When he has taken it, ‘Saddle him for me!’ you will say to him. When he has saddled it, then, ‘Here you are, grandson!’ he will say to you. Do not heed his speech. ‘Put me on his back!’ do you then say to him. If you do this, you will live; you will defeat him. But if you take the horse before he has set you on its back, that horse will destroy you; it will eat you,” she told him; “But if he puts you on its back, then indeed you will come home. Having stayed there four nights, you will win forty horses from that old man. But though again and again I have taken pity on young men and instructed them even in this wise, yet they have not obeyed me. That is why any number of young men have not returned from there, but have been destroyed by him,” she told him; “Very sad is your father, and your mother, and your elder brother, and those your sisters-in-law who are fond of you,” she told him.

text_en: “Dear me, no, brother! I know how much you loved me. It is true that when I came and entered your tipi your wife was sitting alone. When I wanted to go out again, ‘First eat,’ she told me. ‘No, you are alone in the tent,’ I said to her. ‘Oh, it does not matter that I am alone, seeing how fond we are of you.’ So I sat down and she gave me food. When I had eaten, and was rising to my feet, ‘First let me comb your hair,’ she said to me. ‘No, you are alone in the tent,’ I said to her. When I tried to go out, she blocked me in the doorway. [no translation] she said to me; ‘If you do as I ask, much as I have loved you, I shall take even better care of you.’ ‘Why, how could I do such a thing? My brother is so good to me,’ I said to her. ‘He does not need to know of it,’ she answered me. Then, when she stepped aside, I came out. I was embarrassed, for I looked upon all my sisters-in-law even as upon my mother, when they were so good to me,” he told him; “It was for this reason that for a long time I did not come into your tent, because she who sits here had put me to shame. footnote_en: [1] LB on cacêkahkwânah :  The word cikahkwân : “lance,” (plural -ah , or reduplicated cacêkahkwânah ) is used also of small darts with which boys played a game:  one threw his dart so that it stuck upright in the ground, and the opponent tried to throw his so as to split the other. The same word in animate gender (plural -ak ) is used of the girls' and women's gambling toy which consists (seen on Star Blanket Reserve) of four slabs of wood shaped like a knife-blade with surfaces slightly convex, and measuring perhaps 8 by 3 inches.  On one side of two slabs are bear-tracks; on one side of the other two, weasel-tracks.  The four slabs are grasped in one hand and tossed; the throw counts according to the combination of bear-tracks, weasel-tracks, and blanks that turn up.

text_en: “There now, now let your father and mother go fetch the meats, and let them take some for you to eat. On all the drying-frames that are on the camp-site let them hang the meats, and for this drying-frame of yours let them take the fattest one, to provide meat for them to eat!” said the boy who was a prattler; “If they do this way and do not peep, things will always go as well as this. But if they peep, things will not go well. Even if Partridge-Claw here drives buffalo, things will go just as well, if only your father and your mother do not try to look. By the time Partridge-Claw has had two turns at driving in buffalo, there will be enough, I guess, for a stay over the summer. You will have a big supply of meat. This Partridge-Claw is not really a child. And I, too; because we felt sorry for you when you were starving, is why we came to your dwelling,” he told her; “Tell your father and mother: tomorrow again Partridge-Claw is to drive buffalo. Some four days after that he is to drive them again. In the end you will have a big supply of food,” he told his wife.

footnote_en: [5] LB on wîh-wawîwinawisiw :  Obscure; perhaps a nonce-formation.  If really derived from wîwah : “his wife” ( nîwah : “my wife,” etc.), perhaps read wîh-owîwinawisiw ;  for the general rule in Central Algonquian is that secondary derivatives of dependent nouns are made from the form with third-person possessor; those in nî-, kî-, wî- prefix o- , e.g., wîstâwah : “his brother-in-law”: uwîstâwiw : “he has (as) a brother-in-law”; and those in nô- , kô- , ô- prefix ow- , e.g. ôhtâwiya : “his father”: owôhtâwiyiw : “he has (as) a father.”  But the Sweet Grass dialect seems to confuse this initial accretion with reduplication, e.g. oyôhtâwiyiw : “he has (as) a father,” cf. below.
